nytimes.com.title: A Plague Mystery in Siberia
nytimes.com.text:
As if there weren’t enough to worry about in the world: Do we also have an outbreak of the plague? The Black Death? Now?
The short answer is: We don’t know. The slightly longer answer is: A woman who worked in a remote Siberian lab that studies plague has died of pneumonia — or so we’re told. The lab has been locked down, and the Russian authorities aren’t saying much, which has fueled speculation and rumors.
But we’ve got you. My colleagues have gathered all the available information to try to make as much sense of it as possible. (Spoiler alert: Don’t panic.)
A mysterious death and an old foe of humanity
So who died, exactly?
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of Irkutsk’s Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, seems to have died of a mysterious pneumonia illness earlier this month. Her death prompted Russian health authorities to quarantine employees and patients at the hospital where she died, along with the institute’s staff and other people who were in contact with her.
Wait — the plague still exists?
Yes. The plague has been with us for a very long time. Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes plague, has infected humans for thousands of years, also circulating among rodents and fleas that serve as long-term reservoirs.

nytimes.com.title: Italy Weighs Controversial Law Giving Bonus Seats to Election Winners
nytimes.com.text:
Italian lawmakers on Thursday prepared to vote on a controversial new law that would award bonus seats in Parliament to election winners, a move supporters say will help prevent governments from collapsing and detractors denounce as unconstitutional and antidemocratic.
Championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has threatened to resign should it not pass, the new law would give a bonus to the winning party or coalition of an election: 70 seats in the lower house of Parliament and 35 in the Senate, provided the party or coalition reaches 42 percent in both houses. Italy has a 600-seat Parliament, with 400 seats in the lower house and 200 seats in the Senate.
Proponents of the law have nicknamed it “Stabilicum,” saying it will ensure a coalition’s ability to govern in a country with a long history of short-lived governments. Critics call it “Melonellum,” saying the law was tailor-made by the current government to bolster its chances at re-election next year. If the measure becomes law, opponents have vowed to petition Italy’s Constitutional Court for a review.
Italian governments have a history of instability; there have been 68 of them since Italy became a republic in 1946, with the shortest lasting a mere 22 days in 1954. Last month, Ms. Meloni, who was elected in September 2022, set a record for leading Italy’s longest-serving government. She is in the last year of a five-year mandate.
“This electoral law provides very strong stability,” which “builds credibility, allowing our businesses to operate with much greater peace of mind, and giving our foreign partners reassurances,” said Andrea Di Giuseppe, a member of Ms. Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party. The law was “very important,” he said in an interview.
The measure has been the topic of heated debate for months, prompting protests and petitions from some civil rights groups and constitutional experts as well as intense discussion in Parliament, even within Ms. Meloni’s center-right coalition.

nytimes.com.title: For Twin Brothers Abducted in the Oct. 7 Attacks, Adjusting to Freedom Is a New Challenge
nytimes.com.text:
The twin brothers Gali and Ziv Berman were abducted by gunmen in the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.
They spent most of their time in captivity apart and were reunited when they were released a year ago.
The brothers were among the last 20 living hostages to be freed.
Now, they are trying to rebuild their lives.
For Twin Brothers Abducted in the Oct. 7 Attacks, Adjusting to Freedom Is a New Challenge
On Wednesday, Israelis will mark the third anniversary of the deadliest day of violence in the country’s history. On the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, a Jewish holiday, Hamas led a cross-border assault from Gaza on southern Israel, overrunning army bases and border communities, and hunting down revelers at a music festival.
Gunmen killed about 1,200 people, according to the Israeli authorities, and took about 250 more back to Gaza as hostages. The attacks ignited a devastating war in the Palestinian enclave, where tens of thousands of people have been killed in Israel’s counterattack and much of the area has been reduced to rubble.
The hostages were returned to Israel in stages. Dozens of them died in captivity, and their bodies were transported home. Several of those who survived have written memoirs. Some have gotten married or had babies.
Gali and Ziv Berman, twin brothers, were 26 when they were captured in Kfar Aza, the kibbutz where they lived. A year after they were released, they are trying to focus on rebuilding their lives. Gali is studying law, governance and diplomacy in college, and Ziv is in a new relationship with a woman who survived the attack on the music festival.
The journey back to something like normality is far from over, and the horrors of Oct. 7 still haunt them and the country.
The return
As Israeli soldiers drove the Bermans out of Gaza on Oct. 13, 2025, after two years of captivity during which they were separated, beaten, deprived of food and mostly kept in dank tunnels underneath the enclave, Ziv said they had “thousands of questions.” They did not know if their family had survived the Oct. 7 attack. They wanted to know the latest about their favorite soccer team, Maccabi Tel Aviv.

nytimes.com.title: Europe’s Trade Tensions With China Are Coming to a Head
nytimes.com.text:
The European Union and China are heading toward a trade showdown.
Europe’s trade negotiators are meeting with Chinese officials on Thursday and Friday in Beijing. A week later, Europe’s presidents and prime ministers will gather in Brussels to discuss industrial competitiveness with China, among other agenda items. Their concern is urgent. The region’s trade deficit with China is running at 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) per day.
European officials blame an undervalued Chinese currency and Beijing’s state-controlled banking system, which has supplied vast amounts of cheap credit to build export-focused factories.
Chinese officials offer a different explanation. They say much of the widening imbalance reflects Europe’s surging imports of electric cars, solar panels, batteries and battery chemicals. European demand for those products has risen as the continent tries to combat climate change, adjusts to the loss of inexpensive Russian oil and natural gas and copes with the war in the Middle East — developments for which China argues it should not be blamed.
Europe is not alone in its concerns. China’s export push has unnerved other trading partners, including the United States, as Beijing’s trade surplus reached a record $1.19 trillion last year.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, warned in an address last month that Europe’s trade deficit with China had reached a “tipping point,” leading to “deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe.”

nytimes.com.title: 3 Killed and Dozens Injured in Attacks on Saudi Airports, as Houthis Claim Strikes
nytimes.com.text:
Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that Houthi strikes on two major airports killed three people and injured dozens more, in attacks that intensified the kingdom’s renewed war against the Iranian-backed militia in Yemen.
The Saudi government said the attacks hit the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said on Wednesday that the militia had attacked both airports with missiles or drones.
The Saudi-led military coalition battling the Houthis said on Wednesday that it retaliated for the airport strikes by attacking dozens of Houthi military sites in Yemen, including missile storage sites and command centers. The Houthis did not immediately respond to that claim.
The Houthis have managed to inflict few known fatalities on Saudi territory in recent years, and the kingdom’s toll would be first confirmed at an airport in the capital, Riyadh. The attacks could presage worse fighting on both sides of the border, just as the Saudi-backed Yemeni government has declared war against the Houthis and presses a military operation to retake strategically important territory from the group.
“I think we will see the Saudis react even more aggressively than they have been doing,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research group, after the latest attacks.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation Authority said the airport attacks occurred on Tuesday and Wednesday but did not specify when each was hit. Two women died and 28 people were injured at Abha, and a Sudanese man was killed and eight people injured at King Khalid, the kingdom’s statement said.

cnn.com.title: US has lost or sustained damage to 81 military aircraft worth up to $3.3 billion in Iran war, congressional report says
cnn.com.text: The United States military has had 81 aircraft destroyed or damaged in the war with Iran, a Congressional Research Service report released this week says. The number includes both airplanes and helicopters as well as drones, with the MQ-9 Reaper drone – used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support and combat search and rescue – accounting for more than half of the losses. But also on the list are some of the Pentagon’s most-prized assets, including an F-35A fighter jet and an E-3 Sentry, the four-engine jet with a large radar dome atop the fuselage used for target tracking and airspace management. The total cost of the aircraft lost is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Defense Department’s plans for replacements, the report said, citing figures from the Congressional Budget Office. The total cost of the war is much higher – at least $45 billion, sources have told CNN. That figure doesn’t include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the region, including those where some of the aircraft losses happened. Some of the aircraft included in the count may have been returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained light damage in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in September. The report is based on numbers contained in statements from the Defense Department; its inspector general; US Central Command, which has been conducting the operations against Iran; and news reports reviewed by the CRS. The report poses several questions for congressional consideration, including whether lawmakers are getting enough information from the Pentagon on the losses to determine effects and remedies. Defense Department reporting on Iran war losses has, to date, been vague. Even the Pentagon inspector general’s report on the losses, released in September, and covering action from February 28 to June 30, cites previous CRS reports for some of its aircraft loss numbers. Other issues Congress needs to think about are whether to provide funding for repairs or replacements; whether there is enough industrial capacity to satisfy those requirements; and the effects on US military sales to foreign partners. It also raises questions about how the Iran war has affected US posture outside the Middle East. “Congress may assess whether losses in certain high-demand platforms that are aging and limited in number, such as the E-3 Sentry, create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters,” the report says. Analysts have said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and earlier confrontations with the Houthi rebels in Yemen, an Iranian proxy group, have taken an especially heavy toll on the MQ-9 drones, which Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress earlier this year was the military’s “most valuable player” in the war with Iran. Forty-five have been lost in the Middle East this year, “an alarming rate,” according to a September report from the Atlantic Council. The Air Force has lost about 35% of its MQ-9s since 2004, it says.

cnn.com.title: Netanyahu says he brought all the October 7 hostages home. These are the stories of those who didn’t come back alive
cnn.com.text: The strike plan called for hitting a vast underground complex in Gaza’s southern city of Rafah, comprised of dozens of rooms and a network of interconnecting tunnels. Instead of a dozen bombs, the Israeli military had decided to drop just two munitions, each aimed at a single room. The objective: killing Muhammad Shabaneh, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade. On May 24, 2024, the bombs hit their marks. But instead of Shabaneh, two Israeli hostages were killed. Two senior Israeli sources said the military had assessed there were no hostages in that part of the complex. Months later, when Israeli ground troops reached the site, they found the bodies of Youssef and Hamza Ziyadne, an Israeli Bedouin father and son who had been kidnapped by Hamas on October 7, 2023. During the deadliest day in the history of the state of Israel, a total of 251 hostages were abducted and taken into Gaza by Hamas-led militants. More than 1,200 people – mostly civilians – were killed in the terror attack. It took two years of war and three ceasefire agreements to return the hostages. Three years later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists that he defied the odds and brought all the hostages back home. “We brought back every last one of them,” Netanyahu boasted at the UN General Assembly last month. Facing elections in three weeks, Netanyahu has repeated that statement on multiple occasions, rarely if ever mentioning that not all of the hostages returned home alive. “The fate of every person touches the fibers of our soul, and therefore we invested unceasing effort until we brought back all our hostages, down to the last of them,” he said on Monday, during the official October 7 memorial ceremonies. The Ziyadnes are among 40 hostages taken into Gaza alive who were killed or died in captivity, roughly one in five of the 206 abducted alive. Hamas held them in tunnels and hideaways where, according to released hostages, they were abused, starved, chained and beaten. Many were killed by their captors. Others succumbed to their wounds or the conditions endured in captivity. Some died in Israeli strikes and operations, or in the shadow of Israeli decisions. For a few, the full circumstances may never be known. This account of how those 40 hostages were killed or died in captivity – and why some were not released before their deaths – is based on conversations with dozens of hostage families, as well as Israeli military and government officials who helped piece together their stories. Nearly half were killed by their captors, according to Israeli military officials and forensic evidence reviewed by their families. Among them were 4-year-old Ariel Bibas and his brother, nine-month-old Kfir, who the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said were killed by their captors’ “bare hands,” while 68-year-old Itzhak Elgarat was tortured to death, according to a former hostage and autopsy results. Hamas did not respond to CNN’s request for comment; Palestinian Islamic Jihad said it “does not kill captives.” At least 11 were killed directly by Israeli military fire or in Israeli ground operations: three young men who managed to escape and were shot by troops who mistook them for Palestinian militants, a shooting the IDF Chief of the General Staff concluded should not have been carried out; a 25-year-old named Sahar Baruch who was killed in a failed rescue operation; several hostages who were killed by Israeli bombs. Some of the killings can be linked to nearby Israeli military activity. When the ground offensive began on October 27, 2023, Israeli military officials said Hamas issued a standing order: If Israeli forces approach, move the hostages, and if it’s impossible – kill them. The hostages in Gaza were very aware of the dangers associated with the Israeli military’s presence. Eli Sharabi, who published his firsthand account of captivity in his book “Hostage,” wrote, “That’s what we fear: that IDF commandos will try to enter the tunnel to rescue us by force. Because we know it would never work, and it’d be the end. The end of us. And the end of them.” A CNN review of the circumstances of the 40 hostages’ deaths found that at least 24 – more than half – can be traced back to Israeli military actions, including Israeli strikes and ground maneuvers that led to captors killing their hostages. In every case of a hostage killed by or in proximity to Israeli fire, the military says it had no prior knowledge they were there. The IDF declined to discuss specific cases, citing the privacy of hostage families, but said “all possible measures were taken to avoid putting (the hostages) at risk,” and noted the challenges posed by “a dense and complex civilian environment.” “To the extent that any harm occurred during the complex fighting, it was unintentional and occurred under operational constraints on the ground,” the IDF said in a statement. “The hostages were abducted and held captive by the Hamas terrorist organization, which bore sole responsibility for the conditions of their captivity.” (The Hostages and Missing Families Forum counts 46 living hostages who died in Gaza, but CNN’s investigation found six of those hostages were killed as part of the October 7 attack.) ‘The picture kept shifting’ A few hours after the October 7 attack began, Netanyahu declared unequivocally, “We are at war.” That evening, his cabinet set its main goal – destroying the military and governing capabilities of Hamas and Islamic Jihad. The ensuing three years of war killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to the health ministry there. Bringing back the hostages was not part of the original war aims, two Israeli officials said. About a week later, as the scope of abductions became clear, the cabinet added another goal: creating the conditions for their return. The military faced an unprecedented challenge: dense urban combat, some 250 hostages scattered above and below ground and two objectives that appeared to pull in opposite directions. Destroying Hamas would require targeting its leadership. But Hamas, Israeli officials said, kept many hostages close to their senior commanders, using them as “human shields” and making every strike a gamble. The working theory, the officials told CNN, was that most hostages would come home through deals, not rescues, and that military pressure was the only way to bring Hamas to the table. (A total of eight hostages would be rescued in IDF operations.) One senior official called it “synergy.” “The ground maneuver will pressure Hamas to release the hostages, and the more hostages we bring home, the easier it will be to maneuver afterwards,” the official reasoned. But that approach also carried inherent risk for the hostages, some of whom would later be killed by Israeli strikes or gunfire. “We never had 100% intelligence coverage about everyone,” a senior military official said. Hamas constantly moved the captives, so “the picture kept shifting.” Within days of October 7, the military had formed a special hostage task force, led by Maj. Gen. Nitzan Alon. Hundreds of soldiers were assigned to a 24/7 mechanism, linking the air force, intelligence and the IDF’s Southern Command to protect the hostages from Israel’s own offensive. Its main tool was a system of restricted zones around suspected hostage locations, known as “polygons,” drawn broadly at first. These polygons narrowed as intelligence improved; they expanded again after fatal mishaps.  Strikes on significant targets, including Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif, and hostage rescue operations, were regularly delayed or called off over concerns for hostage safety, three officials said. Still, as a senior official acknowledged, “It was not without risks and there are places where we failed.” The lost ‘kingdom’ In Khan Younis, the IDF thought it knew where the hostages were. Then, it didn’t. In the first weeks of the war, about 20 hostages were believed to have been held in a huge underground compound, known to the IDF as “the kingdom.” Sources said a polygon had been established there to ensure no Israeli strikes or ground operations endangered the hostages. But after the first ceasefire collapsed in December 2023, the Israeli military launched a major ground offensive in Khan Younis, and the military soon lost track of the hostages. The army believed they had been taken south. It did not know some had been moved to Khan Younis’ northern Hamad City neighborhood. On February 14, 2024, the air force struck a tunnel in that neighborhood, targeting two senior Hamas commanders, unaware of six hostages inside. Only in May did the army grasp what had happened, a military official said. When the bodies were recovered in August, an autopsy found gunshot wounds in all six bodies but could not establish the cause of death. Their captors had also been found dead in the same tunnel, without wounds. Officials believe they were suffocated by the toxins released by the bombs; they cannot rule out the possibility that the hostages were killed by the gases and shot afterwards. Yuval Dancyg, whose father, Alex, was among the dead, says he still doesn’t understand how the army lost track of the hostages in the first place. He said he warned officers in real time that the Khan Younis offensive would kill his father. “They told me not to worry, that they know where he is and they have enough information,” he told CNN. He said the IDF Chief of Staff, Lt. Gen. Herzi Halevi, later acknowledged in a private meeting that the army lacked sufficient information before approving the strike and took responsibility for the fatal error. The army should have been more careful, Dancyg says, but he places most of the blame elsewhere. “The ones that are responsible for what happened to them, first of all, is Hamas,” he said. “But my government could and should have let the hostages out way before. When you have a war with citizens underground and you decide that the war is the most important thing… hostages will get killed.” The price of delay Several senior Israeli officials who were involved in the decision- making have said publicly that more hostages would have come home alive if not for politics. Alon, the general who led the hostage task force, said last week the war “was too long” and could have ended at least a year earlier. Speaking at the Washington Institute, he said Israel could have made the same strategic achievements, and “maybe get some hostages that got killed or murdered during captivity back home alive.” Current and former Israeli officials said Netanyahu frequently stalled progress on the negotiating track and limited his negotiators’ mandate, barring them from discussing an end-of-war deal until the summer of 2025. Dror Shalom, a former senior defense ministry official, said in an interview with Yedioth Ahronoth, “We could have returned dozens of hostages, but because of delays in the process and the rejection of the deals, they simply did not return to us.” The most critical delay, military officials said, came in the spring and summer of 2024. In late May, Netanyahu and his limited security cabinet approved a three-phase proposal that would begin with a six-week ceasefire and the release of 33 elderly and wounded hostages before leading to the release of all others and an end of the war. Then-US President Joe Biden announced the proposal days later, and the United Nations Security Council endorsed it. Hamas took its time answering, two Israeli officials said, but by early July it had signaled it would agree to the May framework, with minor reservations. That’s when Netanyahu decided to harden Israel’s position, military officials said, inserting new demands such as continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi corridor along the Gaza-Egypt border. His security chiefs disagreed, warning the delay could endanger the hostages. The demand had operational and strategic logic, the officials said, but it disrupted what they say was “almost a done deal.” Netanyahu stuck to his new demands. His far-right political allies, Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, were threatening to withdraw their support and topple the government if Netanyahu moved forward with the deal and ended the war. The Prime Minister’s Office has not responded after CNN reached out multiple times. “There could have been a deal in July,” said Oren Setter, a retired IDF brigadier general who served as deputy director for strategy and negotiations at the Hostages Taskforce. “Hamas was under a lot of pressure and was willing to negotiate with flexibility,” he told CNN. “The fact that we stayed on that Philadelphi issue for so long lost us the opportunity.” “We knew that the price could be the life of the hostages,” he added. A few weeks later, that price had names. The ‘Beautiful Six’ By August 2024, Israeli troops had spent months advancing through Rafah and were concentrating on the tunnels under the Tel Al-Sultan neighborhood, where Hamas commanders were believed to be hiding. There was no concrete intelligence of hostages in the area, two officials said, and the IDF’s subsequent investigation put the likelihood of hostages being there as “medium to low.” On August 27, troops found a Bedouin Israeli hostage, Farhan Al-Qadi, alone in a tunnel. He reported recently hearing a woman speaking Hebrew nearby, saying “good morning.” After a 24-hour pause in operations, Israeli troops pressed on in the tunnel system. On August 31, soldiers found six bodies in a tunnel just a few hundred meters away. They had been shot, likely two days earlier, the IDF said. The army’s official investigation concluded they were murdered by their captors, and that the Israeli maneuver, “although gradual and cautious, had a circumstantial influence” on their execution. Officials say five of the six were slated for release under the May framework, had it been agreed to. One was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a 23-year-old Israeli-American citizen kidnapped from the Nova music festival. His mother, Rachel, declines to assign blame. “Pointing fingers does not bring Hersh back, and does not ease my pain,” she said. The bodies of the six, she told CNN, came back skeletal and filthy. They had been starved and tortured. Widely known as the “Beautiful Six,” they were the last hostages to die in captivity. Israeli officials say that by then, the working methods and intelligence coverage had dramatically improved. But the war went on for more than a year. The deadlock broke briefly after US President Donald Trump’s reelection: in January 2025, a three-phase ceasefire took effect. Its terms were nearly identical to the deal that was on the verge of being approved the previous summer. Over the ceasefire’s first six weeks, 30 living hostages and eight deceased were released. Then the truce collapsed and Israel went back to war. The last 20 living hostages walked free on October 13, 2025 under Trump’s 20-point peace plan. On January 26, 2026, Israel recovered the remains of the last deceased Israeli hostage, Ran Gvili, and the count was complete. But when political leaders say they brought all the hostages home, Rachel Goldberg-Polin asks them to stop. “Please don’t say that you brought him home… Hersh is buried in the ground five miles from my home, but Hersh never came back to my home.”

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: ICE agents told to ramp up daily immigration arrests despite GOP unease as midterms near
cnn.com.text: Immigration and Customs Enforcement leadership told agents nationwide on Tuesday to increase immigration arrests by 1,000 more people daily, returning to a previous goal of 3,000 daily arrests, according to two sources familiar with the verbal directive. It’s the latest sign of ongoing pressure on agents as the Trump administration doubles down on its immigration crackdown despite some Republican unease over who the agency is targeting. ICE also recently released a contract solicitation to expand holding space at agency offices, citing “exceptionally high operational tempo with increased arrests.” With the directive on daily arrests, ICE returns to a previous White House imposed push to arrest 3,000 people a day, an unprecedented number that the agency has previously struggled to meet. ICE had recently been taking around 2,000 people into custody daily on average — a target that officials wanted to sustain. They were also instructed to try to reach 19,000 arrests per week, which accounts for the fact that there are generally fewer arrests over the weekend and not as many officers in the field, one of the sources said. The source stressed that the agency is trying to push officers to arrest as many people as possible for deportation. As a point of comparison, in late June, ICE arrested just over 12,500 people in a week, according to the Deportation Data project, marking a high point. In a statement to CNN, a Homeland Security spokesperson maintained that there are “NO quotas on arrests.” “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE has been supercharged to find, arrest, and deport illegal aliens from the United States using every lawful tool available. This is promises made promises kept in action, and the results speak for themselves,” the spokesperson said. Immigration remains a key political issue for the White House ahead of the midterm elections, and administration officials have been sensitive to any potential changes in operations that appear to weaken the president’s approach to his mass deportation pledge. That has occasionally fueled tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and the White House. But some Republicans have criticized the administration’s tactics and decision to increasingly arrest undocumented immigrants without criminal records. Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district, recently broke with the president in a campaign ad ahead of the midterms. The agriculture industry, which generally leans Republican, also recently raised alarm over an uptick in ICE activity that temporarily disrupted their operations. Immigration arrests had already been increasing. In August, for example, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new monthly high for the Trump administration. The previous high had been set just one month prior when the agency arrested more than 46,000 people. Senior Trump officials have repeatedly denied that agents are required to meet arrest quotas, describing the push as a goal, and maintained that agents aren’t punished if they fail to meet that goal. “I have never talked to anybody at the White House about any quota. We do our job every single day and we do it effectively,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on CNN’s “Inside Politics” last month. “Our focus is to go after the worst of the worst, but when we make contact with an illegal, regardless of how many years you’ve been here, we are obligated by statute to at that point arrest you.” The continued ramp up in immigration arrests has required additional support from contractors. Last month, a contract solicitation reviewed by CNN revealed that the department is seeking contractors to build three different types of temporary facilities meant to help alleviate strain at existing facilities. “Temporary infrastructure is urgently needed to expand secure processing and holding of illegal alien (IA) capacity and non-detained hearing space on site,” the solicitation states. They include a field-detention unit, a room for interviews and processing, and a facility intended to be used for virtual immigration court hearings. A Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency has “no new facility plans to announce at this time.” The agency has also adjusted some of the ways it is conducting operations, including vehicle stops. Last week, ICE officers were told that they’d only be allowed to conduct vehicle stops if they have completed related training courses and must ensure that vehicles used for stops are equipped with lights and sirens, according to internal guidance reviewed by CNN. The memo, which a senior ICE official said amended previous guidance, came on the heels of multiple controversial vehicle stops that have resulted in fatal, and non-fatal, shootings and against the backdrop of internal tension within the Trump administration over how to proceed with the stops, which the administration considers a key tool as it increases immigration arrests. At the time, an ICE spokesperson denied in a statement that the guidance was new, saying: “Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers.” The spokesperson maintained that vehicle stops will continue and the memo “makes no changes to how ICE conducts vehicle stops.”

cnn.com.title: Takeaways from the first Iowa Senate debate
cnn.com.text: Donald Trump’s shadow looms over every contest in November’s midterm elections — but on an Iowa debate stage Wednesday night, the president’s name was rarely mentioned. The two candidates battling for Iowa’s Senate seat, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, kept their sometimes sharp disagreements on issues like health care funding, the future of Social Security and lowering gas and diesel prices largely focused on the policies at hand — and on branding their opponent as out of step with Iowa voters. The debate highlighted the realities of several Senate races key to the battle for control of the chamber playing out in red states like Iowa. Hinson is seeking to avoid being saddled with Trump’s sagging popularity without alienating a GOP base still loyal to the president. And Turek must win over at least some Trump voters in a state he carried by 13 points in 2024. Turek said he thinks what Iowans want most is lawmakers who will “provide solutions to people’s problems through bipartisan policy.” Hinson, meanwhile, accused Turek of changing his tune and adopting a friendlier posture toward Trump. “You trashed the president during the primary, and now you’re doing ads saying you’re going to work with him. It’s a tale of two Tureks,” she said. Here are takeaways from Iowa’s Senate debate: Turek aims for the middle Turek, vying to reverse Democrats’ slippage in Iowa over the last decade, was clearly focused on attracting independents and moderate Republican voters. For the most part, Turek tried to make the the case that Trump’s policies are “hurting Iowans in a unique way” without mentioning the president’s name. He said tariffs have driven up the prices of fertilizer and other inputs for farmers in the state; that the war with Iran has sent diesel prices soaring; and that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act gutted funding for rural hospitals and left some Iowans who depended on Medicaid or Obamacare subsidies without coverage. He highlighted Hinson’s votes in Congress aligning with the president’s position on those issues, but did so without naming Trump. But in a rarity for a battleground Democrat, Turek also praised parts of Trump’s signature legislation. “When you put together One Big Beautiful Bill, as it’s called, you’re going to have a handful of things that I actually am in favor of,” he said. “I’ve said that, and I’ve been open about it. I agree with President Trump that we need to get private equity out of housing … I believe that we should have no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security.” He also bragged that he was willing to buck his own party and work with Republicans in the state legislature. He pledged to “do the ‘full Grassley,’” a reference to the state’s senior senator, Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley, visiting all 99 of Iowa’s counties every year. And he said he would not align with Democrats who might seek to impeach Trump if the party takes control of the House and Senate in November’s midterms. “I have no interest in impeachment,” he said. “I think that we need to look forward, not back. My full intention is to go out there and to work on policy that is going to benefit everyday Iowans.” Hinson tries to undercut Turek but also distance from Trump Hinson, meanwhile, sought to undercut the image Turek aimed to build — while also casting herself as independent-minded and willing to break from Trump. She suggested Turek would “vote like an East Coast liberal.” She also sought to navigate around Turek’s criticism of her votes aligning with Trump on the war with Iran and tariffs — in part by pointing a finger at former President Joe Biden, saying she didn’t want a repeat of Biden’s management of the US military’s withdrawal from Afghanistan or the former Democratic president’s handling of the southern border. Hinson was one of the first Republicans to break with Trump on the war with Iran, calling last month for the president to bring that war to a quick end. And on Wednesday night, she emphasized her willingness to push the president. “I’ll be President Trump’s ally when it is important for Iowa, but I will push back on him — he knows this, because I talk to him regularly — on things that are wrong for our state,” she said. But, she added, nodding to the potential majority leader if Democrats win control of the Senate in November: “Hopefully it’s not Chuck Schumer, but if it’s Chuck Schumer, I’ll work with him.” Social Security split Both Turek and Hinson said they see a grim future for Social Security without changes to the program. But they had dramatically different answers when asked how they would preserve Social Security’s solvency. Hinson suggested she is open to phasing in an increase in the age – currently 62 – at which retirees become eligible to draw Social Security checks. “If you’re 20 years old, it’s a very different conversation than if you’re at retirement age,” she said. She also said part of the problem is that younger Americans are bad at saving money and suggested “Trump accounts” created by the Treasury Department would help. “Millennials are the worst group of savers in the country right now,” she said. Turek, though, said he opposes changes to the retirement age, and would rather lift the $184,500 wage base cap on Social Security taxes. “I promise you, it’s going to move things significantly in the right direction,” Turek said, adding: “Let’s make sure that billionaires and large corporations are paying their fair share.”

cnn.com.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has died
cnn.com.text: Margaret Hamilton, the groundbreaking researcher who helped create the field of software engineering and whose code helped land NASA’s Apollo astronauts on the moon to win the 20th century space race, has died. She was 90. Hamilton’s former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, confirmed her death in a post from the department of aeronautics and astronautics. She died September 30, MIT reported. The cause of her death was not disclosed. It was during her time working at MIT, where she took a job in 1959 and remained until the mid-1970s, that Hamilton managed the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory. The division landed a contract with NASA in 1961. She ultimately led a team of 100 engineers that designed the software to guide NASA’s Apollo missions. Through her work, Hamilton is also credited as one of the founders of the field of software engineering — a term she popularized — by helping to establish it as a professional practice. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” Hamilton was honored in 2016 with the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama for her contribution to science and space travel. Pioneering error prevention Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, according to MIT, and studied at the University of Michigan before receiving her degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Indiana. She took a job at MIT while her husband studied law at Harvard. While working to develop critical onboard software for the spacecraft — both command modules and lunar landers — that completed NASA’s historic Apollo flights — Hamilton is credited with making the system more robust and accident-resistant. One oft-cited failsafe she introduced was “the Lauren error,” according to MIT, which was named for her daughter and discovered when the then-4-year-old was fiddling with an Apollo command module simulator. “She liked to play astronaut because she saw me playing that way in certain simulations we would run,” Hamilton later recalled in an oral history project. “This was in a hardware simulation because we wanted to try how the software worked with all the other things — the astronaut, the hardware. So I remember one time when Lauren’s simulation crashed and I thought, ‘Oh my god, how did that happen?’’’ So, Hamilton programmed backstops to prevent an astronaut from running into the same problem mid-flight, an issue that would have yielded far more dire consequences in space. NASA pointed to one notable example where Hamilton’s work helped ensure mission success: During the famed 1969 Apollo 11 mission, Hamilton’s software overrode an errant attempt to swap the flight computer’s primary processing to a radar system. The software’s intervention, which occurred just three minutes before the first ever touchdown on the lunar surface, “permitted the mission to safely continue,” NASA said. After its work on Apollo, the MIT Instrumentation Lab spun off to become the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, now known as Draper Laboratory. Hamilton did not join the company, setting off instead to form her own company, but Draper’s CEO, Jerry Wohletz, said in a statement in MIT’s Wednesday announcement that Hamilton left an “indelible mark.” “Through her leadership and contributions,” Wohletz said, “she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.” In 2003, Hamilton was also awarded NASA’s Exceptional Space Act Award. The technologist who nominated Hamilton for the honor, Paul Curto, said at the time, “I was surprised to discover she was never formally recognized for her groundbreaking work.” “Her concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling, end-to-end testing, and man-in-the-loop decision capability, such as priority displays, became the foundation for ultra-reliable software design,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Pakistan confirms it has troops in Saudi as conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalates
cnn.com.text: Key Saudi ally Pakistan has confirmed it has troops stationed in the Gulf kingdom, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continue cross-border attacks with deadly assaults on airports. “The forces of Pakistan are already there. That I can share with you,” Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, without specifying how many or their capabilities, saying those details were classified. The confirmation from Chaudhry, the chief of the Pakistani military’s media wing, came just days after the two nations and Turkey agreed to the rapid deployment of the forces, as part of a newly minted mutual defense treaty. Over the past two days, the Houthis have killed three people in attacks on Saudi’s Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and King Khalid International Airport, in the capital Riyadh, Saudi officials said. The attacks underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign. The targeting of the airports prompted an updated security alert from the US Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens the conflict “has the potential to escalate.” The Iran-backed Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015. The conflict flared up in July, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unravelled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces. In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, which the Houthis claimed effective control of last month. The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia. Pakistan’s troops in Saudi The escalation has coincided with Saudi moves to strengthen defense cooperation with regional military heavyweights Turkey, a NATO member, and nuclear-armed Pakistan The trio recently signed a pact with NATO-style collective defense provisions, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance. The deployment of Pakistani forces had “not come out of a vacuum” Chaudhry, Director General of the Inter-Services Public Relations, told CNN. Pakistan has had a military presence in Saudi Arabia for decades, he said. Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi’s security was “absolute,” Chaudhry said. He described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all. But he would not be drawn on whether Pakistani troops would be involved in any operations across the border in Yemen. “Whenever there is a military conflict, no participating country starts disclosing how and where it is going to employ its forces,” he said, adding the any involvement would be “defensive in nature.” “The objective of this alliance is not to start labelling enemies, enemies, enemies, friends, friends, friends. The objective is the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia… That will be done,” said Chaudhry. In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Chaudhry said the collective security agreement would also acted as a deterrent. “Anyone having some funny ideas against another will hopefully think twice, thrice, or multiple times before doing that. That stops something terrible from happening.” Coming to Saudi’s defense is nevertheless complex calculation for Pakistan, which has played a key role in mediating between Iran – its neighbor and backer of the Houthis – and the US, since the US and Israel launched their war with Iran. In 2015, Pakistan’s parliament voted against sending troops to assist Saudi Arabia in an earlier round of fighting against the Houthis in Yemen. Chaudhry said Pakistan was still pushing for a deal to end the US-Iran war. “We have done, are doing, and will continue to do whatever is possible and necessary so that the differences and the gaps narrow down and there is a negotiated, peaceful outcome. We want this conflict not to expand.” Houthi airport attacks The Houthi-controlled armed forces said they fired a ballistic missile towards Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport on Wednesday, in an attack Saudi authorities say killed a Sudanese resident and wounded eight others. Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, later said Saudi forces had destroyed the ballistic missile launcher used in the Riyadh attack, adding that preparations were underway for “another imminent attack.” The attack on the Abha International Airport on Tuesday killed two female residents, one Moroccan and one Algerian national, and wounded 28 others, said Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation. The Houthi claimed responsibility for both attacks. This week, Houthi fighters also used ballistic missiles to target the international airport in Aden – which serves as the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, and an important transit hub for areas outside of Houthi control. The missiles landed near the airport’s runway shortly before a Yemenia Airways flight from Cairo had been due to land, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi’s Jeddah, Yemen’s Transport ministry said on Wednesday. The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press ahead with Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at rolling back recent Houthi gains. Last month, the Houthis seized effective control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway for the global oil trade – after claiming key Yemeni positions along the Red Sea coastline. But in recent days Yemeni forces have claimed to have retaken some of those positions. With civilian infrastructure now coming under renewed attack, the hostilities are showing signs of expanding beyond the battlefield in Yemen and posing a growing challenge to Saudi security and transportation networks.

cnn.com.title: Marco Rubio uses a dramatic backdrop to sketch a post-MAGA foreign policy
cnn.com.text: In the golden light of an Athens evening, with the Acropolis over his shoulder, Marco Rubio hardly looked like a man planning to ride off into a political sunset. The secretary of state’s speech in Greece on Wednesday will surely reignite speculation around his future presidential intentions. It implicitly positioned him as both the heir to and the modernizer of the “America First” movement — just weeks before the 2028 race roars into life after the midterm elections. Rubio depicted the West as a continuous inheritance dating from Ancient Greece to modern America, epitomizing “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention” as well as duty and heroism. But he warned that the civilization, ashamed of its achievements and embarrassed by its past, risked “atrophy, servitude and decline.” “Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” Rubio said, giving himself some political cover for the high-profile appearance. One interpretation is that this was yet another bid to retroactively impose doctrinal coherence on Trump’s erratic foreign policy of Iran war-style gut calls, power grabs and a transactional approach to resources. And Rubio is just the latest administration official to bemoan Europe’s supposed decline; failure to tackle mass immigration; and prioritization of the “global community” over national interest. This canon was hallmarked by Vice President JD Vance’s stemwinder in Munich last year. Yet he was seeking something deeper, at times, sketching the framework of a post-MAGA foreign policy in which US sovereignty and action remain paramount, while​ reinvigorating friendships shattered by Trump’s hostility. “We must rebuild our institutions and alliances” to face new great power rivalries and respond to a “new universe” of threats and attacks, Rubio said. His comments also reinforced a message to decayed European militaries that the US now expects alliances to offer tangible military multipliers to Washington. It was a hint that while nothing will be the same after Trump, a future Republican president might still value updated transatlantic ties. Rubio seeks to shape a new American foreign policy — and maybe something more? Rubio also seemed to be fusing three strands of traditional GOP foreign policy — the muscular internationalism of Ronald Reagan, the realism of Richard Nixon and Trump’s coercive nationalism. He might also have been trying to make sense of his own political evolution from aspirational conservatism to his current, darker worldview. (Rubio’s critics portray his conversion to MAGAism as the cynical act of a political chameleon desperate for power.) The speech was also jarring and contradictory. He was the latest Trump acolyte to travel to Europe to explain Europe’s history to Europeans and to adopt an idealized view of Western civilization that fits the needs of America’s Christian nationalist right. When Rubio laments eroded national sovereignty, like Vance, he seems oblivious to enduring national and cultural differences distinguishing French, German, Italian, and other European citizens. He ignored gruesome history that led late 20th-century leaders to constrain raging nationalism within shared political and economic structures. And while Trump’s team believes something is rotten in Europe, many Europeans perceive a corrupt and increasingly authoritarian American is most to blame for obliterating Western values. Noting that “passions” have rocked the alliance, Rubio used a deceptive euphemism for Trump’s bullying. Rubio’s lionizing of the ancient Greeks as foundational to the US also overlooked the founders’ concern that their direct democracy encouraged factionalism and promoted demagogues. Their answer was the Electoral College. Some Europeans will be offended by Rubio’s speech. But he’s seen by allies as the most conventional and sympathetic Trump foreign policy official, so his comments may be less provocative than rebukes by Vance or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Inevitably, such an ambitious speech using the optics of a major campaign address will stir presidential speculation. Visually, Rubio’s setting recalled then-Sen. Barack Obama’s hilltop speech at the Citadel in Amman, Jordan, in 2008. A Rubio run in 2028 seems problematic with Vance in pole position as the vice president. But whether he next takes aim at the White House in two years, in 2032, or later, Rubio showed the world Wednesday his ambition is unquenched.

cnn.com.title: ‘The list of his failures goes on’: El-Sayed’s Obama criticism resurfaced ahead of campaign rally
cnn.com.text: Former President Barack Obama is set to hit the campaign trail for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed later this month, years after El-Sayed criticized Obama’s presidency at times as a failure, saying it left the country no “better off.” In comments reviewed by CNN’s KFile from Obama’s 2012 reelection through the 2020 Democratic presidential campaign, El-Sayed faulted him for perpetuating war, eroding civil liberties, overseeing record deportations and preserving economic and healthcare systems that he said favored corporations over ordinary people. He also dismissed the Affordable Care Act as insufficient and argued that Obama’s incremental approach helped create the conditions for Donald Trump’s rise. The comments, made in editorials, interviews and panels, stand in sharp contrast to El-Sayed’s current alliance with Obama, who is now campaigning for the progressive doctor as he faces Republican Mike Rogers in a tight Michigan Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber. El-Sayed’s criticism of Obama was often searing. In a 2012 HuffPost essay written shortly after Obama won reelection, El-Sayed — who said he had voted for him — accused the president of failing to deliver the “hope and change” that defined his 2008 campaign. “This leader has perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on,” he wrote. “That memory will serve not as a reminder of the history we made that night – but of the silly emotions of a naïve young man who didn’t understand that hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile,” El-Sayed wrote of Obama’s first election. “I have little hope because there has been less change.” “So let’s be clear, for progressives who care about peace, prosperity, civil liberties, and the future of our country, Obama’s reelection last night was no victory. It was the rock we chose over the hard place,” he added. El-Sayed also took shots at the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature accomplishment and legacy across his two terms, calling it a “watered-down reform that kowtows to the interests of healthcare lobbies.” El-Sayed went on to fault Obama across a range of issues, criticizing the expansion of the war on terror into Pakistan and Yemen, the use of drone strikes, the economy, widening inequality and what he described as an erosion of civil liberties. Though El-Sayed made clear he had voted for Obama in both 2008 and 2012, he framed that support as a choice of the lesser of two evils against Republican former Gov. Mitt Romney. In a statement provided to CNN by his campaign, El-Sayed praised the former president. “At 24, I watched President Obama win in 2008. He changed what was possible for someone like me, with a name like mine. Despite being dealt one of the toughest hands of any American president—he handled it. And despite all he did, there remains so much left to do. That’s where the next generation, inspired by him and his leadership, picks up. We stand on the shoulders of giants—and I can’t wait to tell him myself later this month.” El-Sayed’s campaign pushed back on the idea that his past criticism reflected a broader hostility toward Obama, providing numerous examples over the years in which El-Sayed praised him personally. The campaign noted that El-Sayed has repeatedly said Obama’s 2008 victory inspired him to believe someone with his background and name could run for office. It also provided a 2020 exchange in a since-deleted tweet where El-Sayed said he could disagree with “many” of Obama’s decisions and believed the country was “not better off” after his presidency while still viewing Obama as “competent, coherent, and committed to Americans.” His comments were not limited to 2012. Five years later, while running for governor of Michigan, El-Sayed again distanced himself from Obama in a 2017 interview with Vox titled ‘Don’t call this man ‘the next Obama. ‘” Though he praised Obama for expanding perceptions of who could aspire to a career in politics, El-Sayed said there were “a lot of things I disagree with President Obama on” in both domestic and foreign policy and described Obama’s politics as “fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road Democratic policies.” “There’s frustration [among voters] with the fact that they’re being told by elites that their economy is back and that they should just be happy,” El-Sayed said. “But it’s not. Frankly, the economic comeback has largely benefited corporations and has not really benefited people like them.” Still, El-Sayed argued Obama did good things as president, like bailing out the US auto industry, but not enough. “I don’t think he was strong enough on things like health care. I don’t think he was strong enough when it comes to regulating big banks. I don’t think he was strong enough when it came to campaign finance reform, or strong enough on immigration.” A year later, El-Sayed again criticized the Democratic Party in an interview with progressive podcast host Katie Halper in December 2018 after she raised Obama’s response to the Flint water crisis. Asked how Democratic failures helped pave the way for a figure like Donald Trump, El-Sayed said his criticisms came from a responsibility to the people that the government was supposed to serve. “When Democrats buy into an ideology that says that we all ought to focus on the well-being of corporations rather than the well-being of real people, when we forget what suffering looks like, then we make mistakes,” El-Sayed said. He added that voters could then look at the political establishment from both parties and conclude, “you’re all the same, because all of you have failed.” Speaking in January 2020 at a University of Chicago Institute of Politics panel titled “Democrats: Whose Party is it Anyway?,” El-Sayed argued that Democrats needed sweeping structural changes to address inequality rather than more incremental policies, warning that otherwise they would repeat what he called the “same mistakes” of the Obama years. “We are going to continue to make the same mistakes of the past eight years under Barack Obama,” he said. “We are not, as a country, better off eight years after Obama was elected in 2008 than we were when he was elected. And I say this as somebody who loves him deeply.” “Look at where we are right now. Look at where we are right now. We are debating how we beat the most dangerous president in American history,” El-Sayed added. El-Sayed added that while Obama had delivered some important accomplishments, his administration had failed to fundamentally change the economic and health care systems that left many Americans insecure, problems El-Sayed argued helped create the conditions for Trump’s rise. “I appreciate the fact that we don’t give him credit for what he did for the economy in the short term. But the structure of the economy did not change under Barack Obama. The solutions to actually thinking about making sure that our health care system was equitable and sustainable, that did not change under Barack Obama. And unless we’re willing to admit that, then we’re at risk of going right back to the edge of the cliff we fell off in 2016.”

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
cnn.com.text: Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said. The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said. Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter. CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores. Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York. Flores is expected to appear at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer will ask that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial. Maduro’s lawyer is challenging the legality of the arrest and argues the former president should have immunity since the alleged conduct occurred while he was in office. The Venezuelan government is not joining in claiming immunity on his behalf, according to the prosecution. Allegations of torture More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns. Several of the Americans have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained. The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. In lawsuits filed against their employer — Citgo — Tomeu Vadell, Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned. All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report. That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.” This story was updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Evicted 87-year-old who became a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis has died
cnn.com.text: Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home sparked a government crisis in Spain, has died, the Madrid Tenants’ Union announced on Wednesday. Known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, she died just weeks after hundreds of people turned up to her door trying to prevent her from being evicted from the home where she lived for more than 70 years. She was forcibly removed on a stretcher after the private investment company, which owns the building in Madrid’s upmarket Retito district, hiked her rent from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970) – an amount that was unaffordable for the pensioner. “We regret to announce that Maricarmen has passed away today. As you all know, she was evicted on September 23, and has remained in hospital ever since,” the union said Wednesday. Maricarmen’s eviction sparked a wave of nationwide demonstrations over Spain’s housing crisis, with protesters setting up a large encampment of hundreds of tents at Puerta del Sol in Madrid. The landlord was forced to backtrack and agreed to allow her to move back once she was released from the hospital. “Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” the union added on Wednesday. Last month, Maricarmen spoke to supporters via a video from the hospital and urged them to continue to fight for their homes. “Please fight,” she told supporters. “I send you all a very big hug and thank you for everything.” There was an outpouring of grief and anger among protesters following the news of Maricarmen’s death. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed his condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones, posting to X: “A hug also to all those who today feel this loss as our own. Rest in peace.” People at the encampment in Madrid lit candles and held a moment of silence followed by an applause and shouts of “Maricarmen lives, the fight continues” and “We are all Maricarmen.” Some could also be heard chanting, “It’s not a death, it’s murder.” A group of the protesters began marching towards the parliament, with heavy police presence and barriers erected in the area. The protests have been largely peaceful, except for a few clashes between the demonstrators and police. Madrid’s Tenants Union, which was among the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend. On Monday, Sánchez called ⁠an ​early ​election for late November in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests. The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two proposed laws aimed at tackling the housing crisis. Analysts now expect Sánchez to focus on housing in an effort to win over popular support. The Bank of Spain has warned that the country is short of some 700,000 homes. “We need to renew people’s support,” Sánchez said on Monday. “We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.” The conservative Popular Party, which opposed the proposed housing reforms, is leading in opinion polls. It argues that the crisis needs to be solved by building more homes rather than by regulation. Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo on Wednesday also conveyed his condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. “No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall,” he posted to X in what some saw as a veiled criticism of Sánchez. “In the face of a person’s death, only respect is in order.”

cnn.com.title: Trump makes third trip to Texas in less than a month despite Ken Paxton audio leaks
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in less than a month to stump for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president has publicly insulted in personal terms. Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasingly uphill battle to hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas. Republicans are pouring millions into bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facing a closer-than-expected race against Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994. Trump’s Wednesday appearance in San Antonio, one Texas GOP strategist said, will be closely watched in the coming days for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state. The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November is boosting base turnout. But some Republicans, even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too. “It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said. But as Trump arrived Wednesday, Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles. The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios on Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio. Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.” But that followed The New York Times last week publishing audio of Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful. “So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.” Paxton has been plagued by his own set of scandals, including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year. Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office earlier Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton. At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.” Then there’s his frequent ribbing of the state attorney general’s appearance. “Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.” Trump did not repeat that refrain Wednesday night, calling Paxton a “fantastic man” as the two showcased warm relations on stage. “I’m very proud of him and I think he’s gonna be an unbelievable senator,” Trump said as he invited Paxton to speak. Paxton, in turn, expressed gratitude to his guest. “Aren’t you guys glad he came to San Antonio?” he asked an enthusiastic crowd. The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely. “But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added. Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump earlier Wednesday, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his planned appearance on stage with the president. The utility of a Trump visit Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — his approval rating is 34% in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates. And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll earlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino. Trump sought to juice turnout among his MAGA base Wednesday evening with a focus on border security and other red meat issues. He attacked Talarico as a vegan — a claim the Democrat has denied. And there were visible efforts to organize, including information about early voting and mail-in ballots for attendees on screens and in handouts. But Trump’s visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk. “Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said. There were some signs of discontent. At least a dozen protesters, who interrupted Trump’s rally on several occasions, were removed from the event. And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side. “If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative. A test of Trump’s power in an expensive race The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive. The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN has previously reported. Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved. But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map. “A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised  concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary. “If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added. But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points. That’s led to a debate about how much of this year’s close race is a reflection of the candidate matchup or the national environment and an unpopular president. “If Paxton was a normal person, he probably would still eke it out. I mean, the state’s still structurally conservative,” said one DC-based GOP operative. And the stakes of this year’s race could be bigger than just control of the Senate in 2027; it could carry ramifications for 2028 and beyond. The Texas Republican operative compared a potential Talarico win to a “hole in the dam” that could give Democrats momentum to turn the state blue at the presidential level. Paxton appears to recognize the stakes. “If we lose Texas, we lose America,” he said in a social media post announcing Wednesday’s rally. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s cheap suit is out of character and awkward for a few reasons
cnn.com.text: The fact that President Donald Trump was photographed flashing a suit tag from a bargain brand of imported suits should not really be news. Any woman in politics would tell you we should not dwell on how a politician dresses. But the fact that Trump, a billionaire, was photographed wearing a suit jacket with tags from Jos. A. Bank, the relatively inexpensive brand, is interesting for a number of reasons. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. It seems out of character Does the man who bought his own private club at Mar-a-Lago buy suits at the mall? This is the president who sells a $100,000 watch with his name on it and who allegedly inflated his net worth to be included on the Forbes list of billionaires. Status symbols are important to him. He has bedazzled the White House in gold leaf and Corinthian marble and is using taxpayer money, along with donations, to build one of the largest ballrooms on earth. All evidence suggests he likes to appear to be surrounded by the finest things. He accepted the gift of a $400 million luxury jet from Qatar to serve as his Air Force One. But he’s wearing the suit of a sensible sedan driver? The tags on Trump’s suit bear some resemblance to the Traveler collection of suit separates from Jos. A. Bank. The big and tall variant in black is currently on sale for $279. Advertised as wrinkle- and stain-resistant, it would be a good choice for a trip across the country. It’s a bit awkward for his America First approach Jos. A. Bank is part of a larger conglomerate, Tailored Brands, which also owns Men’s Wearhouse. The larger brand does have some products made in the US, like those from its Joseph Abboud brand, which retail for $700. Jos. A. Bank has an American Bespoke line, which is also advertised as being made in the USA, but the tags featured on the brand’s website differ from those flashed by Trump. That means Trump’s suit was likely made in China or Bangladesh — perhaps not the right message for a president who has promised the return of American manufacturing. The American-made ties by Vineyard Vines advertised on Trump’s online store retail for $125. But that’s just a tie.
