Trump can afford any suit he wants Just as Trump’s detractors have mocked his very long ties or the overcoat and gloves he wore to greet China’s leader Xi Jinping on a mild Washington afternoon last month, they have also seen reason to pounce on his budget-friendly suit. It’s possible Americans struggling with the affordability crisis might find the choice down-to-earth and relatable, although Trump is hardly struggling. He should be able to afford any suit he wants. His family business has seen investments in cryptocurrency pay off to the tune of more than $1 billion, according to financial disclosures. His company is selling early access to his social media posts, suggesting Wall Street firms who can afford to pay for access will want to use the information to cash in. He is pushing Americans to embrace data centers that could benefit companies in which he is invested. Is he trying to appear relatable? A conspiracy theorist like Trump could wonder if him flashing an inexpensive suit tag might be something done on purpose, to make him appear of the people. That’s been done before — think back to Al Gore’s sweaters or John Kerry’s camouflage hunting jacket or even George H. W. Bush’s cowboy boots. But it’s doubtful this was anything so calculated. Video of Trump opening his suit jacket shows that it occurred during a moment when he was dancing onstage. Taken along with the news earlier this year that Trump apparently bought Florsheim shoes, another relatively inexpensive brand of workwear, for members of his Cabinet, it may simply mean that Trump’s sartorial sensibility is mellowing with age. Trump said the Florsheim shoes were “spiffy” and an improvement over sneakers, a no-no for a Cabinet member. Back in 2016, when he was first running for president, his aide told The New York Times that Trump wore the Italian luxury brand Brioni, “among others.” Trump had previously talked about buying those suits “off the rack.” Brioni had furnished Trump’s suits during his time on The Apprentice. At the time, Trump owned a new luxury hotel in DC and Brioni had a shop there. Trump has since sold the hotel and Brioni has closed the shop. Some others might have wondered if Trump had some incentive to rep the Jos. A. Bank brand. He did, after all, sell swatches from the suit in which he posed for his mug shot in Georgia. He’s sold Bibles, watches, steaks, wine, water — you name it. But the piece of clothing that will always be most associated with Trump is the red MAGA hat, the symbol of his populist following, now for sale at his online store for $55 and made in America. CNN’s Tristen Rouse contributed to this analysis. This headline has been updated.

cnn.com.title: Russia says no epidemic risk as WHO pushes for transparency on plague lab death
cnn.com.text: Russia’s health watchdog said Wednesday there is no risk of an epidemic following the death of a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Siberia, even as the World Health Organization (WHO) made a plea for more information about the concerning episode. In a statement Wednesday, Rospotrebnadzor said it is winding down a set of preventative measures in Russia’s Irkutsk region where the laboratory is located. Medical monitoring has been completed for “over 90%” of contacts of the deceased worker, and no dangerous pathogens have been found, it added. The death of the lab technician, who worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in Russia’s southeast, has sparked international concern and speculation in recent days about the cause of her illness. Russian authorities sought to alleviate those worries on Wednesday, with the country’s watchdog saying, “As of October 7, 2026, medical monitoring has been completed for over 90% of contacts. No health issues related to infectious disease were detected, and the results of nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.” Local authorities have previously introduced disease-control measures at local hospitals in Irkutsk, a move that fueled questions among some local residents about whether authorities were being transparent. Global health experts urge greater transparency But despite the positive statement from Russian authorities, global health experts are still urging caution, and asking for more transparency from Moscow. WHO chief Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that a “full risk assessment” has not been possible following the death of the Russian worker, adding that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” WHO’s experts also updated their early evaluation that the lab worker’s death posed “low” risk to public health, saying that because she may not have died of pneumonic plague — a bacterial infection that can be transmitted from person to person, but doesn’t spread easily — the risk from the event was now undetermined. Meanwhile, Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of the WHO’s department of epidemic and pandemic management, said the organization had reached out to colleagues in Russia’s Ministry of Health and expected “further answers.” “So we do reach out to them to ask very detailed questions about what tests were done, the results of those laboratory tests,” she said. “What further analysis is being done if the cause is not yet known, what contacts were put under quarantine or under follow up.” “What we have been told is that they had no case of plague registered in this area, and that no high-threat pathogens were detected,” Van Kerkhove said. “So clearly, we would like more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, and if this individual didn’t die from plague, then how did she die?” The Kremlin has dismissed the concerns and said that it has kept the WHO informed “in accordance with established practice.” Under its International Health Regulations, designed to prevent the cross-border spread of disease, WHO member states are obliged to notify it of “events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern.” US presses for more info The Trump administration is also struggling to get clear answers about the incident from Moscow, though Trump said Wednesday that the US does not believe that Shipilova died from exposure to a bioweapon, adding that the Kremlin has since insisted the situation at an anti-plague institute is “under control.” “We don’t think so,” Trump said. “We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.” The US has escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday. “We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.” “It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” Nonetheless, Trump said Russia is “very sophisticated, very smart, and they’re saying it’s very much under control,” even as he allowed that Russian officials had not disclosed much so far.

cnn.com.title: What to know about Kenya’s first Ebola case and how officials are responding
cnn.com.text: Kenya’s first Ebola case, a patient who travelled for weeks by road and air through three countries without being detected until he arrived in Nairobi, has raised questions about border control and how to trace the virus across countries. The patient, a Kenyan man, had been living in Congo for seven years and started feeling ill a month ago. He had traveled by road to Uganda before boarding a flight to the Kenyan capital on Saturday. There, he tested positive for the Ebola virus in a hospital and died Monday. The Africa CDC Director-General, Jean Kaseya, told The Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that all stakeholders need to ask themselves how one case could have driven and flown to so many places without anyone noticing. “We need to ensure that at point of entry, we have a strong surveillance system in place,” he said. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. Officials are trying to trace all who came into contact with the patient The Kenyan man drove for hours by road within Congo and across the border into Uganda. He boarded a local flight while in Congo, and it is unclear if he used any other forms of public transport. Authorities have looked at the flight manifest of the other flight he took from Kampala, Uganda, to Nairobi, and passengers and crew onboard have been added to the contact list. They’re also looking to trace workers who cleaned the plane after it landed, as well as passengers who traveled on the same plane subsequently. Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on Wednesday that contact tracing was ongoing and that the number of contacts had risen to 57, with 10 already quarantined. “Even the people who cleaned that aircraft after it landed on Saturday, they are part of the people we are tracing. The immigration and the customs officials who served that patient will also be part of the contact tracing,” he said. Africa CDC’s Kaseya acknowledged it is a challenge. He said that the Kenyan man had not come up in existing contact lists in Congo. “Before saying that the outbreak is under control, you need to ensure that you have a contact list where all cases are coming from,” he said. Questions raised about how the patient traveled through Uganda It’s also unclear how the patient was able to cross into Uganda, which has closed its border with Congo because of the Ebola outbreak. Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media center, dismissed the question, saying only that journalists should instead ask Kenya how the man was able to bypass surveillance at its airport. “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X. Two of the man’s journeys were by air, while the rest were by road, covering long distances and passing through various towns and cities. On arrival in Nairobi, the patient underwent port health screening but his symptoms were not detected. He then boarded a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated and later tested positive for Ebola. When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health, Patrick Amoth, said on Wednesday that a meeting was scheduled with officials from Congo and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate what transpired during the patient’s journey. Kenya has been boosting its border controls Kenya’s Health Ministry has heightened surveillance at border entry points and created an Ebola hotline for citizens to report symptoms related to Ebola. The country has also designated five health facilities with a total of 241 isolation beds to manage patients, and is working to increase this capacity. The ministry said the country has enough supplies, including personal protective equipment, and has mobilized resources since the outbreak started in May in Congo. The ministry added that it had designated a specific gate at the country’s main airport for passengers travelling from 10 countries located within the outbreak’s epicenter.

cnn.com.title: Trump floats firing top political advisers after report they helped a pro-Russian government
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two of his top political advisers — less than 30 days before the midterm elections — writing that if their outside work presents a conflict, “I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump’s warning came after The New York Times published a report detailing how James Blair, one of the president’s former deputy chiefs of staff who now leads his outside political operation, and Chris LaCivita, Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager, traveled to the Balkans last week for paid work on behalf of a pro-Russian government. Trump was unaware that the two men had traveled to the Balkans – or that the pro-Russian government was among their clientele – until he was briefed on the impending New York Times piece, sources familiar with the situation told CNN. The president then made a series of phone calls Tuesday night asking his allies what their take on the story was, the sources said. One source said Trump appeared annoyed, and another veteran Republican who is in touch with the president told CNN that Trump was “pissed” by the report – particularly at the revelation that the two advisers had been abroad in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, profiting off their association with him. “Tone deaf,” the veteran Republican said of the advisers’ conduct. But another source said Trump was simply seeking a range of opinions on what had been reported. Trump – who has been actively campaigning for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms – ultimately decided he wanted to respond to the story, two of the sources told CNN. So on Wednesday, one of the sources said, he dictated a Truth Social post to aide Natalie Harp while in the Oval Office, commenting to those in the room that both Blair and LaCivita are outside consultants and are allowed to have other clients. One source said that at that moment, he did not seem irked. “Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump posted. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote. The president continued distancing himself from the two advisers and downplayed any conflict of interest later Wednesday. “They don’t have a conflict because they’re independent people,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I assume they have a lot of clients,” he went on. “So I don’t know their contract. If I thought they had a conflict … I would terminate.” He also noted that neither currently works in the White House. “Well they’re allowed to do that,” Trump told CNN. “They have a lot of clients and it’s okay. I’m a client over there, they have a consulting firm I guess, separately, as all people in Washington do. That’s pretty common.” According to the Times, Blair and LaCivita traveled to Republika Srpska, a territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of elections there on Sunday. The trip came as polls show Republicans are facing severe electoral challenges in the United States. Blair and LaCivita “were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that was retained by Republika Srpska’s government to provide counsel on voting issues,” the Times reported. They said the work was for the government and not the nationalist party that controls it, though they are essentially one and the same. Blair currently leads Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., and has been tasked with heading up the president’s midterm elections strategy. LaCivita is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc. The group has been spending tens of millions of dollars trying to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, including some in reliably red territory who now appear vulnerable. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Trump seems pretty sore over Republicans not wanting to campaign with him
cnn.com.text: It has become abundantly clear that Republicans in tough races aren’t especially eager to campaign with President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm election. Few of them showed up to Trump’s midterm convention last month. His travel schedule since then has rather curiously featured lower-tier states like Alabama, Oklahoma and New York and only a handful of real battleground races. And even in Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott is skipping Trump’s upcoming rally (citing scheduling conflicts, of course). Trump increasingly appears rather sensitive about this dynamic — which makes sense, given he’s latched onto the theory that he alone can push his party to victory in less than four weeks, despite his low approval numbers. He went on a tear about his rallies on Tuesday, bringing it up at least five separate times. “By the way, I’m going around doing rallies. The Republican Party is starting to go right through the roof,” he said at a non-campaign event in Baltimore. “Somebody said today, ‘I wonder why?’ Well, I started — I had to get out. I had to do it.” (There is no evidence Trump’s rallies are actually helping, which we’ll get to.) He posted on social media that his “Rally crowds and enthusiasm are unbelievable!” He added: “We are flipping races all over the place. … It’s all happening!” In a separate post, he said simply: “MY RALLIES ARE SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY, AGAIN!!!” In gaggles with reporters, he returned to the topic even when he wasn’t asked about it, claiming at one point that “the rallies have changed things around.” When asked about leaked audio of Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton saying DC was controlling his campaign, Trump responded that Paxton was “doing much better” since Trump started doing rallies a few days ago. And when a reporter asked Monday about campaigning in Michigan, Trump said he would. When asked about campaigning in Maine, he suggested he would go there, too. “I don’t know about Maine,” Trump said. “I think we’re going to Maine, too.” But GOP Sen. Susan Collins has said repeatedly — including at a debate Tuesday night — that she didn’t expect Trump to come to Maine. “That’s just not going to happen,” Collins said in June. This is also an uneasy question in Iowa, where three House Republicans recently broke from Trump somewhat on the Iran war. And Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson seems to want some distance from Trump. When those lawmakers were at a White House event last week, Trump seemed to put them on the spot, bringing up plans for more campaign events with him. “I’m going to come to Iowa,” Trump said, adding: “I will say that we’re going to do a great rally, and we’ll all be there together. We have to get you all elected.” Hinson responded: “We’ll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir.” And back in early September, when it became clear many Republicans in marquee races were skipping the president’s Trump-centric midterm convention, the president claimed it was for reasons beside his historically low poll numbers. “Everybody wants to come,” Trump maintained, adding: “The reason that some people are not coming is because we don’t have room for 500 politicians.” He also said back then that he would be all over the country, campaigning for every Republican in the most competitive races. “I’m going to go to every one of those 35 places, and we’re going to see if we can get everyone elected,” he said September 2. He repeated the same claim at the convention a week later: “I’m gonna go to every one of them, about 35. In a couple of cases, I’ll go twice.” That doesn’t appear to be happening anymore — at least not yet. With less than four weeks to go, Trump has been to only a handful of true battleground areas. And despite Trump’s claim that he’s such an asset, it appears that his “Trump-a-palooza” midterm convention backfired on Republicans. Polls show the generic ballot, a key measure of the midterm, took a turn in Democrats’ favor at almost that precise moment. Of course, Trump simply can’t allow for this perception that Republicans don’t want to campaign with him and that he’s an electoral burden. His ability to rally the base at raucous, large-scale events has been a central part of his political brand, yet he’s confronting a reality where many Republicans seem to view them as net-negatives. The lack of Republicans pining to campaign with him also calls into question his domination of his party, which he has been cultivating for a decade and is central to his hold on what political capital he has left. If he truly lost the base and his ability to make Republicans do what he wants, he wouldn’t have much left. In the four-week span left before the election, it could become abundantly clear just how many Republicans think Trump is an albatross and a lame duck. So he’s over-compensating for that — badly.

cnn.com.title: Huge companies have dominated AI. Two startups with an entirely different approach think they can do better
cnn.com.text: Among the AI heavyweights, Europe has long been missing a contender. The US has produced OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and SpaceXAI; while China has a whole host of AI labs. Now, one French startup is trying to best them all – and at a lower price. On Tuesday, Paris-based Mistral unveiled its long-awaited model, ML4, which the company calls the “best open-weight model in the world.” “Open-weight” refers to systems whose underlying workings are available for others to use and modify. Mistral’s latest model is “on par” with the best-known closed models from the major AI companies in key areas, including “cyber defense, finance, (and) manufacturing tasks,” Mistral VP of Science Pierre Stock said in an interview. Stock said Mistral’s new model was built at a “fraction of the compute” of competitors, making it cheaper for the company to build and for customers to use. CNN was unable to immediately verify Mistral’s cost and capability claims. Mistral is entering a tough market, even without including the trillion-dollar companies already dominating the AI industry. Its “open-weight” approach is already dominated by Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Z.ai. And the release of ML4 is also coming on the heels of another open-weight model release, Beam, from American startup Reflection. Reflection and Mistral’s performance, however, could help answer two questions hanging over the industry: whether open-weight models can compete with the best systems from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic; and whether Western companies can compete with China for the developers, businesses and governments that increasingly want AI that they can control themselves. Mistral’s latest model was built and trained entirely within Europe, which CEO Arthur Mensch told CNN’s Becky Anderson is important as it means staying out of the China-US “duopoly.” “There’s an enormous desire and an enormous need for alternative technology suppliers,” Mensch said. Open models gaining steam Both releases are built around the same basic proposition: giving users more control over the technology. Open-weight models such as Beam and ML4 can be downloaded and customized for specific tasks. The AI systems most people know today – OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini – are closed models, meaning their companies do not share the underlying “weights,” the billions of parameters that shape how the systems respond and act. Open-weight models have generally been seen as lagging the capabilities of the best closed systems. They offer something those systems do not, however: the ability for users to modify the models themselves, often at a lower cost. That trade-off can matter when companies cannot send sensitive data to an outside provider. When AI company Hugging Face was hacked by rogue OpenAI agents that escaped a test environment, the company said it relied on an open-weight Chinese model to defend itself. “What we realized during this attack was using a model on our own infrastructure, because all of that was private data, was mandatory and you can only do that with open models,” Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue told CNN in July. For open model AI companies, episodes like that are central to the pitch. They argue that many businesses do not need the biggest and most expensive models, but instead smaller, customizable systems that can run on their own infrastructure for security reasons. At the same time, they say the capability gap is narrowing while costs remain much lower. Names you haven’t heard of yet, but backers you have While AI companies are famous for the amount of investor dollars poured into them, open-weight startups also have some serious backing. Last month, Mistral announced it had raised more than $3.3 billion, which is more than half of the $6 billion the French company has raised since its founding three years ago. That is still small compared with OpenAI and Anthropic, which have collectively raised more than $300 billion. But Mistral argues that being “starved in compute” because of its resource limitations forced the company to innovate. Reflection, meanwhile, pairs a similar lower-cost pitch with deep-pocketed backers. The company is backed by Nvidia and major venture capital firms including 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. Though it is only two years old, Reflection has raised billions of dollars and was among a small group of AI labs briefed by the White House this summer on the executive order directing the administration to review frontier models on a voluntary basis before they are released. Like Mistral, Reflection said Beam delivers “strong model capabilities at lower cost,” calling it “a powerful workhorse model for enterprise coding and agentic workloads.” Mistral and Reflection are not alone. Other Western companies with open models include Cohere and Thinking Machines Labs, while larger AI companies have also offered open-weight models in the past. Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said over the summer that Meta would soon launch new open models. The push has also drawn support from the Trump administration, which has said it wants to bolster American open-weight models. Speaking on a panel with Reflection’s CEO at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross called open models “vital” for startups and innovation. He said the government is “extremely interested in looking at ways to build US open source, make it competitive, make it the preferential adoption by planet Earth.”

cnn.com.title: Ancient Egyptians sacrificed servants when kings died, forensic tests show
cnn.com.text: Forensic examination of human remains found around the funerary complexes of Ancient Egyptian kings has uncovered evidence that they belonged to servants who were sacrificed when the monarchs died, according to a new study. The remains of these servants, or retainers, were first excavated from the funerary complexes at Abydos, eastern Egypt, which date from around 3000 BC, in the 1920s. Archaeologists at the time suspected that the individuals had been sacrificed, but no evidence of their cause of death was found, study author Roselyn A. Campbell, a postdoctoral researcher at Purdue University in Indiana who examined the skulls from that original excavation, told CNN on Monday. “By consulting modern forensic studies and advances in our understanding of how human bodies react to injuries and to decay processes over time, I was able to identify clear evidence of head injuries in some of these individuals that occurred around the time of death,” she said. “These injuries, combined with the archaeological context, strongly suggest that at least some of the retainers were killed and then buried around the tombs of these rulers,” Campbell added. It was the “sheer number” of graves that led Flinders Petrie, the British archaeologist who originally excavated the remains in the early 20th century, to suspect that the burials were a result of human sacrifice, according to a news release. “In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler’s power,” Campbell said in the release. “Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.” Petrie took photographs of the remains and kept records. He then reburied most of them, apart from the skulls, 46 of which Campbell found at Cambridge University. “The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death,” Campbell said in the release, adding that linear fractures are generally caused by a flat, wide weapon. Of the 46 preserved crania examined as part of the study, potentially lethal trauma was found in 18 of them, equivalent to 39%. Campbell cautioned that this doesn’t mean that the hundreds of other burials in these areas were also victims of human sacrifice. “With such a small and incomplete data set, and so many millennia having passed since these people were buried, we simply can’t be entirely certain if all these individuals were sacrificed, or only some of them, or if there is some other explanation that has been lost over time,” she said. Some of them may have died naturally, or others may have been killed by asphyxiation or another method that isn’t visible, she added. Katherine Slinger, a lecturer in Egyptian Archaeology at the University of Manchester, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that while it had long been assumed that the royal retainers were sacrificed when a king died, little detail was known about the practice. “The manner in which these retainers were killed has previously remained unclear, with theories ranging from strangulation to poisoning,” Slinger said. “This is the first time that forensic evidence has supported this theory of human sacrifice and proved the manner in which at least some of these individuals were killed.” Understanding sacrifice Campbell is now preparing a book manuscript on the topic, slated for publication in 2027, which will look deeper “into who these retainers were, the context of Egyptian thought and society at this time, and more broadly how we study and understand violence and sacrifice in the past,” she said. Karl Harrison, a forensic archaeologist at the University of Exeter, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that the findings are “genuinely really interesting.” However, he warned against over-interpreting the intentions of the ancient Egyptians. “While forensic science can help to understand patterns of injury, care must be taken in assessing what this means in terms of intentionality,” Harrison said via email. “Ephemeral behaviours of past human cultures — especially those without written records or recorded in the writings of other peoples — offer a social complexity that defies our ability to comprehensively reconstruct,” he added. The study was published in the journal Frontiers on Monday.

cnn.com.title: This island was home to the planet’s largest penguin colony. Here’s why it just lost that title
cnn.com.text: An uninhabited volcanic island in the Southern Ocean used to be home to the largest penguin colony in the world — but not anymore. Scientists have discovered the staggering loss of more than half a million chinstrap penguins from the isolated outcrop. Chinstrap penguins, named for the narrow band of black feathers under their chins, thrive in harsh locations and Zavodovski Island fits the bill perfectly. Part of the South Sandwich Islands archipelago north of Antarctica, the island is wild, craggy and windswept. Zavodovski is home to both chinstraps and macaroni penguins, which have distinctive yellow feather plumes on their heads. In 2011, it was named the largest penguin colony in the world, but when British Antarctic Survey researchers traveled to the island in 2023, they found the chinstraps had suffered huge declines. More than half a million have been lost since 2011, representing a quarter of the island’s penguins, according to the the findings published Wednesday in the journal Current Biology. Comparing aerial surveys with satellite data, the researchers found the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025. “It is the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica,” said Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at BAS and the lead researcher. The decline can be linked to human-driven climate change, the report concludes. “Chinstraps are giving quite a clear signal of the impacts of warming,” Ratcliffe said. Zavodovski, which is about is about 1,200 miles from the nearest permanently inhabited settlement, is rarely visited by scientists because it’s so remote and extreme. To reach it, BAS researchers set off from the Falkland Islands and navigated rough seas for two weeks. At points, they were forced to shelter in fjords from raging storms, before they eventually reached the only part of the island where the cliffs and swelling currents are gentle enough to allow people to scramble onto land. They set up camp on the rocks and spent three days tracking and surveying the penguins using drones, aerial photography from a British plane stationed in the Falkland Islands and tracking devices fitted to the penguins. Chinstrap penguin populations have experienced worrying declines in recent years. A 2020 study found drops of nearly 50% in some Antarctic island colonies compared to previous surveys in the 1980s. But, for a long time, it was believed Zavodovski Island had bucked this trend. Instead, the BAS researchers found a sudden and dramatic decline on the island. It now has the highest rate of chinstrap penguin decline in the world. “We’re looking at annual population declines of around 7%,” Ratcliffe said, around two to three times the rate elsewhere. The scientists ruled out a 2016 volcanic eruption as the cause, given the downward trend had started several years before and has maintained a steady pace across the years. They also found no evidence that competition for nesting space or the impact of regional krill fisheries were driving the fall in numbers. They determined the most plausible cause is fossil fuel pollution, which is heating the ocean and disrupting the chinstraps’ key food source krill, which rely on sea ice for food and shelter. As warming forces the krill southward, the penguins can’t follow because the water is too icy for them. The chinstrap penguin “is quite a specialist species that’s got a very limited global range, and that range is getting squeezed,” Ratciffe said. There is some good news in the study. The scientists found the island’s macaroni penguin population increased by 28% between 2011 and 2016, after which it has stayed stable. Their increase adds weight to the climate change theory, Ratcliffe said. Macaronis are happy in warmer water and have a more varied diet, so are not as reliant on the diminishing krill. The scientists suggest that the chinstraps’ precipitous decline on Zavodovski Island, coupled with falls in other parts of Antarctica, may push them into the endangered category on the Red List of Threatened Species produced by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. They are currently designated as a species of least concern. The findings are “really worrying news” for chinstraps as the South Sandwich Islands were thought to be their stronghold, said Noah Stryker, an ornithologist and author who was not involved in the research. “What strikes me about this study is how rapidly things are changing,” he added. Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specializes in remote sensing of penguins said the study is yet another example “of a warming climate impacting even the most remote parts of our planet. The South Sandwich Islands are far from any humans, home to almost a third of the world’s chinstrap penguins — but not even they can escape the impacts of climate change.”

cnn.com.title: Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers breaks with Trump on tariffs
cnn.com.text: Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, is breaking with President Donald Trump over his tariffs on Canada in a new advertisement. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war — now,” Rogers says in the 30-second spot. “As Michigan’s senator, I’ll bring both parties together to lower your prices. That’s job number one.” The former congressman didn’t use Trump’s name in the ad. But it’s a clear reference to the economic impact of the president’s decision to slap 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods imported into the United States. He is the latest in a growing list of GOP candidates breaking with Trump on key issues. Rogers last month said Trump’s war with Iran needs to “end quickly” — a position shared by several other Republican candidates in competitive races for governor or the Senate. The new ad is the most outspoken Rogers has been against Trump’s tariffs. In a statement in August, the former congressman said tariffs are “necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution.” The ad is filmed in a bar, with Rogers opening by making a reference to a Canadian brewing giant, and Detroit’s professional hockey team. “Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings — man, it just doesn’t get any more Michigan than that,” he says. Rogers faces Democratic former public health official Abdul El-Sayed in a race that is critical to the battle for control of the Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to claim the majority — a task that would grow much harder should the party lose the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan. El-Sayed has long been critical of Trump’s tariffs, as well as the war with Iran, both of which he says are driving up prices for Americans. “We all know Canadians. Canadians are like the only people in the world who are going to preemptively apologize for something they didn’t even do. If you’re starting a trade war with Canada, you’re the a**hole,” El-Sayed told reporters last month. “There’s a smart use of tariffs. This ain’t it. This is a vanity war.”

cnn.com.title: French leaders say they’re listening to students. Will it be enough?
cnn.com.text: After a heavy-handed response to the student protests sweeping France, the government has changed tack. It has banned police from using stun grenades after a student’s hand was blown off earlier in the week and there are promises to listen more to protesters’ demands. But with hundreds of schools still facing blockade and calls for more protests, will it be enough? What has the government said? “Empathy” and a little more “pedagogy” is what French President Emmanuel Macron demanded of police forces facing student protesters, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, following a massive day of protests on Tuesday. “The president recalled the necessity to maintain order, intervene each time there’s serious violence, all while asking us to act with the greatest proportionality,” Nunez told radio station RTL Wednesday, after an emergency ministerial meeting. Nunez, a former chief of Paris’ police, said that he had ordered forces to refrain from using the type of stun grenade linked to a teenager losing his hand in protests on Monday. “We don’t deal with a movement of highschoolers like we deal with a movement of adults,” Nunez said. France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that high schools would replace lessons until the end of the week with a “period of internal democracy” to air grievances and discuss solutions. While refuting any suggestion of police repression, Lecornu condemned violence on the margins of protests, which were mostly peaceful Tuesday, despite the dramatic scenes that dominated coverage. In an address to the nation Wednesday, Lecornu said parliament would debate on November 12 a budget proposal that includes 64 billion euros ($71.6 billion) in funding for education, a slight increase from last year. He also said the government has launched five initiatives to respond to students’ needs, including efforts to renovate school facilities, improve students’ schedules and provide more opportunities to express their concerns. “We have a duty to listen to them. Taking young people seriously means supporting their engagement just as much as sharing the difficulties, but also the constraints, with them,” he said. The proposal for discussion is a tried and tested tactic of Macron, who has historically favored attempts to integrate public debate into policy making. His government tried to calm the Yellow Vests protests with a similar listening campaign in 2019. Meanwhile, 18 investigations into officers’ conduct during the protests have been opened by police internal investigators, Nunez said, adding they would examine the proportionality of police actions. Police forces “are there to protect the high schoolers,” he said. Are protests getting worse? On Wednesday, more than 500 educational institutions were due to be partially or fully closed because of blockades – a 41% decrease from Tuesday, according to the education ministry. That will leave 86% of schools open, the ministry added. According to the interior ministry, 488 people were detained around the high school protests Tuesday. The student blockade actions on Wednesday were a fraction of the hundreds of thousands who marched with workers’ unions Tuesday in support of students across France. But it’s a sign of the rancor among students that protests are continuing day-to-day. Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17 and five major teaching unions said they would strike Thursday in solidarity with their students, with little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime. What do students want? More teachers, smaller class sizes and buildings better adapted to the climate are the most common demands of high school protesters. Student union leaders, who represent some of the young people protesting, have also called for a 10-billion-euro ($11.2-billion) investment in high school and university-level education. A 10-point list of proposals drawn up by student unions included rethinking student workloads, ending a controversial university admissions system, ending police violence against students and creating more student accommodation. Sabrine Kharbach, spokesperson of the Student Union federation of unionized students, told BFMTV that blockades would continue until their demands were met. Anaïs Ella, spokesperson for Les Lycéens, a student association, told CNN that Lecornu didn’t address the demands laid out by student unions. She said that some of the prime minister’s proposals – including filling teaching posts in exam-year classes – “was the basics of the education system.” She said that money would solve some of their demands but that a deeper reset in relations between the government and students was needed. “We are the ones most directly affected by the national education system, yet we aren’t actually listened to,” she added. Since the weekend, there have been concerted efforts among students to reject the violence that has marred protests. Student Angelo Via, 19, who protested in the street Tuesday, told CNN there was a feeling of “powerlessness” in the face of violent police actions, despite many students protesting peacefully. He hopes the protests will bring about “radical change,” especially regarding education budgets. What’s next? There will be relief in France at the interior minister’s decision to ban one type of police grenade, as the injuries suffered by some teenage protesters has sparked widespread horror. But the proposal for time for debate has been met with skepticism in some quarters. The main union for school directors, SNPDEN-UNSA, said that the single day set aside for discussions was insufficient to respond to problems in depth. Nicolas Bonnet, national secretary of the union, told BFMTV that, “something other than a mere consultation period was required to get out of this crisis.” There are whispers in France of these protests transforming into another Yellow Vests movement, which was leaderless, nationwide and unified a broad church of grievances. Mimicking the months-long violent protests – the longest in French history – that rocked Macron’s first term, students and journalists have already begun referring to the next day of protest set for Thursday as “Act IV.” Additional reporting by Lucie Lepellec, Lisa Courbebaisse and Michael Rios.

cnn.com.title: ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen voters, records show
cnn.com.text: The Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping election-fraud operation has drawn on tens of millions of records, scrutinized dozens of nonprofit voter-registration groups and considered deploying undercover agents to investigate organizations suspected of helping noncitizens register to vote, according to newly obtained internal documents. The 166 pages of records, released on Wednesday by the advocacy group Democracy Forward, offer a detailed look inside one arm of the Trump administration’s escalating election-integrity campaign, which has marshaled federal investigators, immigration databases and voter records in an effort to identify noncitizens suspected of illegally registering or voting. They show the extensive infrastructure the administration has built within its immigration enforcement agency to pursue probes aligned with Trump’s election fraud beliefs, with multiple layers of data reviews, dozens of organizations investigated, primary elections tracked and weekly reports summarizing the progress of the various projects. Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, described the undertaking as a phased national initiative involving voter-roll acquisition, data analysis, investigative leads and field investigations. The operation drew on extraordinarily large pools of data. A June 1 HSI report said investigators had ingested 50.6 million records from a Justice Department dataset and another 48.4 million records that Heather Honey, a senior counselor to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, had obtained through what the report called “independent sources of information.” The document does not identify those independent sources, but the data may include public voter lists from California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada that DHS purchased and analyzed around this time. In July, Mullin announced that his department found roughly 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just those four states — claims that officials in those states have repeatedly challenged. The 50 million Justice Department records may include unredacted voter lists voluntarily handed over by more than a dozen Republican-led states in the months prior. DOJ has sued 30 other states to force them to share their unredacted rolls for audit. In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said: “DHS has been incredibly transparent about the acquisition and the analysis of publicly available voter files conducted by the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of USCIS. DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of US citizens.” Democracy Forward President and CEO Skye Perryman said in a statement: “It appears the president and his allies want to pick their voters, as opposed to the way things are supposed to function in a democracy where voters pick their leaders.” The documents suggest that the Trump administration wanted to use data-review products offered by the controversial software company Palantir for its reviews of voter rolls. Multiple agency documents reference plans to ingest the state voter roll data into a Palantir tool known as ELITE. Palantir’s website describes ELITE as a “data integration” tool with the purpose of “identifying the location of known foreign nationals who meet criteria for removal.” A Palantir spokesperson told CNN: “Voter roll data has never been integrated into ELITE.” Probing voter registration organizations The documents also show that investigators were looking well beyond individual suspected voters. An internal comparison said HSI was adopting a “network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads.” Investigators reviewed dozens of nonprofits and voter-registration organizations in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and other states and examined organizations linked to an Ohio company suspected by investigators of voter-registration fraud. Many of those reviews turned up no evidence of wrongdoing. Investigators said they found no derogatory information on dozens of New Jersey groups they examined, found no suspicious financial activity in another nonprofit review and closed a separate Ohio inquiry after exhausting its investigative leads. But the records show that by late May, HSI and the FBI were developing investigative plans involving seven Ohio companies that investigators described as “consolidation centers” associated with Black Fork Strategies, a progressive canvassing firm that HSI alleged was connected to several noncitizens registered to vote in Cuyahoga County. On June 8, ICE notified senior officials that agents planned to execute federal search warrants and interview more than 100 current and former employees as part of their investigation into fraudulent voter registration and illegal voting. The heavily redacted records do not explicitly identify Black Fork as the target of those warrants. But three days later, federal agents raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a progressive organizing group with extensive ties to Black Fork. HSI contemplated more aggressive investigative tactics as well. A June report said officials were exploring whether to use undercover agents to engage with organizations suspected of encouraging or facilitating illegal voter registration by noncitizens. New Jersey and Pennsylvania were identified as areas of focus. The document said undercover agents could be used to gather evidence and trace financial backing if investigators determined an organization was actively recruiting noncitizens to register. The records show that HSI also monitored this year’s primary elections for “trends, vulnerabilities, or indicators” that agents believed “may impact election integrity.” Updates on voter fraud probes shared with White House The bulk of the documents contain status updates on HSI’s voter fraud-related investigations. Most of the details are redacted, but the documents offer insights into how HSI and other DHS components were focused on trying to find voter fraud cases to prosecute. In June, HSI officials wrote that their investigations were focused on five states: New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Minnesota and Ohio. Among the various voter fraud topics, HSI was investigating “Counties with 2020 Results” and “Voter Machines,” according to a May update on the probes. It’s not clear what specifically was being investigated, though earlier this year, HSI agents contacted Arizona state officials with questions about the 2020 election in the state’s largest county, Maricopa. A set of DHS talking points included in the new trove described those interactions as “routine law enforcement coordination and information sharing.” Mullin sent letters in August to the White House and Justice Department arguing that foreign-made components in voting machines could “potentially compromise election infrastructure at any stage of the supply chain.” The investigative status updates were shared with White House officials beginning in July, according to emails from the documents. The records also reveal how immigration enforcement gave the administration another avenue to pursue suspected noncitizen voters when a criminal case could not be brought. Internal legal guidance distributed to ICE attorneys in December 2025 said that “in cases in which the evidence is insufficient to support a criminal prosecution,” suspected unlawful voting could nevertheless make a noncitizen subject to immigration consequences. The guidance noted that certain immigration-law provisions covering unlawful voting do not require a criminal conviction and, in some circumstances, do not require proof that the person knew the vote was unlawful. ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor sent out guidance about illegal voting following July reports that New Jersey mistakenly added 6,600 non-citizens to its voter rolls, and nearly 400 cast ballots. ICE officials wrote noncitizens who voted could be deported under the Immigration and Nationality Act. “There is no requirement that the alien have knowledge that he or she has illegally voted, and no conviction is required,” the guidance stated. “HSI is heavily working these cases,” ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall wrote in a July email. The records also detail separate investigations of “anti-ICE” groups in Minnesota, where a massive federal immigration-enforcement operation earlier this year sparked widespread protests, particularly after federal agents fatally shot two Americans. Internal reports describe undercover agents infiltrating and surveilling activist groups as HSI investigated alleged stalking, doxing and other activity targeting immigration officers. By late May, HSI had opened 418 voter-fraud cases and made 64 administrative arrests. But 318 of those cases had not been referred for prosecution. Investigators had also distributed more than 1,500 leads generated from immigration records to field offices across the country. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Kalshi is launching prediction apps with Native American tribes. That’s dividing Indian country
cnn.com.text: Eric Wright thinks Kalshi could change lives on his Indian reservation. He’s the administrator for the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, a small Native American tribe in such an isolated area of northern California that it doesn’t have potable drinking water. But Wright hopes revenue from the tribe’s new Kalshi-backed prediction app will fund much-needed water projects. The Kletsel Dehe is one of four tribes that launched prediction apps with Kalshi on Wednesday, becoming the latest to break ranks from most of Indian country, where opposition runs high because the industry could threaten casinos that provide an economic lifeline to hundreds of tribes. “We aren’t a big gaming tribe that has a ton of economic dollars lying around,” Wright told CNN. “At its core, this is about tribal sovereignty and economic self-determination. Other tribes are entitled to disagree with our decision, but they don’t have veto power over our economic future.” The explosive growth of prediction markets this year is driving a wedge between Native American communities across the country. The four tribes partnering with Kalshi in California and Oklahoma add to a small but growing list of tribes embracing prediction markets. But hundreds of other tribes claim companies like Kalshi and Polymarket are illegally encroaching on their coveted gaming rights, and they’re pushing in court to ban sports prediction markets, which make up over 80% of the business. Rebecca George, who runs the Washington Indian Gaming Association, is part of the broad coalition of tribes trying to rein in the prediction market industry. She’s one of nearly 20 people from all sides of the debate who spoke with CNN for this story. She said casinos helped transform the “third-world conditions” she saw growing up on the Suquamish tribe’s Port Madison Indian Reservation, not far from Seattle. But she’s wary about what might happen to that revenue stream as prediction markets continue to grow. “In Indian country, we’re still fighting for basic infrastructure,” George said. “Kalshi’s co-owners just became billionaires. And we know this is coming off of the backs of the tribes. So, it’s hard not to take personally.” CNN has a partnership with Kalshi and uses its data to cover major events, but CNN editorial employees aren’t permitted to use prediction platforms. From bingo to $46 billion As federal funding shrank in the 1970s, some tribes turned to bingo to raise money, sparking a legal showdown with states that restricted gambling. A landmark Supreme Court case later opened the door for tribal gaming to expand, and Congress passed the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act in 1988, creating a federal framework for tribes to open casinos on their lands. “It’s a bit ironic that the tribes are saying these new up-and-comers found a backdoor to gambling, when that’s basically how tribal gaming came about,” said Jonathan Cohen, an expert on US gambling history. “It only got legal approval after the fact, with bingo halls and card rooms in small casinos.” Nearly 250 tribal governments now operate about 545 gaming facilities across 29 states, according to the federal agency that regulates the industry. These casinos saw record profits in 2025, with gross revenues surpassing $46.2 billion. But there are some clear heavyweights in the sector – about 56% of that money came from the most powerful 9% of tribal facilities. Tribal gaming was already economically rattled by the rapid expansion of sports-betting over the past decade. Leaders from a half-dozen tribal gaming associations told CNN they want to avoid further disruptions from prediction sites, where more than 80% of trading volume comes from sports. Still, most of the fears from Indian country revolve around what might happen to those income streams as sports markets continue growing on prediction sites – as opposed to what’s already happening. Tribal leaders who spoke to CNN didn’t provide data, when asked, showing revenue drops this year. But many believe there are only so many “gaming dollars” to go around, even though executives as sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel downplay concerns of cannibalization from prediction sites. ‘We need roads, we need water’ Glen Gobin remembers growing up in the 1950s, carrying buckets of water from a nearby pump to his grandparents’ house because they didn’t have indoor plumbing at the Tulalip Tribes reservation in Washington state. He now sits on the tribal council and has seen the transformative impact of casino dollars, which funded 100% of a $67 million water pipeline and a $19 million early education center, according to records reviewed by CNN. “First it was about creating jobs,” Gobin said of the first wave of tribal gaming in the 1990s. “Then it was, we need to build homes, we need to build infrastructure, we need roads, we need water, we need sewer plants.” He was part of a group of tribal leaders that met last month with federal regulators in Washington, DC, lobbying for a ban on sports markets. Also in the room was Robbie McGhee, vice chair of the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, the only federally recognized tribe in Alabama. He said about 85% of his budget comes from gaming, and federal funds only cover 20% of a $20 million health care budget for members and children of tribal descent. “We have always done our best to play by the rules… we had to work with our state to come to an agreement for what gaming would look like,” McGhee said, drawing a contrast with prediction companies that sought approval from the federal government instead of the states. He added, “We have built an economy for our governments.” McGhee also eagerly pointed out that non-tribal casinos pay hefty state taxes that fund education and health care. Federally regulated prediction sites don’t pay state gaming taxes, and those companies are thriving: Kalshi is reportedly eyeing a $40 billion valuation, and Polymarket is at $20 billion. Battles in and out of court There are now dozens of cases involving tribes, non-Indian casinos and dozens of states – and most experts believe the Supreme Court will ultimately decide the legality of sports prediction markets. Two California tribes won last month at a federal appeals court, which ruled that sports markets from Kalshi and Robinhood violate tribal gaming rights enshrined in federal law. A Wisconsin federal judge, however, ruled in May that the Ho-Chunk Nation “produced little evidence” that its casinos were losing customers to Kalshi. The judge declined to shut down Kalshi within the tribe’s borders. “It was reactionary at the start,” said James Meggesto, a seasoned tribal gaming attorney at Holland & Knight. “The gaming tribes were tuned in early on. But the last year has seen a real galvanization of the opposition, notwithstanding a handful of tribes that are dipping their toes into it.” When Kalshi co-founder Tarek Mansour announced the first tribal prediction app last month with the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, he wrote that “the future doesn’t have to be organized around conflict.” But the conflict heightened last week, with insults flying back and forth. The New York Post recently reported about a failed attempt at collaboration in 2025 between Mansour and Victor Rocha, conference chair at the Indian Gaming Association. He’s a leading anti-prediction antagonist on social media who has boasted about “curb-stomping” Kalshi with “no mercy.” Last month, Rocha derided a “coffee boy” that he said was sent by Kalshi to court potential new tribal partners at a professional conference in Las Vegas, and he encouraged tribes to sabotage the meetings. Kalshi’s top spokeswoman, Elisabeth Diana, then called Rocha a “scared bully.” The tribes aligning with Kalshi don’t see it as a battle with opposing sides. Michael Stopp is a Cherokee businessman whose company worked on the prediction app launched Wednesday by the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town, in eastern Oklahoma. Prediction apps won’t “take from the pot” of tribal gaming, he said, because digital platforms can’t replace the experience of sitting at a slot machine or playing table games like blackjack. “I didn’t want to just be the redface out there,” giving Kalshi a Native American partner they could “tokenize,” Stopp told CNN. “But we do our due diligence and really vet the companies we work with, and they’ve put together a very good program for these tribes. It is a legitimate opportunity.” Marshall Pierite, chair of the Tunica-Biloxi tribe, said there was a “lukewarm” reception from Indian country when his first-ever tribal prediction market came out last month. But he said some tribal leaders privately asked him “how they can piggyback on our efforts” with Kalshi. “We just love to challenge and change the status quo,” Pierite said. The CFTC’s ‘one-man show’ With the Trump administration’s blessing, prediction markets are structured as financial exchanges for trading – not casinos or sportsbooks for gambling. This means they bypass state gaming regulations and instead get federally licensed to offer “event contracts” by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC. CFTC chairman Mike Selig, a Trump appointee and staunch supporter of prediction markets, invited tribal leaders last month to his Washington, DC, offices for a meeting that attendees said was professional but unproductive. One attendee, James Siva, chair of the California Nations Indian Gaming Association, said “decades of work” on tribal gaming were “circumvented by a one-man show” at the CFTC. (The CFTC is supposed to have a bipartisan five-member board, but Selig has been the sole commissioner all year.) Siva said tribal advocates told Selig there are more than 6,000 tribal gaming regulators across the country. Compare that to the CFTC, which had only 535 employees as of the latest tally in February. The CFTC polices not just prediction sites but also commodity futures and other financial instruments. A senior CFTC official told CNN that agency leaders saw the meeting as “productive” and appreciated the strong tribal attendance. The official said as a result of the meeting, the CFTC assigned a staff member to add tribal engagement to their portfolio. When asked to comment on the critiques from the tribal attendees, CFTC spokeswoman Brooke Nethercott told CNN that “Chairman Selig was happy to engage with tribal leaders and looks forward to continued engagement.” CNN’s Akansha Singh contributed to this story

cnn.com.title: Former Australian Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing Indigenous men
cnn.com.text:
A former Australian Catholic bishop was sentenced Wednesday to six years and six months in prison for sexually abusing two young Indigenous men.
A District Court of Western Australia state jury convicted Christopher Saunders, 76, in August of 13 out of 19 charges of sexual abuse that occurred between 2008 and 2019 in his sprawling Broome Diocese on the country’s tropical northwest coast.
Saunders will become eligible for parole in February, 2031.
Four charges involving a child younger than 13 were dropped on the first day of Saunders’ three-week trial.
Saunders is one of the most senior Australian Catholics to be convicted in a global clergy abuse scandal that has faced the Vatican for years.
Cardinal George Pell was convicted of abusing choirboys, and Archbishop Philip Wilson was convicted of covering up child sex abuse by a priest. But both clerics successfully appealed their convictions.
Prosecutors alleged Saunders lured young Indigenous men to his church-owned house with alcohol and cigarettes paid for with church funds.
Saunders led the remote Broome Diocese from 1996 until he resigned in 2021. The Outback diocese covers an area larger than France with only 50,000 people. Most of the region’s Catholics are Indigenous.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, said the sentence recognized the gravity and serious nature of Saunders’ offenses.
The sentence also recognized the profound impact on the victims and survivors of Saunders’ crimes, Costelloe said.
“To each victim and survivor who courageously revealed what they had endured, we want to say this: We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church,” Costelloe said in a statement.
The Vatican began investigating Saunders in 2022, then handed the Western Australia Police Force a report on its findings the following year. Police charged Saunders in 2024.

cnn.com.title: Who is Zack Polanski, the ‘eco-populist’ rattling the UK’s establishment?
cnn.com.text: The leader of the UK’s Green Party, Zack Polanski, will on Thursday challenge the political establishment by taking on the ruling Labour Party in a special election for the seat held by former prime minister Keir Starmer. Polanski, with his deep reserve of progressive policies and an active presence on TikTok cuts a markedly different figure to Starmer, who consistently alienated his Labour Party’s left-wing and developed a reputation as a stilted, ineffective communicator. That contrast helped Polanski and the Greens gain traction as a popular left-wing alternative to the governing, center-left Labour Party, which has been bleeding voters in recent years over its stance on issues like welfare spending, trans rights and the war in Gaza. Polanski even said on more than one occasion that his party “is here to replace Labour.” But that momentum has largely stalled since Starmer resigned as prime minister in the summer following enormous pressure from his party. He stepped down as a member of parliament (MP) last month, triggering the by-election. In Starmer’s place, a more formidable opponent has emerged. Andy Burnham, the current prime minister, is widely seen as a better political operator and more capable of appealing to a broad spectrum of voters, including the progressives Polanski has been targeting. So the outcome of this by-election – in the central London constituency of Holborn and St. Pancras – represents more than just Polanski potentially becoming an MP. It pits the Greens and Labour directly against each other for the first time since Burnham took office, acting as the first major electoral test for the new government as well as a barometer of the Greens’ ability to compete with a rejuvenated Labour. If Polanski wins on Thursday, it will be a stern warning for the new prime minister and could be an early indicator that Britain’s left flank has irrevocably split. But if he loses and Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali holds the party’s seat, it will serve as a sign that Burnham has managed to pull progressives back into the Labour Party and slow its electoral decline. Differing stances over the war in Gaza and antisemitism are central to that split, and to this by-election. Many Muslim voters have said they will not vote Labour because they think the government has not acted strongly enough over Gaza. This weekend, the Greens adopted a controversial motion classifying Zionism, which Jewish groups sometimes define as a right to Jewish self-determination, as a form of racism, calling it an “ethnonationalist political project.” Polanski, who is Jewish and changed his name from David Paulden when he was 18 to honor that heritage, did not vote on the motion nor mention it in his speech to the conference. He describes himself as an “anti-Zionist.” Israel responded by banning Polanski from visiting the country. On Wednesday, a fresh storm broke out in British media over a reported friendship between the Green Party member who proposed the motion and a man convicted in the United States on al Qaeda terrorism charges. Any split in the left comes at a critical moment in British politics, with Labour (and the Greens) also focused on containing a rising right-wing wave, most clearly signaled by the rapid ascent of the hard-right populist party, Reform UK. Who is Polanski? A self-described “eco-populist,” Polanski, 43, was catapulted onto the national stage last fall when he secured a surprise victory in the Greens’ leadership election, beating two of the party’s four MPs to claim the top job. Before that, he was still a little-known local politician, representing the Greens in the London Assembly. The broad brushstrokes of Polanski’s image go something like this: to his admirers, he is an antidote to the stiff technocratic tendencies of more mainstream politicians; a gifted communicator willing to adopt the bold left-wing policies Labour has largely shied away from. To his detractors, he is vague and unable to pin down the details of his own policies. More recently, his social media use sparked controversy after he criticized the police’s response to an antisemitic attack in north London and, in a separate incident, reposted a photo that some interpreted as threatening Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK. Still, under his leadership, the party has commanded national attention, building on its best general election performance when it secured four parliamentary seats in 2024. By May, the Greens’ rise seemed astronomic – they briefly polled as high as Labour and the center-right Conservatives, the two parties which have dominated British politics for decades, and enjoyed historic gains in spring local elections. While Polanski has tried to link the climate crisis to other issues, he has largely prioritized immediate everyday concerns, such as the cost of living and suggestions of public ownership of water and other utilities, alongside other progressive initiatives like championing a wealth tax and rent controls, while also adopting a pro-Palestinian stance. Polanski has claimed credit for pushing Labour further to the left, most recently saying his party was responsible for influencing Labour’s shifting stance on the Middle East, including the government’s recently announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Actor turned politician A former actor, Polanski’s strength lies in his communication. He hosts his own nightclub nights and holds weekly conversations with academics, activists and journalists on his podcast “Bold Politics” on ideas like an extreme wealth line (a proposed globally agreed limit for an individual’s net worth), re-nationalizing water companies and rejoining the European Union. But he is prone to slip-ups too – in one disastrous interview shortly after becoming leader he seemed to confuse the national debt and deficit. Months later, he more carefully laid out his economic policy at a left-wing think tank event, though it remains “vague,” said Laura Serra, a political scientist at the London School of Economics. “People don’t really know what they (the Greens) stand for, what they’re going to do,” she added. While Polanski’s almost constant media presence has given him a far higher profile than previous Green leaders, analysts argue that the party’s increasing popularity has less to do with him and more to do with the shifting political climate in the UK. And at the same time, Green parties across Europe have become more influential, propelled by growing support among recent graduates and benefiting from “changing societal cleavages,” said James Dennison, a political scientist at the European University in Florence, who has studied the Greens for more than a decade. “The change is more rapid in the UK, and it’s exaggerated partially because of the electoral system, so it takes them longer to break through, and when they do, they go faster.” Polanski self-consciously forms part of a wider populist trend too; he describes his approach to messaging as “substance with clickbait” and an alternative designed directly to confront the right-wing populism of Reform, and its Trump-supporting leader Nigel Farage. “Populism is about the 99%, the vast majority… against the very, very wealthy… Trump and Farage come from the 1% and want to protect the interests of the elite,” Polanski told Bloomberg earlier this year. This simultaneous rise of the Greens and Reform could fracture Britain’s political landscape, in which the first-past-the-post electoral system typically favors two or three major parties. So, regardless of who wins on Thursday, the Greens even being competitive in a traditional Labour stronghold like this is indicative of how the smaller, more radical parties are increasingly challenging the mainstream.

bbc.com.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.
"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.
But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

bbc.com.title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity, external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.
Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.
An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.
Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command.
Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.
We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.
In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.
"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."
Where is Austin Tice?
Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.
