As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.
Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.
Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.
Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.
One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".
Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.
The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.
Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran.
A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place - involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran - to bring Hassan to Lebanon.
The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran - secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in.
Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.
There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.
Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.
They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".
Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

bbc.com.title: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances and distinct dialogue delivery, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told BBC Marathi.
One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.
He was rushed to hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.
"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.
On Thursday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.
Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".
Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention.
Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. He won his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award as well for his portrayal of the gangster Anna in the film.
He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft.
His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. His other characters, including the patriotic hero of Tirangaa and Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, also won him accolades.
Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.
Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.
The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the wide range of his work. He played different but contrasting roles like that of a notorious gangster or a policeman with equal ease. He also sometimes worked behind the camera as a director and writer.
His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a also testament to his wide-ranging career.
Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before making his debut in films, he was involved in theatre, where he developed his gritty style of dialogue delivery and also mastered the intensity he brought to his on-screen characters.
Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.
Patekar was also known for his activism and didn't mince his words while criticising the government of the day. He was direct, and almost brazen and unapologetic, when it came to criticising ministers and their policies and that too quite publicly.
Issues related to farmers were particularly close to his heart.
His work also went beyond just giving statements. In 2015 he and actor Makarand Anaspure established the Naam Foundation, which has worked on farmer welfare and water conservation in Maharashtra.
But his career was not without controversies.
In 2018, allegations of sexual harassment made by actor Tanushree Dutta against Patekar over an alleged incident on a film set a decade earlier helped spark India's #MeToo movement. Patekar denied the allegations.
In 2019, he was cleared of the charges after police said they had not found sufficient evidence against him.

bbc.com.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.
The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.
"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.
There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.
The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.
Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.
And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.
Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.
To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.
In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
The street does not always win.
In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.
The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.
His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.
But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

bbc.com.title: Three people killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom.
Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.
In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.
The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.
Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca.
Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added.
The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.
The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country.
Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".
The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.
But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.
In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".
The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".
The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.
The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

bbc.com.title: Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.
Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.
Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.
His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.
A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.
Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.
Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.
Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.
"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

bbc.com.title: Trump wants a new Camp David-like retreat at his Florida golf club
bbc.com.text:
- Published
US President Donald Trump is looking to create a presidential retreat similar to Camp David at his Florida golf club.
The club would foot constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and provide free memberships to future presidents - and accommodations to visiting foreign dignitaries.
"It's only about two minutes away from the airport … and they could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like a sort of Camp David retreat," Trump said on Wednesday.
If it comes to fruition, Trump's transformed golf estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David, once a Great Depression-era camp in the woods for federal employees. It would also mark another tradition transformed by Trump.
The US president has sought to cement his legacy through changes to the White House, including gilded gold leaf accents in the Oval Office, demolition of the East Wing and construction of a ballroom. He is pushing ahead with plans to erect a massive triumphal arch elsewhere in Washington.
He has hosted national security meetings and other events at Camp David, known as the president's country residence. The Camp David property - set deep in Catoctin Mountain Park in Frederick County, Maryland - was first taken over as a retreat by President Franklin Roosevelt, who nicknamed it "Shangri-La".
The area is rustic, and in some ways resembles the military facility it officially is - Naval Support Facility, Thurmont. The entire facility is staffed by uniformed members of the US Navy and Marine Corps.
The secure facility is largely hidden from public view, with Marines guarding the perimeter and airspace above restricted. It is not marked on maps of the national park, even if its location is known to locals.
Press is only very rarely allowed on the grounds - meaning that photography of the wood and stone cabins and lodges that make up most of the facility are tightly controlled.
On a recent visit by the BBC, for example, reporters in the White House press pool were under strict instructions to avoid taking images in unauthorized areas or providing details on the camp's layout.
Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, on the other hand, is connected to the rest of the city by ample roadways, some of which are lined with supporters or protesters when the president is there.
The 27-hole golf course and club bills itself as having "a lively social scene" and fine dining - and is visited often by Trump's political allies during his many weekends in Florida. It includes a luxurious clubhouse, a gift store and hosts frequent social events for members.
The president's argument that the area is "secure" is notable. In recent months, Trump has frequently used national security and safety arguments to justify various projects in Washington DC, including his White House ballroom project the planned Triumphal Arch.
Asked by reporters if he would call the new presidential retreat at his golf club "Camp Donald", Trump replied, "Well, it's already called Trump International. It's one of the best golf courses in the world."
He said among advantages is the absence of high buildings and homes looming "so you don't have ... people hiding behind windows".
"They can get maximum safety," the president said. "It's a great idea and it'll be used a lot."
Trump said at the Oval Office on Wednesday that Secret Service officials first suggested the idea of using the golf club as a presidential retreat, and that he thinks it is "a great idea".
"It's about as safe as they could possibly get," he said.
The BBC has contacted the Secret Service for comment.
A letter dated 3 September from the golf course's attorney to the county commission in Florida said Trump offered to deem the club as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course" for presidents and visiting heads of state, according to USA TODAY's Palm Beach Post.
The letter, obtained by the local outlet, states that the golf club would provide access to all its facilities at "no cost to the federal government" and provide free membership to future presidents.
The golf club would front constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and local residents, according to the letter.
"This wouldn't be for me," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday. "This would be for all future presidents."

bbc.com.title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages.
Asahi, Sapporo, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC that their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC), adding that they would fully cooperate with the regulator.
The four firms dominate Japan's beer market, with their drinks a common sight in supermarkets and convenience stores across the country.
Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory's beer business is not publicly-listed.
"I do not deny that an investigation is being conducted today, but I'd like to refrain from commenting on the details as a preliminary review is underway," JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo said, according to local media.
The BBC has contacted the JFTC for comment.
According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022.
All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation.
Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act".
It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation".
Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise."
A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed "an on-site inspection" had taken place "in connection with a potential violation of Japan's Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices".
The company said: "We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC's investigation."
Asahi said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission" and that it will fully cooperate with the regulator.
It follows an investigation by the regulator in June over alleged cartel activity by some of Japan's biggest ice cream makers, including Meiji and Pocky maker Ezaki Glico.

bbc.com.title: Cornell rape case accuser has received ‘threats’, attorney tells BBC Newsnight
bbc.com.text:
Cornell rape case accuser has received ‘threats’, attorney tells BBC Newsnight
The lawyer for the woman who alleges she was raped at a Cornell University fraternity house says both he and his client have received death threats following the publicity of the case.
Thomas Giuffra is representing a woman, known in legal documents as Jane Doe, who alleges she was raped at a frat house on campus in 2024. No criminal charges were initially filed in connection with the allegations. The case has since been reopened following a civil lawsuit filed by Doe.
Giuffra spoke to BBC Newsnight about recent developments in the case and Donald Trump's recent comments about it.

bbc.com.title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies
bbc.com.text:
- Published
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol - a square in Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing - with a collective gasp followed by a minute of silence.
Dozens of candles were lit around the square while more candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then marched from Puerta del Sol to the Spanish Congress, chanting "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
One protester told the BBC that people would remain in the square "as long as necessary".
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences and wrote on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur

bbc.com.title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
bbc.com.text:
- Published
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.
India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.
That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.
Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.
Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.
Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.
Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.
The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.
In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.
Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.
Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.
Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.
Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.
Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.
Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.
"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.
"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.
"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."
Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.
In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.
The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.
Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.
Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.
Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.
The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.
She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.
An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.
Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.
That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.
The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.
Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.
Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.
India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.
With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

bbc.com.title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare

bbc.com.title: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Court of Appeals in New York has heard arguments from both lawyers for families of 9/11 victims and the government of Saudi Arabia as it decides whether the families' long-running legal case against the Middle Eastern country can move to trial.
Almost 3,000 people were killed on 11 September 2001 after hijackers seized four US passenger jets and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon, and a Pennsylvania field, following resistance from passengers.
The families allege that a Saudi government employee, Omar al-Bayoumi, knowingly supported two of the hijackers and that he was working with a network of officials linked to the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs.
Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.
The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.
The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead.
In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.
In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial.
Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision.
Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact – including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state – had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.
9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant".
"He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."
One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.
Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.
As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.
Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing.
"25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

bbc.com.title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.
The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.
US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.
The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan which brought the charges.
Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.
Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.
Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.
The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.
Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".
Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

bbc.com.title: 'House of Horrors': California couple accused of abusing surrogate-born children
bbc.com.text:
'House of Horrors': California couple accused of abusing surrogate-born children
A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness. The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
The Los Angeles District Attorney has described the mansion where the children were living as a "House of Horrors."
The BBC's Madeline Gerber breaks down the case and describes the inside of the mansion.

bbc.com.title: How toxic haze is causing Singapore’s landmarks to disappear
bbc.com.text:
How toxic haze is causing Singapore’s landmarks to disappear
Indonesia is facing one of its worst wildfires seasons, with around one million hectares of land burned so far this year.
In Singapore, iconic landmarks are being shrouded in toxic haze from the fires. The BBC’s Tessa Wong is there and breaks down how the wildfire smoke is impacting countries around South East Asia.

bbc.com.title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to medical care.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.
However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.
Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.
Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.
In a statement, advocacy group Dying with Dignity called the government's decision "profoundly disappointing".
"We anticipate that a very small number of individuals with severe and persistent mental illness would be eligible for Maid under this criterion, but their suffering is no less real than those who live with physical illnesses," said Helen Long, the group's CEO.
But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.
"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.
Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death".
Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that he anticipates a lengthy legal battle on the issue.
"People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said.
More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.
In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.
It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".
The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.
Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".
Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access, external to medically assisted death but that support falls when it comes to patients with mental illness alone.
- If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
- In Canada, support can be found at the Suicide Crisis Helpline by dialling 988

bbc.com.title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
bbc.com.text:
- Published
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.
It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.
The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.
And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.
Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.
"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.
Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.
Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".
Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.
Yaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.
In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.
"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.
A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".
"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."
Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.
He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.
Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.
Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later.
"It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."
At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister.
"You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"
Three years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.
Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign.
"We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."
Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.
But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.
We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.
Netanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.
A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".
Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.
For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.
Yaakov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides.
"There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."
The shadow of the attacks hangs over this election, dividing Israel once again along political lines.
For supporters, it confirms that Benjamin Netanyahu is still needed to keep Israel safe.
Critics say his political survival puts Israel at risk.

bbc.com.title: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and how did she survive?
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has woken up and begun speaking from her hospital bed almost a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers said.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.
Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.
As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.
Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, it is unclear whether she has any long-term health defects. Medical staff have been working to clear the drug from her body, a process that they expected to take about a week. She has been removed from a ventilator.
Zivot said Pike had been able to communicate in a "basic way", including by giving her name and making an incorrect attempt to guess the date.
Meanwhile she is reportedly handcuffed to her bed.
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike, though executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. Meanwhile, it has been announced that the state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee, the state governor, to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their plan to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?
While there is a lengthy history of botched executions across the US, Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived after receiving a lethal injection.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
