Among a smattering of white faces on Dunstable Road was a traffic warden, who declined to give their name but said: “I’ve always felt perfectly safe, and if ever there has been a minor incident, generally a member of the public or a shopkeeper has come to my aid.”
Joshua Bozier, 36, a homeless man, said: “To be honest, I feel safer here in Bury Park than in the town centre. I know everybody here, whereas I’ve been spat at and urinated on in the centre. I’ve lived all over and Luton’s not what it’s made out to be.”
He said Robinson “spilled a lot of shit”, but he did point to the past conduct of some Islamist activists in the area, who in 2009 demonstrated against the Royal Anglian regiment’s homecoming parade from Afghanistan.
Only a tiny proportion of the town’s Muslim community were involved, but the incident became a useful symbol for the far right.
Dr William Allchorn, an associate professor at Richmond American University and an expert on the far right, said the relationship between the EDL and the Islamist activists “was mutually reinforcing and for people looking for a European example of the supposed consequences of multiculturalism, Luton came with an unusually ready-made set of images, personalities and stories.
“A series of confrontations occurred at exactly the moment when a new anti-Muslim form of street politics was developing, and an unusually effective political entrepreneur in Tommy Robinson was able to turn those local events into a national and eventually international story.”
Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, accused Stephenson of pushing the same “rightwing nonsense” as Robinson. The police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, Labour’s John Tizard, wrote to the Tory MP to say: “These statements are not supported by evidence and bear a troubling resemblance to far-right agitators seeking to divide communities.”
Luton’s independent mayor, Javed Hussain, said he was baffled by Stephenson’s claims as he strolled through Bury Park, pointing out Christian, Sikh and Muslim places of worship and emphasising local regeneration.
“I’m at a loss to know why he is saying this because Luton is a very multicultural, diverse town, as well as very vibrant one, so it’s disheartening,” he said.
“Yes, in this area there may be a large number of people from an Asian background, but people from all over do travel here for all sorts of reasons, whether to shop or eat.”
Research by the council has also found that cohesion was strong enough for the town to avoid the fractures that led to violence in other English towns in the past, though there were warnings that more needed to be done, such as broadening cultural experiences for school pupils.
Not unsurprisingly, community relations are never far from the lips of local policymakers. While proud of the aspirational ethos among second- and third-generation British Asians in Luton, including his own family, Hussain said: “Look, if there was something I wish we could do more of, it would be to support children from council estates that are predominantly white. There is always more to do.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘That is a lie’: alleged Alan Jones victim denies family tried to get money out of broadcaster, court hears
theguardian.com.text:
An alleged teenage victim of Alan Jones has denied his family tried to deceive the broadcaster and get as much money out of him as they could during a tense cross-examination in a Sydney court.
Asked whether he was intent on getting as much financial assistance as he could from the former 2GB host, the witness replied: “That is a lie.”
The youngest complainant in the trial has told the court he was 17 when Jones allegedly put his tongue inside his mouth and touched him on the bottom during a visit to the shock jock’s property in the Southern Highlands.
Known as complainant A, the witness said he visited the Fitzroy Falls farm several years after he started corresponding with Jones at the age of 13.
He posted a letter to Jones asking for help after his father left, a family member died and his single mother was struggling financially.
Complainant A is one of five men who allege Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020.
The host has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.
Jones’s barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, has been cross-examining the young man for two days about the extent of his mother’s involvement in the hundreds of emails which were sent to Jones between 2013 and 2016.
The witness has accepted that his mother provided financial details and documents and made suggestions about what to write, but insisted the correspondence was largely his own work.
Bashir asked: “Were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails just signed off from [A] that your mother had input into?”
Complainant A replied: “No.”
Bashir said: “I suggest that you were - what do you say to that?”
A replied: “That you’re wrong.”
Bashir took the witness to a particular email and asked the witness if he agreed that he wanted Jones’s assistance with his mother’s mortgage.
The complainant repeatedly refused to agree, saying “I am not going to be railroaded” and “I am not going to have my words twisted, Ms Bashir”.
Bashir asked: “You understood your mother had the intention of obtaining as much assistance from Mr Jones as she could?”
A replied: “That is a lie.”
The terse exchanges between Bashir and the witness elicited several objections from prosecutor Georgina Wright, who on Wednesday said: “I object to this, your Honour. This is annoying.”
After hours of detailed questions about whether the complainant wrote a specific email about a contract more than a decade ago, Judge Glenn Walsh intervened.
“He can’t approve a contract; he is 14 years of age,” Walsh said.
The court heard one email Jones sent to A when he was 16 years of age said he had provided in excess of $100,000, “the cost is out of hand” and needs to come to an end. “Enough is enough,” he said.
The teenager replied to Jones that he and his mother could start making repayments to reimburse him. Jones wrote he did not expect to be repaid.
The incident left him scared for the consequences of pushing Jones away, he said. “I needed to be grateful, and being defiant is not being grateful and making a scene is not being grateful.”
The trial continues under Judge Walsh.
- Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial

theguardian.com.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
theguardian.com.text:
South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.
The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.
The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.
On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

theguardian.com.title: Jurors in Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial shown photo of alleged ‘execution-style’ gunshot wound
theguardian.com.text:
Marks made by a gun at close proximity were found on Jesse Baird after his decomposing body was discovered, a jury has heard.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Baird, his ex-partner, and the TV presenter’s new partner, Luke Davies.
The third week of his double murder trial has pivoted to how investigators found the new couple’s remains in rural NSW.
Crime scene officer Greg Moon, who coordinated a forensic sweep of the Greek monastery at Bungonia where the men’s bodies were found, continued giving evidence on Thursday about the condition of the remains.
Most of the family members of Baird and Davies have not been present in court for the grisly forensic evidence.
Closeup photographs of the gunshot wound sustained by Baird were shown to the jury, but not to people in the public gallery.
Moon walked the length of the jury box during his evidence to individually show each juror pinprick marks around the wound known as stippling, caused by particles coming out of a gun when it is fired.
The crown alleges Lamarre-Condon, now 31, killed Baird “execution-style” at close range.
However, the former officer’s barrister says Baird, 26, and Davies, 29, were killed in self-defence when they engaged the accused in two separate violent struggles.
Moon said examining the stippling can indicate the distance between the gun and its target.
“The closer the firearm is to the target, the stippling will be quite condensed around the gunshot wound,” Moon said.
“The only area I saw stippling was around that gunshot wound on the right temple.”
Justice Natalie Adams warned jurors on Thursday they would see confronting photos as part of their civic duty.
“Skin will be in a decomposed state … it’s not going to look what you think it’s going to look like,” the judge said.
The bodies were discovered inside two surfboard or standup paddleboard bags, with the smaller bag containing the body zipped up inside a larger one, Moon said.
He said the bodies were discovered one on top of the other with rocks and small branches placed on top.
Fellow investigator Christine Abela said she immediately knew something was amiss when she first arrived at the rural property more than a week after the two men were killed in the summer of 2024.
“There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday.
“The scent of a decomposing body.”
Abela detailed how investigators found concrete blocks, a gym weight and a cut padlock at Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly unsuccessfully attempted to sink the bodies in a dam.
Moon said there were multiple indicators that the remains had been at the monastery, about 20km away from the farm, for several days.
“A large number of maggots and other insects were present in the bags along with other decompositional fluids,” he said.
Lamarre-Condon’s efforts to clean up and dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies have come under scrutiny during the trial.
His barrister says the actions to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia, 200km south of Sydney, were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.
Earlier in the trial, jurors were shown CCTV of the alleged actions the senior constable took in the hours after the killings, including buying a second surfboard bag and hiring a larger second vehicle.
The footage, released by the court on Thursday, allegedly shows the heavily disguised Lamarre-Condon returning to the alleged murder scene laden down with cleaning products and a tarpaulin.
The 12-week trial continues.

theguardian.com.title: Teenager becomes first person to have testicular tissue transplant in UK
theguardian.com.text:
Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children.
The 19-year-old had his tissue removed and frozen three years ago before undergoing treatment for a serious blood disorder. He said he was “incredibly grateful” to the medical team behind the pioneering procedure, which represents a potential breakthrough for male fertility preservation.
Chemotherapy can permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm, leaving children who undergo it at risk of infertility in adulthood. Three years after his chemotherapy, tests showed he had no sperm in his semen.
Now a team of NHS medics in Edinburgh have transplanted his previously frozen testicular tissue back into his body, in the hope that it will begin to produce sperm.
The operation is the first of its kind in the UK, and only the second reported to have taken place worldwide. “Fertility is something I’ve struggled with personally for a long time,” said the patient, who asked to remain anonymous.
“I’ve always wanted to have children of my own but at some point, I found myself starting to slowly accept that that might never be possible for me. Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future.”
The student added: “We don’t know yet whether it will work, but knowing that there is now even a possibility means more to me than I can really put into words.
“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone for giving me this opportunity and for all the work that has made it possible. I also hope that being part of this research means that, in the future, other young people in the same position can have that hope too.”
Freezing semen is an established fertility preservation method for older teenagers and adult men.
But for pre-pubescent boys this is not an option. The new treatment potentially opens a door to fertility preservation for children needing cancer care and other treatments which require the use of chemotherapy.
The tissue taken for transplant contains spermatogonial stem cells, which are responsible for producing sperm from puberty onwards.
Doctors should know in a matter of months whether the procedure, which took place in August, has enabled the 19-year-old to produce viable sperm.
The transplant, carried out by medics at NHS Lothian and backed by funding from Children with Cancer UK, follows a decade of research by the University of Edinburgh.
Rod Mitchell, professor of developmental endocrinology at Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair, and a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at NHS Lothian, said: “This is a big step towards helping boys facing treatments that damage their fertility to have children of their own.
“Ten years ago, we started our research programme to freeze and store pieces of testicle from boys before they start chemotherapy, to preserve their fertility.
“We are beginning to see some of these young men return to explore their fertility options. This study offers real hope for future fertility in boys facing cancer treatment.”
Tracey Gillies, the medical director at NHS Lothian, said the operation was a “landmark procedure” and marked an important step forward for children whose fertility may be affected by treatment they needed to overcome serious illness.
She added: “We are grateful to the patient and his family for helping advance research that could transform care for others in the future.”
In May, the Guardian reported how a man whose testicular tissue was frozen before he had chemotherapy as a child and retransplanted 16 years later had been able to produce sperm.
More than 1,200 patients in the UK and 3,100 worldwide had had testicular tissue stored for potential future use, the University of Edinburgh said.

theguardian.com.title: Sardinian village where more women reach 100 may be new centenarian ‘blue zone’
theguardian.com.text:
The secret to longevity is being a woman – specifically, a woman in one part of Sardinia. At least, that is the conclusion of a study on centenarians in a tiny mountain village on the Italian island.
Sardinia became known as a haven for longevity, especially for long-lived men, in 1999 when a cluster of remote villages nestled in the slopes of its central and eastern provinces were classified among the world’s five “blue zones” – geographic areas with high concentrations of centenarians.
Now Bolotana, located in the Margine area of central Sardinia about 70 miles (110km) from the island’s original blue zone, has emerged as a new potential candidate, researchers say, generating centenarians every year in a trend driven by women.
A study by professors at Sardinia’s University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham in the US, published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Aging, found that 13.8% of women in the village who reach the age of 70 will live to 100 – placing it second in the world for female longevity after Hong Kong.
In Italy, where the number of centenarians has more than doubled since 2009, 3.5% of women who make it to 70 will achieve the milestone.
The researchers analysed records of people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925 and found that 38 had lived beyond 100, putting their longevity rate at 57% higher than the Italian national average.
The study began in 2024 and as of last year there were 12 centenarians among a population of 2,266 in Bolotana – roughly 12 times the Sardinian average.
Six have since died and the six who are left are all women, the two eldest being 102. More residents are expected to reach the milestone age by the end of this year and during 2027.
The findings also showed that, compared with the world’s other four blue zones – Okinawa in Japan, the Nicoya peninsula in Costa Rica, Ikaria in Greece and Loma Linda in California in the US – Sardinia’s zone was expanding.
“The important thing is that, for the first time in more than 25 years, we have found a place for longevity outside of the conventional blue zone [in Sardinia],” Giovanni Mario Pes, the study’s lead scientist and a co-creator of the blue zone concept, told the Guardian.
“But while Bolotana shares the same characteristics, it is even more exceptional. Whereas the original zone had an unusual balance between the two sexes, here female longevity prevails.”
Pes said that while it was already well established that women lived longer for biological reasons, “the extraordinary thing is that the longevity of the women in Bolotana is three times higher than that of most western women”.
Pes, a Sardinian whose great-grandfather lived to 110 and whose mother is 101, declined to be drawn into hypothesising over the secrets to the village’s longevity, saying the study was “limited to pointing out the existence of the phenomenon”.
However, after spending time with sprightly centenarian women there, he said what struck him most were the “very intense and very real social relations” maintained throughout their lives.
He gave the example of Giovanna Marras, 101, who lives with her sister. “They live together, they cook together, they talk to each other easily,” said Pes. “There was absolutely no sign of cognitive decline.”
Francesco Manconi, the mayor of Bolotana, offered some theories. “I’m not a scientist but it’s probably a mix of things,” he told Corriere della Sera, citing a clean, fresh diet, although he said nobody renounced seada, a traditional local pastry filled with cheese, or mustazzolus, a spiced biscuit often eaten at breakfast.
The “uncontaminated nature” surrounding the village could also play a role, Manconi added, as well as physical activity, despite Bolotana not having a gym. “Elderly people have always walked a lot … as much as 20km [a] day. And I would say they were mostly women.”
As of November 2025, official statistics showed there were 23,548 residents in Italy who were aged 100 or over, up 2,000 from the previous year. Of those eclipsing a century last year, 82.6% were women.
Women also take the lead among Italy’s 724 semi-supercentenarians, who people aged 105 and over – and among the 19 supercentenarians, those in the 110-plus age bracket.

theguardian.com.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
theguardian.com.text:
Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.
Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.
The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.
Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.
Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%
The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

theguardian.com.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
theguardian.com.text:
The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.
“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.
Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.
The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.
The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic Youth.
Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

theguardian.com.title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America,” and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/ Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of Republican governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

theguardian.com.title: Trump repeats his false claim that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego – as it happened
theguardian.com.text:
Trump repeats his false claim that Iran, which has no nuclear weapons, could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego
Near the end of his speech in San Antonio on Wednesday, which has just concluded, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that the war he started with Iran in February was necessary to prevent Iran from destroying American cities like Los Angeles or San Diego in a nuclear attack.
“I am ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said. “We had no choice because we can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.”
What the president did not say is that US intelligence agencies wrote in March 2025, in an annual threat assessment provided to Congress, that Iran abandoned its pursuit of nuclear weapons more than two decades ago.
“We continue to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and that [Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei has not reauthorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003, though pressure has probably built on him to do so,” the intelligence community reported last year. Three months later, in June 2025 , Trump ordered US military strikes on Iran’s main nuclear-enrichment facility, which, he said, had been “obliterated”.
Still, on Wednesday, Trump repeated his claim that the war on Iran he launched in February of this year with Israel had been necessary to stop Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems?” Trump said in Texas on Wednesday. “And I said it the other day, ‘let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles’ … You want to see some bad things happen? You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”
“We’re not going to let that happen,” the president said of the supposed threat from a country that has not had a nuclear weapons program for 23 years and has no missiles capable of reaching any part of the US. “We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen,” Trump said. “And they’d use it, too. They’d use it. They would use it.”
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
In remarks in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump tried to channel the anti-Muslim racism that helped get him elected in 2016, by skipping straight from a dire warning that Iran would use a nuclear weapon if it had one to the wild, false claim that Barack Obama could have stopped the Ft Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, but chose not to.
Trump repeated his false claim that the war he started with Iran in February was necessary to prevent Iran from destroying American cities like Los Angeles or San Diego in a nuclear attack. In fact, US intelligence agencies assessed in 2025 that Iran had abandoned its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.
Trump’s midterm rally speech was disrupted up to a dozen times by protesters.
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda.
Trump stokes anti-Muslim racism with false accusation that Obama chose not to stop Ft Hood gunman Nidal Hasan
In his remarks in San Antonio, Texas earlier on Wednesday night, Donald Trump tried to channel the anti-Muslim racism that helped get him elected in 2016, by skipping straight from a dire warning that Iran would use a nuclear weapon if it had one to the wild, false claim that Barack Obama could have stopped the Ft Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, but chose not to.
“We also recently announced that we’re going to deliver final justice to an evil killer, the Ft Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan, who murdered 14 innocent souls and wounded dozens more here in Texas, yelling ‘Allah Akbar’, ‘Allah Akbar’ while he was doing it,” Trump said of the Army psychiatrist who killed 12 soldiers and a retired guardsman in a gun attack in 2009.
“And we just found out,” Trump added, falsely, “that President Obama had the emails from Hasan to a known terrorist murderer, well-known, saying he was going to wage jihad against his fellow soldiers. But Obama and his group did nothing about it.”
As Trump made this false charge, his supporters jeered loudly.
In fact, as was widely reported in 2009, US intelligence agencies did intercept over a dozen messages Hasan sent to Anwar al-Awlaki, a cleric at a mosque in suburban Virginia where Hasan worshiped. But some of those messages were gathered in 2008 before Obama was president, and there has never been any indication that the messages indicated plans for an attack, as Trump claimed, or that either president George W Bush or Barack Obama was ever briefed on them.
According to a study of the messages published in 2018 by the program on extremism at George Washington University, Awlaki only replied to two of Hasan’s messages, sent to him through his website, and the subject of both was an essay contest Hasan wanted to establish. Awlaki never answered any of Hasan’s questions about Islam, the GWU researcher Katharine Poppe reported.
Trump announces that Presidential Medal of Freedom for Roger Clemens, baseball pitcher dogged by doping allegations
Near the end of his speech at a midterm campaign rally for Republicans in San Antonio, Texas on Wednesday, Donald Trump announced that he was awarding the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Roger Clemens, who retired as one of the greatest pitchers in Major League Baseball history, but has been denied admission to the Hall of Fame because of allegations that he used performance-enhancing drugs.
Clemens, who had introduced Trump, thanked the president for the award, but made no comment on the doping allegations that have dogged him since he was named as a steroid user by George Mitchell, a former US senator. The allegations against Clemens, who has always denied drug use, were based on the testimony of his former trainer, Brian McNamee, who said he repeatedly injected Clemens with steroids and human growth hormone.
When Clemens repeated those denials at a Congressional hearing in 2008, he was charged with perjury and obstruction of Congress by the federal government before eventually being acquitted by a jury in 2012.
“It’s a ridiculous thing that you’re not in the Hall of Fame with that kind of a record,” Trump said of Clemens. “And by the way, people talk drugs: he never admitted to anything,” the president said. “He never admitted to anything. He’s just a physical monster, okay?”
Trump repeats his false claim that Iran, which has no nuclear weapons, could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego
Near the end of his speech in San Antonio on Wednesday, which has just concluded, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that the war he started with Iran in February was necessary to prevent Iran from destroying American cities like Los Angeles or San Diego in a nuclear attack.
“I am ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said. “We had no choice because we can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.”
What the president did not say is that US intelligence agencies wrote in March 2025, in an annual threat assessment provided to Congress, that Iran abandoned its pursuit of nuclear weapons more than two decades ago.
“We continue to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and that [Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei has not reauthorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003, though pressure has probably built on him to do so,” the intelligence community reported last year. Three months later, in June 2025 , Trump ordered US military strikes on Iran’s main nuclear-enrichment facility, which, he said, had been “obliterated”.
Still, on Wednesday, Trump repeated his claim that the war on Iran he launched in February of this year with Israel had been necessary to stop Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems?” Trump said in Texas on Wednesday. “And I said it the other day, ‘let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles’ … You want to see some bad things happen? You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”
“We’re not going to let that happen,” the president said of the supposed threat from a country that has not had a nuclear weapons program for 23 years and has no missiles capable of reaching any part of the US. “We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen,” Trump said. “And they’d use it, too. They’d use it. They would use it.”
Trump vents anger at Texas Democrat Henry Cuellar for not becoming a Republican after he pardoned congressman accused of bribery
At the Republican midterm campaign rally in San Antonio, Donald Trump just vented his rage at Henry Cuellar, a Texas Democratic congressman he pardoned last year, for not switching parties.
Trump claimed that he had made no deal with Cuellar before he signed a pardon that ended the federal government’s effort to jail the congressman and his wife on a dozen charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy.
However, the president clearly indicated that he had expected the congressman to become a Republican out of gratitude.
“So many considered this to be a tremendous act of disloyalty, and certainly showed him to be an extremely ungrateful kind of a person,” Trump said.
Urging voters to defeat Cuellar by voting for his Republican challenger, Trump said: “We’ll call that payback for a disloyal, ungrateful person. A person whose life has been saved only to go back into the clutches of the people that tried to destroy him. So Henry Cuellar is a guy who is considered low-life in Congress, not respected, and right now should be serving a long term prison sentence with his wife and a top level penitentiary.”
Trump repeats false claims of booming US economy and invented investment figure, ignoring inflation and spiking fuel prices
In his speech to supporters in San Antonio, Texas, which is still in progress, Donald Trump has been repeating the same false claims about the US economy he has made again and again in recent weeks.
Ignoring soaring inflation and fuel prices exacerbated by the war he started with Iran and has been unable to stop, Trump repeated his entirely imaginary claim that he has already secured $21tn in foreign direct investment in the US since returning to office lat year.
In fact, as CNN reported last month, federal data shows that new foreign direct investment in the US was about $232bn in 2025, and Trump appears to be “counting trillions in vague investment pledges – pledges that were about “bilateral trade” or “economic exchange” rather than investment in the US – and “vague statements that didn’t even rise to the level of pledges.”
Trump also repeated his false claim that tariff revenues have swelled federal coffers so much under his administration that he was able to pay a $1,776 bonus to military service members and would also cover the $5,000 checks to all US adults he is promising voters if they keep Republicans in the majority in the House and Senate.
The $1,776 payments to troops that Trump first announced in December, which he said would be paid for by tariff revenues, were not funded by the import taxes Trump imposed. As the Associated Press reported at the time, the money was actually drawn from a congressionally-approved housing supplement – money service members were already set to receive.
Trump rally speech in San Antonio interrupted by multiple protesters as he repeats lie about Talarico
Donald Trump’s midterm rally speech in San Antonio, Texas has been disrupted by protesters at least six times so far.
Television coverage of the rally showed that one of the protesters was violently assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he attempted to leave the arena.
“You know, many of these protesters are paid,” Trump said, repeating a baseless claim he has been making for a decade. “These are paid protesters. They’re paid by enemies of our nation. Now, I’m telling you, they pay them for this.”
The interruptions seemed to momentarily derail the president as he repeated a lie about James Talarico, the Texas Democrat he claims is a vegan who only pretends to eat meat and secretly vomits every time he does. There is no evidence for this imaginary tale the president has repeated multiple times in recent weeks as Talarico has pulled ahead of the Trump-backed Republican candidate for the US Senate, Ken Paxton.
Trump began his riff with the rare admission that he has been mispronouncing the word vegan, as “vaygan”.
“He is a fake,” Trump said of the Democrat. “He’s a vegan. You know, my wife told me, ‘Sir, do me a favor. You have to do me just a little bit of a favor. It’s not vaygan; it’s vegan.’”
As the president told this story about being asked to pronounce the word correctly, he appeared to get confused about who, exactly, had corrected him. Trump does not usually refer to his wife calling him “sir”. Moments later he said that the person who made this request of him was a man.
“I don’t know about that stuff. I’m not into it. And he said: ‘It’s vegan! Please pronounce that word properly. I called it, vaygan, vaygan. I thought it – how the hell would I know? I like steak.”
Trump showers praise on 'fantastic' Ken Paxton, the Texas Senate candidate caught on audio calling Trump a drag on his campaign
After as brief introduction from Roger Clemens, the disgraced former baseball star accused in a high-profile report of using performance-enhancing drugs, Donald Trump has taken the stage at a midterm campaign rally for Republicans at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, Texas.
The president began by attacking the Texas Democrat James Talarico, using the nickname “Talafreako”, which the candidate has put on campaign merchandise.
Trump then praised Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general who is running for US Senate against Talarico, as “probably the greatest attorney general in the history of the state of Texas. He is tough. And he was with us all the way. And so I just want to thank him. He’s a fantastic – he’s a fantastic man and what a job he’s done.”
Trump made no mention of the fact that Paxton was recently caught on audio revealing that he considers Trump’s unpopular war on Iran, and the resulting high gas prices, a drag on his campaign.
Trump lashes out at 'ungrateful' Texas Democrat he pardoned for not becoming a Republican
We are now waiting for Donald Trump to arrive at a Republican campaign rally at Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, Texas, where the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton finished speaking 30 minutes ago.
Moments before Air Force One touched down at Kelly Field in San Antonio, Trump fired off a lengthy diatribe attacking Texas congressman Henry Cuellar, a Democrat he pardoned last year, attacking him as “ungrateful” for not becoming a Republican.
I did the pardons, and made no deal, where a crooked politician would have, but I thought there would be a good chance that Cuellar, who was persecuted by Democrats because they didn’t like him, would have routinely gone over to the Republican Party — The people that saved him from years in prison. Shockingly, Cuellar announced, only a few days later, that he is going to remain a Dumocrat. Many considered this to be a tremendous act of disloyalty, and certainly, showed him to be an extremely ungrateful person … Henry Cuellar is a LOSER who, right now, should be serving a longterm jail sentence with his wife in a top level penitentiary.
Federal lawsuit from Democrats says eight more pro-Trump ads are ready to air, including attacks on Biden and Obama
The federal lawsuit Democrats filed on Wednesday to stop the Trump administration from using millions of taxpayer dollars to air a series of pro-Trump ads includes details of another eight ads that have already been prepared for broadcast – all of which celebrate Donald Trump, and appear to violate a federal ban on the use of public money for “self-aggrandizement” or “purely partisan” messaging from the government.
The Democratic National Committee says in the suit that “there are at least 13 campaign-style political ads in a Dropbox account controlled by LMD Agency Inc, the government contractor bringing the ads to air”. Each ad in the Dropbox account includes on-screen text saying that the ad celebrating Trump in the run-up to midterm elections his party is in danger of losing was “Paid for by the U.S. Government”.
In addition to the five pro-Trump already broadcast since last month, the suit describes another four in detail:
An ad titled “UFC 250”, which celebrates the fights staged at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.
An ad titled “King of the Jungle”, which shows a lion hunting in the wild and disparages Trump’s political enemies, including former president Barack Obama and other Democrats. In February, Trump shared a racist video on social media that portrayed him as a lion and Obama and his wife, Michelle, as apes.
An ad titled “Resilience”, which includes images of Trump announcing his candidacy for the presidency in 2015; his mugshot from Fulton county, Georgia, in 2023, when he was charged with racketeering and a conspiracy to overturn the results of the 2020 election in the state; video of the assassination attempt on him during the 2024 election campaign.
An ad titled “God Made Trump”, a fan-created hymn of praise to Trump that was shown during the Republican midterm convention.
According to CNN, which gained access to the Dropbox last week, another ad in the series features attacks on Joe Biden, including the mocking image of the former president as an autopen installed by Trump on an exterior wall of the White House.
Democrats sue Trump administration, asking judge to declare Trump ads paid for with taxpayer dollars illegal propaganda
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda.
The ads promoting Donald Trump, including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
After a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote the president during the final month of the midterm campaign season, the president claimed on Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super PAC he controls to pay for the ads instead. The next day, however, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating the military intervention in Venezuela ordered by Trump, that new ad was also paid for by the public.
The DNC complaint, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges that the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”.
The complaint gets right to the point in its opening lines:
The Trump administration is using taxpayer dollars to air political advertisements, a blatant violation of the statutory ban on the use of appropriations for ‘publicity or propaganda purposes’. President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
The suit also notes, as the Guardian reported last month, that the first ad in the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called ‘Fifa peace prize,’ to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”.
The text of the complaint also references new polling from Reuters/Ipsos released on Tuesday which found that an overwhelming majority of Americans, 86%, called it inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election. The survey reported that 80% of Republicans called the ads inappropriate, with only 17% of the president’s party approving of them.
According to the suit, the ads have been broadcast on ABC, NBC, MS Now, CBS, CNN, Fox News and Newsmax and appeared during a variety of programs, including popular NFL and college football games, and news and entertainment shows on which the president has been criticized, including Meet the Press, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and Saturday Night Live.
Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November”.
“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he added.
In a speech heavy on symbolism and historic reference, Marco Rubio urged Europe from the rugged hill where democracy was first experienced in Athens to remain faithful to the traditions that have kept the west alive.
With the Acropolis behind him, illuminated by the last light of day, the US secretary of state called for a renewal of the western spirit.
“Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he said before a crowd of politicians and diplomats gathered at the ancient Pnyx hill, where popular assemblies first met. “The course we take will determine whether the west maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.”
In echoes of the blistering speech JD Vance gave at the Munich security conference last year, Rubio reminded his audience that the Trump administration had decided to “choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power”.
He added: “It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the ‘global community’ over one’s own people. And I think here, too, we have much more to learn from the men of ancient Greece. They knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else. Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.”
Greek security services pulled out “all the stops” to ensure that the speech could go ahead, the Guardian has learned. For the duration of the two-night stopover, Athens has been thrown into enforced lockdown amid draconian security measures, with rallies and large gatherings banned.
Rubio, widely seen as a leading contender in the Republican nomination to succeed Trump in 2028, insisted he be given the opportunity between leading the sixth round of US-Greece strategic dialogue – talks that saw several significant cooperation agreements signed – and meeting the Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, this evening.
Applause for the address was far from rousing, however, with leftwing opposition MPs and media going so far as to call it “provocative” and accusing the center-right government of pandering to the Trump administration.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, has slammed the Trump administration’s move to block the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) from observing the midterm elections.
This will mark the first time in more than 20 years that the group, the world’s largest regional security organization, would not be present to monitor the elections in the US.
“The Trump Administration’s failure to continue this practice is yet another step that risks undermining public trust in America’s safe and secure election system,” Shaheen said.
A reminder that monitors do not interfere with the voting process itself, but observe it.
“I was an official election monitor in the country of Georgia in 2012 and most recently in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022, so I know first-hand the importance of showing up for allies and partners to improve the public’s confidence in election integrity,” said Shaheen, an outgoing senator from New Hampshire who is also the top Democrat on the foreign relations committe.
Russia and Belarus are the only other countries who have excluded OSCE observers in nationwide elections.
The move comes as Trump’s justice department has pledged to send 1,000 election monitors to polling sites across the country in November. In response, the NAACP filed a lawsuit to block the administration’s effort, noting that their presence could “interfere with the right of voters to participate in the election free from intimidation”.
Donald Trump said he has “no regrets at all” about endorsing Ken Paxton in the Senate race in Texas, after the Republican nominee reportedly complained about the impact of the Iran war and high gas prices on his precarious performance. According to an audio recording obtained by Axios, Paxton can be heard responding to questions about the main issues affecting his race at a fundraiser in Washington DC. “It’s not tariffs,” he said. “It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel.” A number of polls have Paxton, also the Texas attorney general, trailing his Democratic rival, James Talarico, as Republican groups spend tens of millions of dollars to support his election bid.
Meanwhile, the president is on his way toSan Antonio, Texas, where he’s set to hold another campaign rally to drum up support for Paxton. This is Trump’s second visit to Texas in the past week. He’s set to speak at 7pm ET.
Trumpalsosaid today that he would “immediately” fire his political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair “if there’s a conflict,” following a New York Times report that the two political operatives visited the Russian-aligned Bosnian territory of Republika Srpska. In a Truth Social post, Trump noted that the two operatives “do not work for me, other than as outside consultants”, adding they are allowed to do “work for others, just like all consultant”. LaCivita was formerly a senior adviser on the president’s 2024 campaign, and Blair was formerly a White House adviser who took a temporary leave of absence to head up Maga Inc – the Trump-aliged Super Pac.
Mike Rogers– the Republican nominee for the open US Senate seat in Michigan –is trying to show a bit of daylight between his platform and the Trump administration’s trade war with the state’s neighbor, Canada. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy,” Rogers, a former congressman, says while perched at a sports bar drinking a Canadian beer. “We need to end this tariff war – now.” In the Oval Office, Trump, said he viewed the ad “as though [Rogers] wanted Canada to make a deal”, before launching into a familiar rant about how the country has been “ripping off” the US for “many, many years”.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) investigated hundreds of non-profit groups that helped people register to vote, according to internal government documents obtained by legal non-profit Democracy Forward. Dozens of groups, from across the country, were investigated. Some of these non-profits partner with larger groups, like Voto Latino – which focuses on voter registration and get-out-the-vote efforts for Hispanic and Latino citizens.
Trump again acknowledged the reporting that two of his top political advisers, Chris LaCivita and James Blair, spent time in the Balkans last week, in the Russian-aligned Bosnian territory of Republika Srpska.
The New York Times reported that the pair were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars through a DC-based law firm, retained by the territory’s government. Earlier, Trump said he would “terminate” the operatives “if there’s conflict”.
However, as he left the White House for Texas, the president appeared more unfazed: “They’re allowed to do this. They have a lot of clients in this. I’m a client of theirs. They have a consulting firm, as all people in Washington do. That’s pretty common.”
Hegseth welcomes USS Abraham Lincoln crew back to US after record-breaking deployment
Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, welcomed back the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln back to the US in San Diego today.
A reminder, the aircraft carrier has been at sea for more than 300 days, after its deployment was extended in May, amid the ongoing Iran war.
“You responded from minute one, constant combat operations, which Iran never expected-the kind of fire and fury that you were able to bring off this flight deck, along with other incredible Americans,” Hegseth said. “The only reaction the American people and the American media should have is pride.”
However, time on the ship has been marked by controversy. According to Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy assignment – the longest continuous period at sea without a port call.
On Wednesday, Hegseth repeated his frequent critique of the media, and accused some members of the press of turning the record-breaking deployment into “some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.
Last week, Hegseth appeared to reference the mental health crisis on board while speaking to lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.
MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities. At the time, Hegseth dismissed reports about deteriorating conditions on board as “completely misrepresented”.
My colleague, Anna Betts, has been speaking to families of crew members ahead of the Lincoln’s return. You can read her full report here:
In the Oval Office, Trump dismissed any concerns about Mike Rogers’ recent campaign ad, where the Republican nominee for US Senate in Michigan calls to “end this tariff war – now”.
The spot appears to be another instance of Rogers trying to create daylight between his bid and the administration’s policies. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy,” he says in the ad.
Trump, however, said he “viewed it as though [Rogers] wanted Canada to make a deal”, before launching into a familiar rant about how the country has been “ripping off” the US for “many, many years”.
A reminder that trade talks broke down in August between the US and Canada – resulting in a flurry of reciprocal tariffs of up to 50% between the countries.

theguardian.com.title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites
theguardian.com.text:
OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.
Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.
OpenAI was contacted for comment.
An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.
The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.
OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.
During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.
“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.
Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”
Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.
The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.
“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”
The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.
“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.
“Best, OpenAI Security Team.”
Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.
“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.
“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”
Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.
The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.
“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.
“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”
Do you know more? Email josh.butler@theguardian.com

theguardian.com.title: Texas kills man in first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa Pike
theguardian.com.text:
A Texas man was put to death Wednesday in the first US execution since the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8.03pm after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative, at the state prison in Huntsville.
Howard’s lawyers sought to halt the execution, arguing to the Texas court of criminal appeals there were similar risks of executing Howard using the same lethal injection drug that was used on Pike. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and had complained her arms felt like they were going to explode as she was given the drug.
“Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps,” Howard’s attorneys argued.
The court denied the request for a stay and later denied a second attempt to stop the execution over the drug. The court denied both without elaboration. The US supreme court also denied a late appeal Wednesday evening without comment.
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more lethal injections scheduled after Howard. He is the 30th person executed nationwide in 2026.
Howard was found guilty of capital murder in 2001 for robbing a convenience store in Silsbee, a town north of Beaumont, and fatally shooting 42-year-old clerk Vickie Swartout.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to members of his victim’s family, who watched through a viewing window just feet from the death chamber.
“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said, shortly before the injection got underway. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.”
His legal team argued that, at the time of the crime, Howard was intellectually disabled and thus ineligible for the death penalty, as the supreme court ruled in 2002.
Pike regained consciousness on Tuesday. Her lawyers say she has pneumonia and is unable to move her arms.
Pike’s was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, and governor Bill Lee has barred any further lethal injections for the rest of the year. He has also ordered a probe into why Pike’s execution failed. Pike’s lawyers had previously argued her blood disorder would make a lethal injection painful. Speculation has also swirled over the quality of the pentobarbital.
“There is a similar risk,” Howard’s attorneys wrote in the Wednesday motion filed with Texas’s court of criminal appeals, “that Texas’s execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind.”
Last week, the fifth circuit court of appeals declined a request to stop Howard’s execution.
Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday morning.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

theguardian.com.title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
theguardian.com.text:
Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.
Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

theguardian.com.title: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time
theguardian.com.text:
Patricia Krenwinkel, a former Charles Manson follower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.
This is the third time that Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions and denied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.
Krenwinkel, who was 21 at the time of the 1969 killings, has been imprisoned longer than any other woman in California, and the parole board has repeatedly acknowledged her record of rehabilitation over 57 years in prison, concluding she would not in her elderly age be a danger to society.
She was convicted in 1971 for her role in the violent crime spree over two nights that claimed the lives of actor Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her four friends, and grocery owner Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. The killings were gruesome and became one of the most notorious crime stories in the US.
Krenwinkel was 19 years old when she “fell under Charles Manson’s control” and was exploited and psychologically abused by the cult leader, her attorneys have said.
“Reaching this moment has taken decades of hard, deliberate work to confront who she was, what she did, and the devastating harm she caused,” her longtime lawyer, Keith Wattley, said in a statement after the parole grant. “She fully accepts responsibility for her actions, everything she contributed to, and every life she destroyed in 1969. Pat does not excuse or minimize that harm.”
Over her decades in prison, Krenwinkel has had a clean disciplinary record, and nine consecutive psychological evaluations in the past 40 years have found her to be a low public safety risk, according to Wattley, who has represented Krenwinkel for 16 years. He said she has participated in extensive therapy and group counseling, earned a college degree and trained service dogs for people with disabilities.
“I have seen the depth of her remorse and the extraordinary work she has done to change her life. I firmly believe she is ready to return home,” Wattley added.
Debra Tate, Sharon Tate’s sister, has repeatedly objected to the release of Krenwinkel and other Manson followers.
When Newsom denied Krenwinkel parole in 2022, after the board first found her suitable for release, the governor acknowledged that she had been a “victim of Mr Manson’s abuse” and said she had “matured in prison and engaged in commendable rehabilitative efforts”. But he argued she had “not developed sufficient insight into the causative factors of her crime and her triggers for antisocial thinking” and was still dangerous.
When Newsom again denied her parole in 2025, he also acknowledged her “serious chronic medical conditions” had diminished her strength, but concluded she “must do additional work to deepen her insight before she can be safely released”.
The governor is required to consider her elderly age and that she committed the crime as a youth in his review of her case.
Krenwinkel’s attorneys and advocates have repeatedly argued the governor was caving to political pressures by denying parole to people convicted in high-profile cases. Newsom previously vetoed the release of Leslie van Houten, another former Manson follower, but an appeals court sided with her and granted her freedom in 2023. Newsom also faced scrutiny for overturning the parole grant of Sirhan Sirhan, convicted of assassinating Robert F Kennedy, even after two of Kennedy’s sons favored his release.
The push for Krenwinkel’s release comes at a time of growing concern about the increasing number of elderly people languishing in US prisons after decades of incarceration. Krenwinkel’s longtime friends from inside California’s women’s prison told the Guardian last year that she was a mentor and support system to others in the prison.
Wattley, founder of UnCommon Law, a non-profit organization that represents people at parole hearings, urged Newsom to “uphold the law” and approve Krenwinkel’s freedom: “The parole process exists because people can change, rehabilitation matters, and public safety must be grounded in evidence. Pat’s case raises a fundamental question: if three parole grants don’t lead to release, what is the point of this process?”
Spokespeople for Newsom did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Wednesday.

theguardian.com.title: Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach
theguardian.com.text:
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.
In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called on Europe to “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.
The highly produced speech contained a forceful rejection of the kind of globalist politics that Trump has blamed for America’s and Europe’s ills, including growing illegal immigration and the outsourcing of manufacturing. In it, Rubio warned that the western world was at an “inflection point” and defended America’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.
“The word nationalism became a dirty word, so we tore down our monuments,” Rubio said. “We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the country they would inherit.”
Now, he said, the western world had found itself at a crossroads, where it either must “maintain its place at the head of the world or [resign] itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline”.
“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice,” Rubio continued. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”
The speech comes as relations between the US and Europe are facing numerous strains, including the US war in Iran, Washington’s scattershot support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia, disputes inside Nato including Trump’s recent demands for sovereignty over Greenland, and a growing ideological divide being driven by powerful officials including the US vice-president, JD Vance.
The shift in the Trump administration’s use of national power has unsettled many European allies, who have continued to seek compromises in order to keep the Trump administration onside on major issues including support for Ukraine and economic cooperation through the European Union.
