theintercept.com.title: He Confessed to an Afghanistan War Murder. The U.S. Military Promptly Closed the Case.
theintercept.com.text:
In the spring of 2023, on a partly sunny day where the temperature flirted with 70 degrees, an Army veteran of the Afghanistan War walked into the unique Prairie-style police headquarters in Banning, California. In a private room in the detective bureau, the former specialist, who served with the storied 82nd Airborne Division, sat down with a special agent from the Army’s Criminal Investigation Division — better known as CID — to make a confession.
The veteran had served with roughly 20 mortarmen and scouts from a platoon in the 2nd Battalion, 508th Parachute Infantry Regiment assigned to Combat Outpost Ware in Afghanistan’s Arghandab River Valley in 2010. A lush land of grape groves and pomegranate orchards, towering sunflowers and marijuana plants, the Arghandab was crisscrossed by canals and was a flashpoint in Kandahar Province, the spiritual homeland of Afghanistan’s once and future rulers, the Taliban.
The soldiers from the 82nd Airborne played a cat-and-mouse game with the Taliban. America’s official policy was counterinsurgency, or COIN: a re-tread of a failed strategy of the Vietnam War that promised a kinder, gentler brand of warfare aimed at winning Afghan hearts and minds. But in the Arghandab Valley, the COIN of the realm was kinetic.
The Taliban seeded the orchards with improvised explosive devices set off by a foot on a pressure plate, a boot on a tripwire, or Taliban hands gripping a remote control. The Americans countered with overwhelming firepower: attack helicopters, armored gun trucks, and infantrymen toting M4 carbines. It was a “rough time for the unit,” another veteran of the platoon remembered. They saw a great deal of “contact,” engaging the Taliban more times than another unit member could recall.
But the former mortarman in Banning had come to talk about one particular incident that, more than a decade later, he could not forget.
The CID agent gave the veteran a “cleansing waiver of rights” to read and sign. It advised the veteran that he had the right to remain silent, that any statement he made could be used against him at trial, and that he was providing testimony “freely and voluntarily.” The veteran waived his rights and signed the document on March 28, 2023 at 1:31 p.m. He acknowledged, according to exclusive criminal investigation documents obtained by The Intercept, that he killed an unarmed man and wounded a woman. More than that, he said that he “needed to be held accountable for his actions.” He told CID that he had “committed a war crime.”
Twenty-five years ago, in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, an angry America went to war in Afghanistan. The conflict would become, by some counts, the longest in U.S. history, stretching across four presidential administrations. It ended where it started, with the Taliban in control of the country after a crushing 2021 defeat for the U.S. and the Afghan allies it propped up for two decades.
The U.S. lost around 2,400 troops in Afghanistan at a staggering cost of around $2.3 trillion. Afghans suffered far worse. In October 2001, President George W. Bush announced that “the oppressed people of Afghanistan will know the generosity of America.” But from almost the opening American salvo, they began dying at U.S. hands.
During just the first five months of the conflict, there were no fewer than 136 media reports of U.S. attacks that killed between 1,200 and 3,155 civilians. Year after year, U.S. and coalition airstrikes killed Afghans – sometimes scores of civilians, sometimes hundreds. The deaths continued to the war’s final moments when an August 2021 drone strike targeting a suspected terrorist in the country’s capital, Kabul, instead killed 10 civilians, seven of them children. More than 70,000 Afghan and Pakistani civilians are estimated to have died as a direct result of the war, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project.
While the carnage of the American air war garnered the biggest headlines, Afghans were also gunned down, again and again, by U.S. ground troops. Following a 2007 ambush, Marines killed 19 civilians and wounded 50. An initial investigation found the Marines used excessive force when they killed civilians after a suicide bombing. Later, the Americans were recast as victims. In 2010, a “kill team” from the Army’s 5th Stryker Brigade slew at least three civilians over four months and mutilated the dead for war trophies. Eleven of the 12 soldiers charged were convicted of crimes, but most were released from prison by the mid-2010s. Staff Sgt. Robert Bales massacred 16 Afghan civilians in 2012. A Special Forces A-Team was accused of killing close to 20 civilians in 2012 and 2013. The remains of 10 victims were later found buried outside their base. A U.S. investigation exonerated the Americans of any wrongdoing. Only one man was punished: Zikria Kandahari, the unit’s Afghan interpreter.
Pete Hegseth, now the self-styled Secretary of War, served with the Army National Guard in Afghanistan during that era. In Trump’s first term, when he was a Fox News personality, Hegseth lobbied on behalf of three men who were convicted or facing charges related to war crimes committed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Trump intervened in all three cases, granting two pardons and reversing a demotion.
During his confirmation hearing last year, Hegseth complained that “restrictive” rules of engagement had made it “difficult to actually do your job on the battlefield,” repeatedly recalling his own service. “I was the senior counter-insurgency instructor in Afghanistan. My job was to understand how the Taliban and Al Qaeda operated,” he explained. “They knew our rules of engagement, and when they were more restrictive, they took advantage of them.” He continued: “We don’t need burdensome rules of engagement that make it impossible for us to win these wars.”
But what the veteran in Banning described to CID agents was anything but burdensome.
In April or May — he couldn’t recall which — of 2010, that veteran said he was carrying an M4 carbine as his unit moved about 3 kilometers into the Arghandab and occupied an abandoned building at the edge of a village. When the Americans were attacked, they returned fire, killing a couple Taliban members.
The unit readied themselves, expecting the Taliban to regroup and mount another assault. The Americans intercepted a radio transmission. A translator told them that a single male militant on a motorcycle, transporting rocket-propelled grenades, was headed toward them, according to the documents. The unit’s chain of command authorized the use of force.
When a motorcycle rider came into view, a sniper took aim and fired off one round. He missed.
The respite for the motorcycle man was short-lived, however. About 500 feet away, close to 20 Americans raised their rifles.
An M4 carbine — a magazine-fed, gas-operated, air-cooled, shoulder-fired weapon — shoots lightweight bullets at extremely high speeds. In the spring of 2010, M855 5.56-mm bullets were de rigueur for U.S. forces. Fast with low mass, the rounds produce a tremendous amount of kinetic energy. When they slam into a human body, that energy is transmitted to the soft tissue of the victim creating a “wound channel” that causes massive blood loss.
The Banning mortarman fired off one round. Others from the unit opened up, too.
The motorcycle man never reached his destination. If someone was waiting for him to arrive on that spring day in 2010, they still are.
The Banning veteran and others walked up to the Afghan man and “witnessed a military aged male deceased with multiple gunshot wounds to the face and other areas of his body,” wrote the CID special agent, transcribing the mortarman’s testimony. “No RPG’s were present.”
Nobody knew how many rounds hit him, but the damage to the Afghan man’s body was so extensive that he was “unidentifiable,” according to another witness. The mutilation was so devastating that the Americans were unable to even collect his “biometrics”: fingerprints, iris scans, facial images.
The dead man, said the veteran, wasn’t alone. There was a wounded woman, too. He told the CID agent that the “woman was crawling on the ground.” There may also have been a baby or child present as well — CID’s redactions make it impossible to know for certain.
After the veteran made his confession, in late March 2023, Army criminal investigators started consulting U.S. sources. Despite detailed unit records for more than 100 notable incidents in April and May 2010, an Army historian could locate none for the killing of the motorcycle man.
When CID began interviewing unit members, the company commander — by then a lieutenant colonel — said the incident did not sound familiar to him. The unit’s first sergeant told CID that while he saw most “troops in contact” reports, he didn’t recollect the incident. He acknowledged that the details “sounded plausible.”
Others recalled the incident in detail but excused it. One soldier who never saw the motorcycle man before he was killed said, for example, that it “sounded like” the man handed off the RPG to someone before he was shot. Another former specialist — who by 2023 was a warrant officer — told CID that unit members “fired on the military age male on the motorcycle.” He also recalled that “a woman was on the motorcycle,” too. He told the Army investigators that it was “unfortunate that no RPGs were present” but believed “the incident was handled properly” since “they were authorized to fire from their command team.”
Having never even attempted to identify the Afghan man, the woman on the scene, or the possible child; having never sought out any evidence beyond the testimony of members of the unit; and despite a signed, sworn confession by one of the shooters, Army CID concluded — within six weeks — that there was not “probable cause to believe that any soldier committed the offense of murder.”
CID refused to make the special agent in charge of the case available for an interview. “Unfortunately, we are unable to support your request to interview DACID personnel involved,” Special Agent Mark Lunardi told The Intercept, before leaving his job. More than a year ago, after multiple follow-up requests for information, Thomas Hamilton of CID’s press office wrote: “I will get back to you as soon as I can.” He has, despite repeated follow-ups, failed to respond.
For more than a century, the U.S. military has shown a consistent disregard for civilian lives. It has repeatedly cast or misidentified ordinary people as enemies; failed to investigate civilian harm allegations; excused casualties as regrettable but unavoidable; and failed to prevent their recurrence or to hold troops accountable.
A 2020 study of post-9/11 civilian casualty incidents found most have gone uninvestigated. When they did come under official scrutiny, the “military too often relies solely on its internal records and sources —which can be flawed and incomplete — to assess civilian harm,” the Center for Civilians in Conflict and Columbia Law School’s Human Rights Institute reported.
These findings were bolstered by the groundbreaking work of the podcast “In the Dark.” Their 2024 investigation — a corollary to a reexamination of the 2005 killings of civilians in Haditha, Iraq — found U.S. troops had committed 781 possible war crimes in Afghanistan and Iraq that the U.S. military actually investigated. In at least 65 percent of cases analyzed by “In The Dark,” investigators didn’t believe that a crime had taken place — even in cases where perpetrators had, like the Banning veteran, confessed. The 2010 killing of the Afghan motorcycle man is, however, not one of the cases in their database.
In the 151 cases in which investigators found probable cause that a crime had occurred, that the rules of engagement had been violated, or that a use of force hadn’t been justified, true accountability was rare. While 572 alleged perpetrators were involved in these cases, only 130 were convicted; the records show they rarely received significant prison terms. Much more often, their cases were dealt with by commanders with broad discretion to punish their troops with extra duty, demotions, or reprimands, in lieu of formal prosecutions. Fewer than 1 in 5 perpetrators, investigators found, appeared to have been sentenced to any type of confinement. The median sentence was just eight months.
Todd Huntley, an active-duty Judge Advocate for more than 23 years who deployed to Afghanistan twice with a Joint Special Operations Task Force, believes killings like the one described by the Banning veteran were a common occurrence. “There were probably hundreds of incidents that were just like it that we’ll never know about,” he told The Intercept. A current government official, who was involved in the wars in the Greater Middle East, said the total could reach into the thousands.
Since taking the helm of the Pentagon last year, Hegseth has launched overlapping efforts to weaken transparency, scuttle accountability, hobble military justice, and undercut protections for civilians in conflict zones — from replacing the Pentagon press corps with pro-administration sycophants, and firing the top legal authorities of the Army and the Air Force, to pursuing changes that would encourage lawyers to approve more aggressive tactics and take a more lenient approach to those who violate the laws of war.
The Intercept has previously reported on Hegseth’s gutting of civilian harm mitigation and response efforts. In late April, Hegseth repeatedly dismissed congressional concerns about civilian harm and respect for the laws of war in testimony before the House Armed Services Committee. “The Department of War fights to win,” Hegseth replied when asked if he stood by his statement that the U.S. would afford enemies “no quarter” — a war crime. A recent report by the Pentagon’s top watchdog says cuts to civilian harm mitigation and response efforts have been so severe under Hegseth that the United States cannot adequately protect civilians in conflict zones. This was driven home at the outset of the Iran war when the U.S. attacked the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children.
The CID records of the motorcycle man investigation are redacted in ways that make it impossible to ascertain key facts about additional civilian harm. “An [REDACTED] woman was on the motorcycle with the military aged male and [REDACTED] from the engagement,” according to the summary of a statement by one unit member. The Banning veteran also “stated he [REDACTED] an unarmed [REDACTED] woman during his deployment.”
The redactions also prevented The Intercept from identifying the veteran and fellow unit members to gather additional information. “If it wasn’t for the soldier involved coming forward, this incident would never have come to light,” Huntley, now the director of the National Security Law Program at Georgetown University Law Center, told The Intercept. “The 13-year delay in reporting made any investigation difficult as others involved couldn’t remember details and the redactions in the report make it impossible to learn anything else about the incident.”
Only one member of the unit contacted by The Intercept agreed to speak about the incident. The veteran acknowledged, on background, that the incident occurred, but would not say if he was one of those interviewed by CID.
Still, the case of the motorcycle man offers a stark counter-narrative to Hegseth’s assertions about the war on terror — and the basis for his efforts to undermine protections for civilians today.
The rules of engagement in Afghanistan in 2010 were so lax that a man was killed for no reason and with no repercussions.
It was so unremarkable that no record of the engagement could be located. It was so commonplace that senior unit members couldn’t recall it.
It was so typical that only one man even thought to report it — and he waited 13 years.
It was so characteristic of U.S. military policy that no inquiry was conducted into the rules of engagement in force at the time.
And the incident was so in keeping with U.S. military tradition that, despite a murder confession and little question that an unarmed man was gunned down, Army CID and the 82nd Airborne’s chief of military justice quickly concluded there was no probable cause for charges, and the investigation was closed.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

lemonde.fr/en.title: Saudi Arabia says three dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Saudi authorities said Wednesday, October 7, that three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom's international airports, including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. The Iran-backed fighters earlier took responsibility for a flurry of attacks that included firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as the conflict deepens with Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
"On Tuesday and Wednesday...Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities," the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement. An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport and a Sudanese national was killed at the airport in Riyadh, the agency said, with 36 people wounded in the attacks.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it "destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform" used in the attack on Riyadh. In a subsequent statement the coalition directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate. "The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting [the two airports] will not go unpunished," it said on X.
The coalition said as a result it struck and destroyed 82 "legitimate military targets," including Houthi mountain-based ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centers, communication systems and Houthi gathering sites. The Yemeni group, which controls most of the country's northwest, is battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and it captured swathes of coastal land.
The fighting has displaced more than 200,000 people within the country, the United Nations said Wednesday. Yemen's internationally recognized government this week declared a major counter-offensive and claims to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by Agence France-Presse (AFP) have not reported any major changes on the ground. Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
Flight diverted
"Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God's grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday on X.
The Saudi-led coalition said the missile was intercepted. The Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in Aden, the interim capital for Yemen's government.
The government's Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport. The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia's Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, spokesman Saree said, claiming they had "hit their targets accurately." It is the second time this week Houthis claimed to have attacked Riyadh's main airport.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Egypt charges six journalists with terrorism offenses
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Egyptian prosecutors accused six journalists from an independent fact-checking platform on Wednesday, October 7, of terrorism-related offenses, alleging they worked for the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and received foreign funding to spread "false news." The journalists, who make up the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, were arrested during raids across several governorates on September 28 and 29, according to the outlet's management and rights groups. Matsadaash, whose name means "Don't Believe It" in Arabic, has operated since 2018 and often investigates statements by officials and state bodies.
The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), which represents the journalists, said they had reported torture following their arrests, allegations denied by the Interior Ministry. In a statement on Wednesday, prosecutors said the case stemmed from investigations into activities by Brotherhood leaders abroad. They alleged those leaders had directed members to create online platforms to spread "rumors and false news and statements," undermine confidence in state institutions and incite people to take part in demonstrations.
The statement identified Matsadaash as "one of the group's media platforms" operated from abroad. Investigators also alleged the defendants received "monthly funding" in foreign currencies through transfers from a company owned by a Brotherhood member living overseas. According to the prosecution, one defendant admitted that he and the others had been instructed to publish "false news about state institutions and their officials in preparation for bringing them down." Another defendant allegedly admitted the platform was used to "highlight shortcomings" by state officials in a way that fuels public discontent.
Prosecutors said an examination of two journalists' social media accounts found posts "supporting the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood group." Matsadaash and its co-founder, Abdelrahman Mansour, a prominent activist from Egypt's 2011 uprising now based in New York, deny the allegations. The Muslim Brotherhood was banned in Egypt in 2013 following the overthrow of late Islamist president Mohamed Morsi.
A conviction on charges of belonging to the group can carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment. The arrests have drawn condemnation from dozens of rights and press freedom groups, who have called for the journalists' release. Egypt, which has long faced criticism over restrictions on media activity, is now holding 26 journalists in connection with their work following the latest arrests, according to EIPR.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French high school protests: 'Young people are not fooled by the discrimination and contempt that society directs at them'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
From the very beginning of the high school student movement that has been shaking France for the past two weeks, disparaging comments about the young people taking part have intensified. The government, for its part, dismissed the movement as nothing more than an issue of "urban violence."
What does this contempt for young people really mean? Could it be that they are a socially discriminated minority? Does something like "childism" exist, in the same way as "sexism" or "racism"? These are the questions raised by Laelia Benoit, child psychiatrist and sociologist at the Yale Child Study Center, affiliated with the French National Institute of Health and Medical Research (INSERM), and author of Infantisme ("Childism," 2023).
"Manipulated," "incoherent," "immature," "brainless": In your view, how do these recent remarks about high school protests reveal childism?
Childism is defined as a set of systematic prejudices and discrimination against minors (children and adolescents), simply because of their age. From the very beginning of this movement, all the usual mechanisms of childism appeared in certain political and media discourse, which we had already studied in relation to youth climate protests. One of the most common arguments is that these young people are being manipulated by forces beyond their control, especially political ones. Assuming that a high school student cannot think for themselves and that they are necessarily being used by adults, social media or political parties is first and foremost a way of denying them any ability to act politically.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'The Social Reckoning' by Aaron Sorkin dives into the toxic effects of Facebook and Instagram
lemonde.fr/en.text:
LE MONDE'S VERDICT – WHY NOT
Aaron Sorkin, 65, the writer behind The Social Reckoning, has undeniably been one of the most prominent American screenwriters in recent years. Series such as The West Wing (1999-2006), and to a lesser extent, The Newsroom (2012-2014), as well as films like The Social Network (David Fincher, 2010) and Moneyball (Bennett Miller, 2011) are all testament to his reputation.
A passionate commentator on sociopolitical issues and a master of dialogue that electrifies the action, Sorkin is a man of ideas and words, brilliant when other directors bring his scripts to life. Yet when he steps behind the camera himself, he tends to lose his footing. Molly's Game (2017), The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020) and Being the Ricardos (2021), though competent, have hardly made a major mark on cinema. These films, among others, serve as a reminder of the important distinction between scriptwriting and directing, especially at a time when, by reducing art to a slogan, style is too often sacrificed to subject matter.
And what a subject The Social Reckoning has! The film is adapted from a groundbreaking investigative series by American journalist Jeff Horwitz, who, drawing on files leaked by whistleblower Frances Haugen, showed in 2021 in the pages of the Wall Street Journal just how fully Facebook and Instagram executives, above all Mark Zuckerberg, understood the deeply toxic (mental, political, social) effects of their platforms' algorithms and content on users. And yet, the relentless pursuit of profit ultimately outweighed any moral concerns among the company's leadership.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Russian journalist Anna Politkovskaya believed that a society that accepts lies ends up accepting violence as well'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On October 7, Vladimir Putin celebrates his 74th birthday. That same day marks 20 years since the murder of journalist Anna Politkovskaya [1958-2006], who was executed in the entryway of her apartment building in Moscow. The gunman was waiting for her there; his accomplices had followed Anna all day and kept him informed of her movements.
For Anna Politkovskaya, a society that accepts lies ends up accepting violence as well. Her reports from Chechnya, written during and after the war, exposed the shocking propaganda and lies of the Russian occupying forces. She also denounced the relentless use of physical violence in an environment almost devoid of rights. She knew the risks she was taking, but she also knew how unacceptable it was to remain silent.
I remember how, in the Moscow newsroom of Novaya Gazeta, she would wait to see whether editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov would approve her latest article, whether she had gone too far for a newspaper that, as early as 2004, lived in constant fear of being shut down by the authorities. That was the situation, and yet it felt as if not everything was lost. Who could have imagined that, 20 years later, Putin would still be in power and waging a war that would cost hundreds of thousands of lives?
I met Anna after the end of the main phase of the Second Chechen War (1999-2000), the first conflict started by Putin. She traveled constantly to the Caucasus, referring to these trips as "work assignments": To her, this war was a disaster for all of Russia. She believed it had seeped into everyone's pores, and those who refused to conform were silenced.
My film Coca – the Dove from Chechnya (2005) showed how Chechen women, armed with a camera and a notepad, documented atrocities committed by the Russian army. They worked, in vain, to get an international court to convict the perpetrators, based on their painstaking research.
When I met her during those years, Anna was often accompanied by her Chechen friend, Zainap Gashaeva, a central figure in my film, who was born in Kazakhstan, where Stalin had deported the Chechen people. Both were women in the field. During those years, thousands of people vanished without a trace and never reappeared. The women I filmed showed me binders filled with photos of these missing people. Anna tried to retrace their fates and find those responsible. She acknowledged that the war had changed her, that she had become tougher, and she was more determined than ever.

lemonde.fr/en.title: How the Kremlin is orchestrating the takeover of Russian assets from Leroy Merlin, Auchan, Nestlé and FM Logistic
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Two weeks after the confiscation of the Russian assets of Leroy Merlin, Auchan, Nestlé and FM Logistic, Vladimir Putin played the innocent. "We are not taking anything from anyone, we are not stealing anything and we are not nationalizing anything," insisted the Russian president on Thursday, October 1, at the Valdai political forum, one of his annual meetings with Russian elites. No one in the room contradicted the Kremlin leader when he said the Western companies' assets could eventually be returned to their owners.
In practice, these assets, targeted by a Kremlin decree on September 17, as well as those of the German retail group Metro, which have also since been confiscated, have been placed "under temporary administration." They were taken over by an unknown Russian micro-enterprise, effectively a shell company that is expected to serve as an intermediary before the assets are acquired by groups close to the Kremlin.
At Valdai, Putin did not mention this at all. When asked whether these assets could return to their original owners in the event of a "favorable scenario" with Western countries, he replied, "Yes, they will get them back." However, he did not specify what he meant by this "favorable scenario," which could include an end to the war in Ukraine, a highly unlikely prospect. "All of this is just empty rhetoric. With the failure of peace negotiations and the likely electoral defeat of [Donald Trump's party] in November, Vladimir Putin now feels even freer. To intensify the war in Ukraine. And to seize European assets in Russia," warned a source in Moscow with close knowledge of the country's business circles.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Trump says he wants to turn Florida golf course into retreat 'for all future presidents'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday, October 7, that he wants to turn his luxury Florida golf course into a retreat for future presidents modeled on the historic Camp David getaway. The 80-year-old billionaire said that US security officials had suggested the plan to transform the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach into a sanctuary for his successors.
"Seems that all presidents play golf, and I was asked by Secret Service and the military," Trump – who is himself a huge golf fan – told reporters in the Oval Office. "It's only about two minutes away from the airport, so they literally would be at that site, and they could spend a weekend there – like a retreat, like sort of a Camp David retreat."
"And they asked if I'd be willing to do it, and I said I would be. This wouldn't be for me, this would be for all future presidents." Trump said there would be security advantages to the site, where gunman Ryan Routh tried to assassinate the then presidential candidate in September 2024. Routh was jailed for life earlier this year. "There are no high buildings looming over it. There are no houses on it," he said.
Trump already spends many winter weekends on the fairways at the club. It is a short drive from his opulent beachfront Mar-a-Lago residence, which he dubbed the "Winter White House" in his first term. Trump did not address whether US government money would go toward the plan for his club.
'Happens to be a highly-rated course'
But it is the latest in a series of projects in his second term that have seen Trump stamp his physical mark on the US presidency, while raising questions about where the funds come from. Trump is building a $400-million ballroom at the White House that he says is paid for by himself and private donors, though the costs for extra security features are being borne by US taxpayers.
The former property tycoon has also faced ethical questions about his decision to host this December's G20 summit at his Doral golf club near Miami. He was forced to give up a similar plan in his first term following a major backlash.
A White House official told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that the Trump property in West Palm Beach has all the "features that are necessary for any presidential retreat" and "happens to be a highly-rated golf course."
A lawyer representing the Trump course wrote to local officials in September, comparing the proposed retreat to Camp David, Windsor Castle in Britain and France's Elysee Palace, the Washington Post reported.
Trump is, however, not a fan of Camp David, having visited the presidential bolthole in the scenic Maryland hills near Washington on only a handful of occasions during his two terms in office. Other presidents have made frequent journeys and hosted historic foreign summits there, including when Jimmy Carter welcomed Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin in 1978 to sign the Camp David Accords.

lemonde.fr/en.title: In Gaza, after 20 years without elections, an uncertain vote
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In Gaza City, scarred by Israeli bombs that have erased its iconic towers, Assil al-Louh has no shortage of reasons to want elections. At 32, she has never been able to take part in one. The last national vote held in the Gaza Strip was in 2006, when Hamas claimed victory and then ruled the territory with an iron fist. The mother of three, who has a degree in information technology and is now unemployed, would like to see new Palestinian leaders emerge. "People need to change for mindsets to change," she told us by phone – the only way to reach Gaza's residents, as Israel has barred foreign media from entering for nearly three years.
But to vote now? She barely hesitates: "We are not ready." In Gaza, where more than 80% of buildings have been damaged, priorities lie elsewhere: finding drinking water, searching for food, protecting children from Israeli attacks. "There aren't even passable roads," al-Louh added. She has survived five Israeli offensives since 2008. The last one killed her 29-year-old brother in December 2024. Nearly 3 million Palestinians, including 1.24 million Gazans, are, in principle, being called to elect their Parliament on November 28.

lemonde.fr/en.title: In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman wants to bring the new left to city hall
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On the evening of June 2, after the primary in Los Angeles's mayoral election, Nithya Raman no longer seemed to believe she would make it through. The final results were not yet in, but the chances of advancing were fading for the 45-year-old Democratic candidate, who has served on the City Council of the United States' second-largest city since 2020.
Having entered the race late, on February 7, challenging the sitting mayor Karen Bass – also a Democrat – Raman appeared to be signaling the end of her campaign. In her speech, she thanked her team and her husband, screenwriter Vali Chandrasekaran, and mentioned her 10-year-old twins, praising their patience with a mother who, since their birth, "has always been running for something."
Then the tears came. Her voice trembling, she said she was fighting to make sure her city is "worthy of the children who live in it." This rare display of raw emotion from the otherwise disciplined, Harvard-educated and meticulously prepared candidate quickly made the rounds in the media and on social networks.
A few days later, the final results came in. Raman managed to clinch a spot in the runoff, behind the 73-year-old incumbent mayor. With 29% of the vote, she narrowly edged out Spencer Pratt, a Republican reality TV star who had stirred controversy with radical statements and provocative AI-generated videos. The runoff will be a contest between two Democrats – an unexpected scenario, especially since almost every incumbent mayor of Los Angeles has historically been reelected in the primary.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Brazil remains the last significant thorn in Washington's side in Latin America. But for how much longer?'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The timing is out of sync across the Americas. The United States is wondering how strong the Democratic wave will be in the midterm elections on November 3, while in the southern part of the continent, left-wing governments are being swept away one after another.
The results of the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 4, and the lead taken by Flavio Bolsonaro, one of the sons of Jair Bolsonaro, the latter dubbed the "Trump of the Tropics," must have been welcomed at the White House. Such occasions for celebration have become rare there.
The original model could now hope to see a major barrier lifted to implementing his doctrine for the "Western Hemisphere," meaning the Americas. Over the months, Chile, Peru, Bolivia and Colombia have all shifted to the right, following Argentina's lead, by embracing the themes and methods of Trumpism to varying degrees. After bringing Venezuela to heel in January with the removal of Nicolas Maduro – which allowed Washington to claim control of a significant portion of the world's leading oil reserves – Brazil remains the last significant thorn in Washington's side. But for how much longer?
A member of the BRICS group (now comprising 11 members representing the Global South) and a champion of multilateralism that resists empires, the Latin American giant stood up to Donald Trump by criticizing and condemning his counterpart, despite threats and the hammer of tariffs. Jair Bolsonaro took mimicry so far as to attempt to overturn the results of the last presidential election by force in January 2023. Imitation, as they say, is the sincerest form of flattery.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Thousands march ahead of Brazil election runoff: 'Never Again Bolsonaro'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Thousands of people joined a student march Wednesday, October 7, in downtown Rio de Janeiro to protest against election favorite Flavio Bolsonaro and the prospect of the far-right's return to power in Brazil, as the campaign for a runoff election swung into action. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out in front in Sunday's first-round election, sending shock waves through Brazil's left, which is scrambling to claw back votes ahead of an October 25 runoff.
With drums, fireworks and spirited chants, thousands of students spilled into downtown Rio de Janeiro declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and calling for votes for leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Protesters evoked life under Jair Bolsonaro, who was in office from 2019 to 2022 and is remembered for his government's handling of the Covid pandemic, which he dubbed a "little flu" and which claimed more than 700,000 lives in Brazil, the second-highest death toll in the world after the United States.
The march was strikingly more crowded and animated than Lula's rally at the same spot on Friday before the election, after a campaign many had criticized as lackluster.
Fears of social spending cuts
Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed sweeping budget cuts, using a pair of scissors to echo the chainsaw of libertarian Argentine President Javier Milei, whose economic reforms he has praised. Brazil is battling soaring public debt exacerbated by high interest rates, and the election result saw the Sao Paulo stock exchange rally to record highs.
Amid uncertainty over what cuts Flavio will make, protesters recalled those made by Jair Bolsonaro to federal universities, research scholarships and the government-subsidized Farmacia Popular program, which provides free or discounted medicines. Some protesters expressed concern about Flavio Bolsonaro's plans to seek amnesty for his father, currently serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his 2022 election loss. Several other pro-democracy rallies are planned in the coming days.
Campaign reset
Both Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula are shaking up their campaigns to prepare for the runoff. Flavio Bolsonaro has focused on building coalitions and doubled down on his plans to shrink the state and modernize the tax system. He also promised to use the right's new dominance in Congress to make constitutional reforms.
Lula, who at almost 81 years old is seeking a fourth term in office, has hit reset with a major focus on social media – where the right has long held the advantage – posting a video selfie on Wednesday for the first time. "Come on, folks, let's hit the streets; let's go talk to people," he said in the video posted to Instagram and TikTok.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French scientist Henri Kagan wins long-awaited Nobel Prize in Chemistry
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Better late than never. French chemist Henri Kagan, 95, finally received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday, October 7, together with Japanese scientist Kenso Soai, 76. Kagan, a professor at Paris-Saclay University, had narrowly missed the prize once before, in 2001, even though, at the time, he was already recognized as one of the pioneers in the field for which the honor was awarded: asymmetric catalysis.
"We are extremely happy. This corrects a historical injustice," said Jacques Maddaluno, an emeritus researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) and former director of its Institute of Chemistry. "He is a brilliant scientist, full of humanity and humility." "French chemistry is very fortunate," added Emmanuelle Schulz, director of the Institute of Molecular Chemistry and Materials of Orsay (ICMMO), which descends from a laboratory Kagan co-founded.
Asymmetric catalysis, Kagan and Soai's specialty, is one of the fields most frequently recognized by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences because it deals with a fundamental question: What shapes do molecules adopt in three-dimensional space, and how can those shapes be controlled? With five fingers and a palm, one can make either a left hand or a right hand, which are mirror images but cannot be superimposed. A right-handed glove does not fit the left hand. These are called chiral forms.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Evicted retiree, 87, who sparked Spain housing protests dies
lemonde.fr/en.text:
An 87-year-old Madrid woman whose eviction triggered nationwide protests over Spain's chronic housing crisis and a political debate that culminated in early elections died on Wednesday, October 7, a tenants' union said. "We are sorry to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement about Maricarmen Abascal, adding that her cause marked "a turning point in the history of this country."
Abascal became a symbol of Spain's housing market on September 23 when she was evicted from her life-long Madrid home on a stretcher after the real estate firm that owned the apartment drastically hiked the rent. Outrage at her eviction triggered national demonstrations, with hundreds of people camping in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square in the most symbolic of the protests.
The movement piled pressure on the minority leftist government to present urgent housing measures, including more restrictions on evictions and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts. But their rejection in parliament last week prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election for November 29 in which housing will feature prominently. "The housing debate is at the center, but the cost to get here has been too high," the tenants' union said of the election, originally due in 2027.
Abascal had been hospitalized with exhaustion after her eviction, but a deal had been reached with the company that owned her flat, allowing her to return home. "This solution has come too late. A totally avoidable situation after a torturous process," added the tenants' union.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French PM denies police were ordered to 'confront' student protesters
lemonde.fr/en.text:
French security forces do not have orders to "confront" protesting high school students, the prime minister said on Wednesday, October 7, as allegations of police brutality mounted following days of protests that have shaken the country.
Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the movement demanding better conditions in high schools began, and more than 6,500 people – mostly minors – have been arrested. After rights groups, unions and the students accused authorities of using disproportionate force, the government said it would suspend the use of stun grenades by police at student-led demonstrations.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said, in a televised address on Wednesday evening, that the country could not be "indifferent" to the concerns of high school students, acknowledging that the "anger of young people does not come from nowhere." He denied that security forces have "orders to confront" the young people, and promised the government would present a plan to respond to the crisis at the end of October.
Protests called for Thursday
Meanwhile, protest organizers urged fresh demonstrations on Thursday as several education unions called for new nationwide strikes. While most schools reopened on Wednesday, more than 500 remained at least partially closed, with students blocking doors with mounds of trash bins.
"We know that if we stop making our voices heard, the movement will lose momentum," said Marilou, a high school student in Fontainebleau, near Paris, who didn't want to share her full name. "We want real action, and until we get it, we'll keep mobilizing," she told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Student protestors have complained of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures. They have requested a meeting with Lecornu, saying they have costed proposals to present. "I want to urge students – both high school and university – to stay mobilized starting tomorrow. Because the balance of power is on our side," said student union leader Ryad Rani.
Stun grenades banned
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told the radio broadcaster RTL early on Wednesday that he had suspended the police use of stun grenades in response. "I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," said Nuñez. He stressed that this suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened."
Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged over that incident on Tuesday. Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Nuñez said.
Several lawyers representing teens taken into police custody say they have faced physical violence and insults. Ainoha Pascual, a lawyer representing three minors in Paris, said they had been "terrorized." "A very large majority arrive in custody injured," having taken baton blows or being dragged on the ground, she added.
Multiple crises
In Wednesday's address, Lecornu also promised to release diesel stocks in a bid to bring down fuel prices, and reiterated an aim to cut the country's soaring budget deficit to 5% of GDP next year.
The French government is wrestling with multiple crises including the protests and its 2027 budget, as well as a looming election next year to choose Macron's successor, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls.
"It took several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students," said Manuel Bompard, a hard-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader. The government has blamed LFI for stoking tensions around the protests.

lemonde.fr/en.title: What's in Le Pen's fiscal 'magic measures'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Can Marine Le Pen fit the circles of her presidential platform into the square of fiscal orthodoxy? The outcome of that highly challenging task could partly determine the result of the 2027 French presidential election, according to those close to her. On Tuesday, October 6, the far-right candidate presented her budgetary roadmap for the next five-year presidential term at a press conference at the luxurious new headquarters of her Rassemblement National (RN) party.
The form was more convincing than the substance. As usual with the French far right, the vast majority of her promised savings focused on three areas: the contribution to the European Union, alleged fraud, and foreigners. The calculations were based on optimistic economic assumptions. For the first time, Le Pen also promised significant cuts to the healthcare system, social housing and the number of civil servants.
The plan left economists wary and sparked a strong political backlash from both the right and the left. No presidential candidate had, until now, attempted such a transparent operation regarding their budgetary choices. And for good reason: The challenge exposes whoever takes it on to attacks. The RN willingly took on the risk. "For 2027, we cannot remain discreet about savings," said MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy, the close ally of Le Pen in charge of orchestrating this shadow budget. "It's a parachute, harness and seatbelt. If there's a debt crisis, we'll be seen as the most credible."

lemonde.fr/en.title: What is the EF-SON stun grenade France has suspended after it mutilated a high schooler?
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The weapon that tore off the hand of a 15-year-old high school student in Lens, France, on Monday, October 5, was a new-generation stun grenade that has been used by French law enforcement forces for only one year.
On Tuesday, the French national police's director general, Louis Laugier, ordered the "provisional suspension" of the use of the weapon at high schoolers' protests "until the circumstances of the young man's injury in Lens are established."
"I am suspending its use for the high school student protests until all the facts are known regarding what happened in this case," confirmed Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on RTL radio on Wednesday morning. He added that the French police oversight body, the IGPN, had opened 18 investigations into alleged misconduct by officers during the protest movement.
The grenade in question, the EF-SON, is manufactured by the French company Alsetex, a longtime commercial partner of the Interior Ministry. It has been available to French law enforcement since summer 2025, alongside another stun grenade model, the GL-304, made by the Brazilian company Condor. The EF-SON can be fired using a grenade launcher. With a diameter of 40 millimeters, it is not compatible with the Cougar launcher, which has been widely used by French police for a decade, but it can be used with the Cobra launcher, a dual-barrel launcher that French police also began using in 2025.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Israel, three years after October 7: A nation's traumas and blind spots
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On this land where the blood of the victims of October 7, 2023, was spilled, just a few kilometers from Gaza, where the blood of Palestinians is still being spilled, Mazal Tazazo, 36, carefully recounted the hours of anguish she experienced during the terrorist attack launched that day by Hamas. She had come to dance at the Nova festival, and in the early morning, the celebration turned into a massacre. In this natural setting, 378 people out of 3,500 participants were murdered, one by one, by Hamas fighters.
Forty-four others were taken hostage and brought to Gaza, dead or alive. The site also became the epicenter of the sexual violence committed that day by Hamas. Wounded in the head, Tazazo hid under eucalyptus leaves and branches for hours. She pretended to be dead among the bodies of her friends, then concealed herself at the back of an abandoned car before being evacuated with other survivors. "A miracle," she said with a smile that her eyes contradicted.
Paid by the Israeli Foreign Affairs Ministry, she comes to the site, which has become a memorial, three times a week to recount the circumstances of the attack to visitors. "People have to wake up!" she said on Monday, October 5, to a group of Indian influencers seated in a semicircle and surrounded by hundreds of photos of victims, their faces showing their stolen youth. "People in Europe, they don't understand that they give our enemies the legitimacy to hate Jews, to hate Israelis," she insisted a little later, in the shade of the eucalyptus trees, expressing both the absolute violence of the October 7 terrorist attack and her incomprehension at the loss of support from much of public opinion.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Emmanuel Roman, head of finance giant Pimco: 'Markets are sending France a serious signal. The situation is grave'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Emmanuel "Manny" Roman is the chief executive of Pimco, one of the world's largest asset managers, with $2.3 trillion in assets under management. The company specializes in bond markets and invests in debt, including that of France.
The Frenchman, who lives in California, where Pimco is headquartered, fears that interest rates will continue to rise. He is frustrated with the French political debate, rejecting the proposal by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the radical left's candidate in the 2027 presidential election, to cancel part of the national debt, while also doubting the budget-cutting promises of Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate for the Elysée.
French 10-year interest rates have approached 5%. Does France still have the confidence of financial markets?
I would like to put this in a global context. We are seeing rising rates worldwide, mainly due to inflationary pressures in the oil sector and demand from hyperscalers [AI companies], which borrow to fund data centers, chips, and so on. We see this increase everywhere – in the United States, in Japan. That said, in Europe, France is clearly more affected than Germany or even Italy, for budgetary and political reasons. Markets are sending it a serious signal. The situation is grave.

spiegel.de/international.title: Abuse in France: "Is Anyone Thinking of the Children?"
spiegel.de/international.text:
When Stéphane Grimbaud thinks back, it must have begun in December 2025. He was sitting with a picture book at his son's bedside, a book about a boy who gets to go to the school cafeteria for the first time. Grimbaud's son Arthur is four years old and loves food. "See," Grimbaud said, "the boy is just like you. He's looking forward to the cafeteria."
When Arthur really likes something, it is immediately obvious. "I love the cafeteria!" he shouted. Then he paused – before saying: "You know, Papa, I don't like the cafeteria anymore." He had probably been served something he hadn’t liked, Grimbaud thought, in his recollection. A year earlier, his son had started "école maternelle," a mix of preschool and kindergarten, which is mandatory in France for three-year-olds. Special mealtime requests of the kind parents could make in the "crèche," or daycare, were no longer accepted. The children are supposed to get used to rules.

Will he do it, Papa?" the boy asked his father. Children sometimes say cruel things, he told his son, but they usually don't mean them. "He's not a child," Arthur said. "It’s Olivier (name changed). welt.de.title: Trump bei Auftritt in umkämpften Texas von  Protesten gestört
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump hat bei einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung in Texas für den republikanischen Senatskandidaten Ken Paxton geworben. Dabei wurde Trump am Mittwochabend wiederholt von Demonstranten unterbrochen. Mindestens ein Dutzend Protestierende störten seine Rede, einige wurden von der Polizei abgeführt. Unter ihnen war auch ein Mann, der offenbar nahe an der Bühne stand. „Er geht jetzt zurück zu Mama“, sagte Trump. „Aber was er nicht weiß: Seine Mutter hat für Trump gestimmt.“ Trump bezeichnete Paxton, den er im Vorwahlkampf unterstützt hatte, als den „vielleicht besten Generalstaatsanwalt der Vereinigten Staaten“. Bei der Senatswahl im November kämpfen die Republikaner um die Mehrheit im Senat. Texas gilt traditionell als republikanische Hochburg, doch die Demokraten hoffen angesichts von Trumps schwachen Zustimmungswerten, steigenden Benzinpreisen und des Krieges mit dem Iran auf Erfolge. Trump bezeichnete die hohen Treibstoffpreise erneut als „kleinen Preis“ für den Krieg. Dabei ging er auch auf seine jüngsten Äußerungen über mögliche iranische Angriffe auf US-Städte ein. „Ihr wollt Probleme sehen? Dann lasst sie San Diego angreifen, lasst sie Los Angeles angreifen“, sagte Trump. „Wir werden das nicht zulassen. Wir schützen unsere Städte. Wir schützen unser Land.“ Der Auftritt war Trumps dritter Besuch in Texas innerhalb eines Monats. Die Republikaner haben dort bislang mehr als 300 Millionen US-Dollar in den Wahlkampf investiert. Trump kündigte zudem an, dem früheren Baseballstar Roger Clemens die Presidential Medal of Freedom, die höchste zivile Auszeichnung der USA, verleihen zu wollen.

welt.de.title: „Geburtstagsgeschenk für Putin“  – Rakete trifft Wohnhaus, 28 Tote
welt.de.text: Bei einem der schwersten russischen Luftangriffe auf die Ukraine sind am Mittwoch nach ukrainischen Angaben mindestens 28 Menschen getötet ​und 100 weitere verletzt worden. Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj sprach von einem der „niederträchtigsten Angriffe“. Die schwersten Verluste gab es in der Stadt ⁠Pryluky in der nördlichen Region Tschernihiw, wo eine russische Rakete ein fünfstöckiges Wohnhaus zerstörte. Regionalgouverneur Wjatscheslaw Tschaus zufolge starben dort 20 Menschen, darunter fünf Kinder. Insgesamt feuerte Russland nach Angaben Selenskyjs in der Nacht 70 Raketen und Dutzende Schahed-Angriffsdrohnen auf die Ukraine ab. Das russische Verteidigungsministerium teilte mit, seine Streitkräfte hätten einen „massiven Schlag“ gegen militärisch-industrielle Einrichtungen ausgeführt. Zu den Zielen hätten ⁠Anlagen des ukrainischen ​Rüstungsunternehmens Fire Point gehört, ‌das Marschflugkörper und Drohnen herstellt. Zudem seien die Hafen- und Werftinfrastruktur in der Schwarzmeer-Region Odessa sowie ein Schiff mit Militärgütern auf dem Weg dorthin ins Visier genommen worden. Die ukrainische Luftwaffe erklärte, sie habe gut 80 Prozent der angreifenden Drohnen abwehren können. Die größte Herausforderung blieben jedoch die russischen ballistischen Raketen, sagte Selenskyj. Er bekräftigte seine Forderung nach mehr Patriot-Luftabwehrsystemen. Diese sind die einzigen Waffen im ukrainischen Arsenal, die solche Raketen abfangen ‌können. Die weltweiten Bestände sind jedoch durch den Krieg im ⁠Iran und den Konflikt in der ​Ukraine erschöpft. Die EU reagierte mit neuen Sanktionen, die sich gezielt gegen den russischen militärisch-industriellen Komplex und die ⁠Hersteller ballistischer Raketen richten. Selenskyj wies darauf hin, dass die Angriffe mit dem Geburtstag des russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin zusammenfielen. „Das ist die Art von Geburtstagsgeschenk, das Putin sich selbst gemacht hat: ‌die Tötung von Kindern, ⁠die Tötung von Menschen“, ‌sagte er in ​seiner abendlichen Videoansprache. ⁠Selenskyj zufolge trafen ukrainische ​Truppen ihrerseits in den vergangenen 24 Stunden vier Ziele in Russland, darunter zwei Ölanlagen. ‌Die ​Ukraine erhielt am Mittwoch zudem eine neue Finanzhilfe der Europäischen Union ‌in ‌Höhe von 1,2 Milliarden Euro.

welt.de.title: „Hybride Bedrohung“ – Deutschland und Großbritannien stärken Cyberabwehr
welt.de.text: Deutschland und Großbritannien intensivieren ihre Zusammenarbeit bei der Bekämpfung von Cyberangriffen, Sabotage und anderen hybriden Bedrohungen. Das teilte die britische Regierung zum heutigen Besuch des britischen Premierministers Andy Burnham bei Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) mit. Die beiden Regierungschefs werden in Berlin unter anderem den deutsch-britischen Freundschaftsvertrag von 2025 in Kraft setzen. Beide Länder „verpflichten sich zu einer Partnerschaft zur Abwehr hybrider Bedrohungen, um gegen feindliche Aktivitäten vorzugehen, die Sicherheit und Wohlstand in unseren beiden Ländern bedrohen“, teilte die Downing Street mit. „Die hybride Bedrohung durch unsere Gegner – insbesondere Russland – erstreckt sich über Europa und darüber hinaus und bedroht unsere gemeinsame Sicherheit.“ Beide Nationen wollten durch Informationsaustausch und die Koordinierung bei Überwachung, Abschreckung und Unterbindung von Bedrohungen „feindliche Akteure“ schwächen, hieß es weiter. Burnham sagte: „Angriffe auf unsere Infrastruktur, unsere Unternehmen und unsere Demokratien sind keine ferne Bedrohung. Sie reichen bis in die Wohnungen und Arbeitsplätze der Menschen hinein und sind darauf ausgelegt, uns schwächer und gespaltener zu machen.“ Für den Freundschaftsvertrag, den sogenannten Kensington-Vertrag, werden heute bei einer Zeremonie die Ratifizierungsurkunden ausgetauscht. Mit der Vereinbarung stellen die beiden Länder ihre Beziehungen sechs Jahre nach dem Austritt Großbritanniens aus der Europäischen Union auf eine neue Grundlage. Das 27 Seiten starke Dokument wurde beim ersten Besuch von Merz als Kanzler in Großbritannien im Juli vergangenen Jahres unterzeichnet. Flankiert wird es von einem Aktionsplan mit 17 Punkten zu einer vertieften Zusammenarbeit in den Bereichen Wissenschaft, Technologie, Verteidigung, Sicherheit und Wachstum. Burnham hatte zuletzt als erster britischer Regierungschef seit dem Brexit konkret von der Möglichkeit zur Rückkehr in die EU gesprochen, der Weg dahin wäre aber auch bei einer Entscheidung für entsprechende Gespräche weit. Deutschland ist laut britischen Angaben der zweitgrößte Handelspartner des Vereinigten Königreichs und trägt rund 155 Milliarden Pfund (umgerechnet rund 183 Milliarden Euro) zur britischen Wirtschaft bei

welt.de.title: Antrag auf Hausarrest – Maduros Frau will aus dem Gefängnis
welt.de.text: Cilia Flores geht es nicht gut. Die gestürzte First Lady Venezuelas sitzt seit Monaten in einem Bundesgefängnis im New Yorker Stadtteil Brooklyn. Sie hat zwei Zähne verloren, rund elf Kilogramm abgenommen. Und auch ihre Herzerkrankung habe sich verschlimmert, sagen ihre Anwälte. Nun wollen die Verteidiger erreichen, dass die 69-Jährige das Gefängnis verlassen darf.  Flores wartet gemeinsam mit ihrem Ehemann, dem gestürzten Präsidenten Nicolás Maduro, auf ihren Prozess wegen schwerer Drogen- und Waffenvorwürfe. Ihre Anwälte beantragen, sie unter Hausarrest zu stellen. Dort soll sie sich einem von den Gefängnisärzten empfohlenen Eingriff unterziehen und anschließend erholen können. Die Staatsanwaltschaft bestreitet nicht, dass Flores gesundheitliche Probleme hat. Sie hält ihr allerdings entgegen, empfohlene diagnostische Untersuchungen abgelehnt zu haben, solange sie nicht aus der Haft entlassen werde. Flores habe damit „faktisch selbst eine medizinische Notlage geschaffen, auf die sie sich nun beruft, um ihre Freilassung zu erreichen“. Der 92-jährige US-Bundesrichter Alvin Hellerstein, der das Verfahren gegen Maduro und Flores leitet, hat für Donnerstag eine Anhörung angesetzt. Dann soll über Flores’ Antrag entschieden werden. Sollte sie das Gefängnis tatsächlich verlassen dürfen, hätten die Bundesbehörden nicht mehr unmittelbar die Kontrolle über jeden Aspekt ihres Alltags. Flores’ Ärzte empfehlen eine Herzkatheteruntersuchung. Mit der medizinischen Versorgung im Gefängnis sei Flores grundsätzlich zufrieden, sagte eine Person, die mit ihr gesprochen hat, WELT. Doch die 69-Jährige fürchte sich davor, den Eingriff vornehmen zu lassen – und anschließend aus der Narkose aufzuwachen, möglicherweise mit Handschellen an ein Bett gefesselt oder umgeben von Dutzenden anderen Gefangenen. „Sie hat große Angst davor, aufzuwachen und sich dann in einer Situation wiederzufinden, über die sie kaum Kontrolle hat – und dass dann etwas passiert“, sagte die Person. Flores’ Anwälte schlagen deshalb vor, sie in einem privaten Wohnhaus unterzubringen. Wo genau, geht aus den öffentlich zugänglichen Gerichtsunterlagen nicht hervor. Bewaffnete Sicherheitskräfte sollen sie dort rund um die Uhr überwachen. Organisiert würde die Bewachung von einem Unternehmen unter Leitung von Louis Milione. Er war früher Spezialagent für Anti-Narkoterrorismus-Einsätze und später die Nummer zwei der US-Drogenbehörde DEA. Die Staatsanwaltschaft hält von diesem Modell wenig. Flores versuche, „ihren Wohlstand zu nutzen, um eine Sonderbehandlung zu erhalten“, argumentieren die Ankläger. In anderen prominenten Strafverfahren hätten Richter vergleichbare Modelle abgelehnt – unter anderem bei Sean „Diddy“ Combs, Ghislaine Maxwell und Jeffrey Epstein. Vom Machtzentrum in den Gefängnisalltag Noch bis zum 3. Januar sah Flores’ Leben völlig anders aus. Als Ehefrau Maduros und frühere Vorsitzende des venezolanischen Parlaments gehörte sie zur Machtelite des Landes. Dann stürmten US-Spezialkräfte das schwer gesicherte Anwesen in Caracas, in dem sich Maduro und Flores aufhielten, und nahmen das Paar fest. Anschließend wurden beide nach New York gebracht, wo sie sich vor einem Bundesgericht verantworten müssen. Seitdem sitzen Maduro und Flores in einem Bundesgefängnis in Brooklyn, gelegen zwischen einem Pier und einem Friedhof in einem bislang kaum gentrifizierten Teil des Stadtbezirks. Flores war dort nach ihrer Ankunft zunächst sechs Wochen lang allein in einer Zelle untergebracht, berichtet die Person, die mit ihr gesprochen hat. Danach kam sie in den allgemeinen Frauenbereich. Dort leben nach Angaben eines Gefängnissprechers derzeit rund 35 Insassinnen. Ein Teil ähnelt einem Schlafsaal: Die Betten stehen in Reihen in einem großen Raum. Daneben gibt es einen Gemeinschaftsbereich, in dem sich die Frauen aufhalten können. „Für Gefängnisverhältnisse ist es nicht unangenehm“, sagt die Person, die mit Flores gesprochen hat. Männliche und weibliche Gefangene werden vollständig voneinander getrennt. Flores und Maduro können sich deshalb im Gefängnis nicht sehen. Hinzu komme, dass es unter den Insassen gelegentlich zu Auseinandersetzungen komme, die angesichts ihres Gesundheitszustands ein zusätzliches Risiko für Flores darstellten, argumentieren ihre Anwälte. Der Streit über ihre Gesundheit ist dabei nur einer von mehreren Nebenschauplätzen eines Strafverfahrens, das nun noch erheblich brisanter werden könnte. Wie mehrere US-Medien am Mittwoch berichteten, bereiten Bundesstaatsanwälte neue Anklagepunkte gegen Maduro und Flores wegen der mutmaßlichen Folter von US-Bürgern in venezolanischen Gefängnissen vor. Den Berichten zufolge geht es um mehr als ein Dutzend Amerikaner, die während Maduros Herrschaft von der venezolanischen Regierung festgehalten wurden. Auch weitere Personen könnten im Zusammenhang mit den mutmaßlichen Misshandlungen angeklagt werden. Die zusätzlichen Vorwürfe könnten bereits am Donnerstag offiziell bekannt gegeben werden. Maduros Anwalt Barry Pollack erklärte, bislang nicht über bevorstehende neue Anklagepunkte informiert worden zu sein. Damit könnte sich das ohnehin komplexe Verfahren gegen das frühere venezolanische Führungspaar noch einmal erheblich ausweiten. Ein Geschworenenprozess steht dennoch nicht unmittelbar bevor. Ein Termin ist bislang lediglich vorläufig für Juni 2027 angesetzt. Schon die Auseinandersetzung über die bisherigen Anklagepunkte dürfte sich noch lange hinziehen. Maduro und Flores werden unter anderem Verschwörung zum Drogenterrorismus und zum Import von Kokain vorgeworfen; hinzu kommen Waffenvorwürfe. Beide haben auf nicht schuldig plädiert. Ihre Anwälte haben inzwischen eine Reihe grundsätzlicher juristischer Angriffe auf das Verfahren gestartet. Im September beantragten die Verteidiger, die bisherigen Anklagen wegen der Immunität des Paares abzuweisen. Maduro sei weiterhin das rechtmäßige Staatsoberhaupt Venezuelas, argumentieren sie. Flores bekleide ihrerseits weiterhin offizielle Funktionen als First Lady und in der Führung des venezolanischen Parlaments. Maduro zieht Vergleich zu Donald Trump Maduros 60 Seiten umfassender Schriftsatz beruft sich unter anderem auf eine Entscheidung des Obersten Gerichtshofs der USA aus dem Jahr 2024. Darin hatte das Gericht Donald Trump weitreichende strafrechtliche Immunität für Amtshandlungen als Präsident zugesprochen. Die Verteidiger von Maduro und Flores argumentieren nun, auch die ihnen von der US-Staatsanwaltschaft vorgeworfenen Handlungen könnten als „Amtshandlungen“ im Rahmen ihrer staatlichen Funktionen gelten. Bemerkenswert ist dabei: Seit Maduros Festnahme hat Venezuela in einem US-Gerichtsverfahren für Delcy Rodríguez Immunität als Staatsoberhaupt geltend gemacht – nicht aber für Maduro. Und dann ist da noch eine grundsätzlichere Frage: Warum darf dieses Verfahren überhaupt in den Vereinigten Staaten geführt werden? Auch hier setzen Maduros Anwälte an. Einer der zentralen Anklagepunkte lautet auf Verschwörung zum Drogenterrorismus. Maduro soll demnach am Drogengeschäft mit von den USA als Terrororganisationen eingestuften Gruppen beteiligt gewesen sein, darunter die FARC und das Sinaloa-Kartell. Seine Verteidiger argumentieren jedoch, die ihm vorgeworfenen Handlungen lägen außerhalb der Reichweite der amerikanischen Strafjustiz und könnten deshalb nicht vor einem US-Gericht verfolgt werden. Mit einer Entscheidung Hellersteins über diese grundlegenden Anträge wird erst im kommenden Jahr gerechnet. welt.de.title: New Yorks Bürgermeister Mamdani wirft Israel „Genozid im Gazastreifen“ vor
welt.de.text: Anlässlich des dritten Jahrestags des Hamas-Überfalls auf Israel hat der linksgerichtete New Yorker Bürgermeister Zohran Mamdani der israelischen Regierung einen „Genozid im Gazastreifen“ vorgeworfen. Mamdani kritisierte am Mittwoch unter Verweis auf US-Waffenlieferungen an Israel zudem, dass „unsere Steuergelder diese Kriegsverbrechen finanzieren“. Der 34-Jährige ist seit Januar als erster Muslim Stadtoberhaupt in New York. Mamdani erklärte, der 7. Oktober sei „zutiefst schmerzhaft für so viele New Yorkerinnen und New Yorker“. Einerseits markiere er drei Jahre seit den „entsetzlichen Kriegsverbrechen der Hamas“ gegen Israel mit mehr als 1200 Toten und 251 Verschleppten. Zum anderen setze sich das Leid durch „den verheerenden, andauernden Völkermord“ Israels in Gaza fort, bei dem mehr als 74.000 Palästinenser getötet worden seien. „Drei Jahre später müssen wir es ablehnen, eine Welt zu akzeptieren, in der Besatzung und Apartheid fortbestehen, in der Kriegsverbrechen ungestraft bleiben und unsere Bundesregierung mit jeder Waffenlieferung ihre Mitschuld fortsetzt“, schloss Mamdani. Netanjahu wirft Mamdani Antisemitismus vor Der New Yorker Bürgermeister hatte den israelischen Regierungschef Benjamin Netanjahu in vorherigen Äußerungen einen „Kriegsverbrecher“ und „Architekten eines Genozids“ genannt. Netanjahu wirft Mamdani seinerseits Antisemitismus vor. Bei der UN-Generaldebatte Ende September sagte Netanjahu zudem, „zahlreiche Juden“ in New York fühlten sich unter dem muslimischen Bürgermeister nicht mehr in Sicherheit. Als Reaktion auf solche Vorwürfe kündigte Mamdani Ende September neue Maßnahmen gegen Antisemitismus an. New York hat die größte jüdische städtische Gemeinde außerhalb von Israel weltweit. Dort leben rund 960.000 Jüdinnen und Juden, das entspricht rund zwölf Prozent der Bevölkerung.

welt.de.title: Israelische Armee enthüllt – Hamas plante zweiten 7. Oktober im Westjordanland
welt.de.text: Die israelische Armee hat Pläne der Hamas aufgedeckt, das Massaker vom 7. Oktober zu wiederholen – diesmal in israelischen Siedlungen im Westjordanland. Zum dritten Jahrestag des Hamas-Überfalls haben israelische Militärkreise die Pläne gegenüber Journalisten dargelegt, darunter auch Reporter von „Bild“, das wie WELT zum Axel Springer Global Reporters Network gehört. Die Pläne fanden israelische Soldaten nach dem  7. Oktober (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/themen/israel-palaestina-konflikt/)  in Gaza. Darin beschreiben die Terroristen laut den israelischen Sicherheitskräften Schritt für Schritt, wie sie israelische Ortschaften im Westjordanland erobern und besetzen wollten. Es war dasselbe Muster wie im Süden Israels: gewaltsam eindringen, Orte überrennen, die Kontrolle übernehmen. Für die Armee ist klar: Die Hamas wollte den 7. Oktober im Westjordanland wiederholen. Dieses Mal mitten im Land, direkt vor den Toren israelischer Städte und Dörfer. Die entdeckten Terror-Pläne haben das Denken und die Taktik der israelischen Armee grundlegend verändert. Früher griff sie meist erst ein, wenn klar war, dass jemand einen Anschlag plante. Damit ist längst Schluss. Aus israelischen Militärkreisen heißt es: Man könne nicht mehr warten, bis man eine klare Absicht der Terroristen sehe. Die neue Regel lautet: Wenn eine Gruppe die Fähigkeiten und die Mittel für einen Angriff hat, schlägt die Armee zu – bevor etwas passiert. Den Fehler, im Vorfeld des 7. Oktober die Gefahr für einen Angriff unterschätzt zu haben, will die israelische Armee nicht wiederholen. Die Frage, ob  Geheimdienste Israels Premier Benjamin Netanjahu vor dem 7. Oktober gewarnt haben (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6a9ff77754ff84194d4caf08/enthuellungen-emirate-sollen-netanjahu-vor-grossangelegter-operation-der-hamas-am-7-oktober-gewarnt-haben.html) , ist inzwischen ein zentrales Thema im Wahlkampf in Israel. „Der 7. Oktober hat alles verändert, auf beiden Seiten“ Vor dem 7. Oktober 2023 waren es meist Einzeltäter, die mit Messern, Schusswaffen, Steinen oder Molotow-Cocktails angriffen. Die Armee reagierte nach einem festen Muster: Täter festnehmen, Familie überprüfen und, wenn ein Israeli getötet wurde, das Haus der Familie abreißen. Dann kam das Massaker, der schlimmste Terrorangriff in der Geschichte Israels. „Der 7. Oktober hat alles verändert, auf beiden Seiten“, heißt es aus hochrangigen israelischen Militärkreisen. Nach Einschätzung der Experten haben die Hamas und andere vom Iran unterstützte Gruppen begriffen, dass sie zu viel mehr in der Lage seien. Statt einzelner Täter setzten sie auf organisierte Terrorgruppen. Sie besorgten Geld, schmuggelten Waffen und suchten gezielt nach Schwachstellen in Israels Sicherheitsnetz. Die größte Angriffsfläche ist laut Militärkreisen die Grenze zu Jordanien. Wegen des Friedensvertrags galt sie jahrelang als ruhig. Heute ist sie die längste und aktivste Schmuggel-Route: Vom Iran gesteuerte Milizen bringen darüber große Mengen Waffen ins Westjordanland. Im Norden des Westjordanlands, in Dschenin, Tulkarem und Nablus, bauten Hamas und Iran laut Insidern sogenannte Katibas auf. Das sind Terror-Bataillone, die nach ihren Orten benannt sind, etwa die Katiba von Dschenin. Das Prinzip: Wer die richtige Ideologie mitbringt, bekommt Geld und Waffen. Im Dezember 2024 versuchte die Palästinensische Autonomiebehörde, die Kontrolle über Dschenin zurückzugewinnen. Laut den israelischen Militärkreisen scheiterte sie: Fünf ihrer Sicherheitskräfte starben, auf der anderen Seite nur ein einziger Terrorist. Im Januar 2025 rückte die israelische Armee selbst ein. Mit der Operation „Eiserne Mauer“ übernahm sie die Kontrollpunkte der Autonomiebehörde und blieb dauerhaft vor Ort. Das Motto lautet: „Aggressivität mit Präzision“. „Das ist ein Feind, der Krieg will, keinen Frieden“ Die Operation zielt auf drei Dinge: die Kämpfer, die an Anschlägen beteiligt sind, ihre Waffen und den Sprengstoff sowie die Rückzugsorte, vor allem in den Flüchtlingslagern. Dabei werden auch Drohnen eingesetzt. Offenbar mit Erfolg: Seit Januar 2025 ist der Terror aus dem Westjordanland nach Angaben israelischer Sicherheitskräfte um mehr als 80 Prozent zurückgegangen. In Dschenin seien die Märkte und Schulen wieder offen, und auch kriminelle Banden seien weniger aktiv. Vorbei ist die Gefahr nicht. Es gibt nach wie vor Einzeltäter, die Steine werfen oder schießen, wenn auch seltener. Doch was Israel weiterhin am meisten beunruhigt, ist die Ideologie der Terroristen. Gefangene hätten in Verhören erklärt, ihr langfristiges Ziel sei es, zu siegen und die Israelis „zu versklaven“. Aus den Militärkreisen heißt es: „Das ist ein Feind, der Krieg will, keinen Frieden.“ Das Axel Springer Global Reporters Network ist eine markenübergreifende Initiative, die Scoops, investigative Recherchen, Interviews, Meinungsstücke und Analysen globaler Relevanz veröffentlicht. Journalisten aller Axel-Springer-Marken – darunter „Politico“, „The Telegraph“, „Business Insider“, WELT, „Bild“, „Onet“ und „Fakt“ – kooperieren bei ausgewählten Geschichten für ein internationales Publikum. Die Berichterstattung erstreckt sich über alle Plattformen von Axel Springer: Online, Print, TV und Audio. Zusammen erreichen diese Veröffentlichungen Hunderte Millionen Menschen weltweit.

welt.de.title: „USA, geh weg“ – Wo Trumps Botschafter für Ärger sorgen
welt.de.text: Für viele Länder hat Donald Trump immer noch keinen Botschafter nominiert. Andere Posten wurden vor allem mit Spendern und Vertrauten besetzt – die in ihren Ländern vielfach für negative Schlagzeilen sorgen.

welt.de.title: „Klitschko glaubt, dass die Taktik von Putin ist, hier für Horror, für Schrecken zu sorgen“
welt.de.text:

welt.de.title: Viele Verletzte bei Attacke mit Machete an Schule in Polen – 19-Jähriger festgenommen
welt.de.text: Bei einer Messerattacke an einer Berufsschule in Polen sind am Mittwochvormittag acht Menschen verletzt worden, zwei davon sehr schwer. Der mutmaßliche Täter, ein 19-Jähriger, sei festgenommen worden, sagte eine Polizeisprecherin dem Sender Polsat News. Der Angriff passierte im Berufsschulzentrum Nr. 4 in der Stadt Ostrołęka in der Woiwodschaft Masowien, knapp 100 Kilometer nördlich von Warschau. Unter den Verletzten sind nach Angaben der Bezirksstaatsanwaltschaft vier Schüler und zwei Lehrer der Schule sowie zwei Unbeteiligte, die sich außerhalb der Schule aufhielten. Einer Lehrerin habe der Angreifer eine Schnittwunde am Arm zugefügt, berichtete eine Mitarbeiterin der Schule. Die Verletzten wurden mit Krankenwagen und Rettungshubschraubern in das Fachkrankenhaus Mazowieckie in Ostroleka gebracht, die am schwersten Verletzten später in ein Krankenhaus in Lomza verlegt. Nach Polizeiangaben handelte es sich um eine Machete. Die Attackierten hätten „Hilfe“ und „Ruft die Polizei“ geschrien. Einige Schüler hätten sich in den Klassenzimmern verbarrikadiert. Die Mutter einer Schülerin, die den Angriff miterlebte, sagte dem Sender TVN, der 19-Jährige sei in die Klasse ihrer Tochter gerannt. Schon da seien seine Hände stark verletzt gewesen.
